A complete decision model

Choose a familiar sequential system and specify its boundary, state,
observation, action, disturbance, objective, information pattern, and one hard
constraint. Every item must refer to the same decision maker and time scale.

Solution to 

Exercise 2

Many answers are possible. For a room thermostat, one consistent model is:
the boundary contains the room, walls, and heater; the state contains indoor
air and wall temperatures; the observation is a noisy air-temperature reading;
the action is heater power; outdoor temperature and occupancy are disturbances;
the objective trades temperature error against energy; the information at time
t is the observation and action history; and
0\leq u_t\leq P_{\max} is a hard constraint. A different answer is valid when
all eight objects use one boundary and one sampling period.

Action channels are physical

In 

Figure 1, explain why replacing every input by
an unconstrained generalized force changes all three decision problems.

Solution to 

Exercise 3

The replacement gives the swing a fictitious pivot actuator instead of
body-shape control and may bypass the chain’s inability to push. It replaces
bounded trolley acceleration in the crane with direct forcing of the load. It
also lets the wave device inject signed force instead of choosing nonnegative
power-take-off damping. Each substitution changes the feasible trajectories,
rather than only the symbols used to describe them.

Sampling changes the transition

For \dot x=-ax+bu with a zero-order-held input, derive the forward Euler
updates at step sizes \Delta t and \Delta t/2. Which discrete coefficients
change with the sampling period?

Solution to 

Exercise 4

At step size \Delta t,x_{k+1}=(1-a\Delta t)x_k+b\Delta t\,u_k.

At step size \Delta t/2,x_{k+1}=\left(1-\frac{a\Delta t}{2}\right)x_k
{}+\frac{b\Delta t}{2}u_k.

Both the state coefficient and the input coefficient change. Two half-steps
also compose a different finite-step approximation than one full Euler step,
although both converge to the same continuous flow as \Delta t\to0.

When shortening adds energy

Multiply -2m\rho\dot\rho\dot\psi by \dot\theta and use
\dot\psi\approx\dot\theta near the bottom of the swing. Why can shortening
the rider’s radius add energy in either direction of travel?

Solution to 

Exercise 5

The approximate power contributed to the suspension coordinate is\left(-2m\rho\dot\rho\dot\psi\right)\dot\theta
\approx-2m\rho\dot\rho\dot\theta^2.

Because m,\rho>0 and shortening gives \dot\rho<0, this term is positive.
The square removes the sign of \dot\theta, so the conclusion holds for
clockwise and counterclockwise passages.

A taut-slack hybrid model

Describe the swing’s taut and slack phases as a hybrid model. Identify the
continuous state, discrete mode, release guard, reattachment guard, and impact
reset; a complete equation of motion is not required.

Solution to 

Exercise 6

Use a continuous mechanical state containing positions, velocities, and rider
configuration, together with a mode
m\in\{\text{taut},\text{slack}\}. The taut mode enforces the chain-length
constraint and requires nonnegative tension. Release occurs when the tension
needed to maintain that constraint reaches zero and would become negative. The
slack mode follows unconstrained ballistic dynamics. Reattachment occurs when
the pivot-to-seat distance reaches the chain length with outward radial
velocity. The impact reset removes the inadmissible radial velocity and
dissipates its associated energy.

What rod-only data cannot identify

The structured controller completes a revolution on the rod model and fails on
the chain model. Why can a larger neural transition model fitted only to rod
trajectories fail to resolve this discrepancy?

Solution to 

Exercise 7

Rod trajectories contain no release, slack flight, reattachment, or impact.
Additional function capacity cannot identify a mode absent from the data.
Chain interventions or an explicit unilateral hybrid structure must first
supply that missing behavior; data can then estimate parameters within it.

A one-factor SwingRL audit

Extend the SwingRL comparison with the seated controller, or disable either
squat or lean in the standing controller. Before running it, predict one
diagnostic that should change. Then explain which modeling assumption the
intervention tests.

Solution to 

Exercise 8

A valid audit changes only one factor, records a prediction first, and compares
the result with the baseline. The seated controller changes rider morphology
and available actuation. Disabling squat removes the
-2m\rho\dot\rho\dot\theta^2 power channel; disabling lean removes the driven
angular terms. Peak unwrapped angle, revolution success, action-channel work,
and the timing of release or reattachment are suitable diagnostics. A result
supports only the changed modeling assumption, not a general ranking of
controllers.

The two previous chapters assumed that the Bellman operator could be
evaluated exactly at any state. Every target (\Bellman v_k)(s_i) contains
an expectation over the successor state,(\Bellman v)(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{r(s,a) + \gamma \int v(s')\,p(ds'|s,a)\right\},

and the fishery computed it with a 21-node quadrature rule, while the
eight-dimensional stopping problem already replaced it by an average over 32
random draws. This chapter asks what that replacement costs, and what it
makes possible. When the transition density is unavailable, because the model
is a simulator or a log of recorded transitions, sampling is the only way to
evaluate the operator, and the sample average is the estimator. Its error is
random rather than systematic, its rate does not depend on the dimension of
the state, and it adds to the per-iteration error that the


previous chapter bounded. Replacing
exact expectations by samples is what turns the approximate dynamic
programming of the previous chapters into what the operations research
community calls simulation-based dynamic programming and the machine learning
community calls reinforcement learning.

Two consequences of sampling organize the chapter. Acting on a value function
v requires the expectation for every action at every decision, so with
samples it requires simulation at decision time; storing the value of each
action instead, the action-value function q(s,a), moves that work into
training. And the maximum over noisy estimates is biased upward, even though
each estimate is unbiased, so the targets of every sampled Bellman update
overestimate, and the chapter ends with the ways to correct it.

Learning Goals

After completing this chapter, you should be able to:

Locate the two expectations in a fitted Bellman update, inside the operator and over the states, and bound the effect of estimating either one on the fixed point

Replace an expectation by a sample average, state the bias and variance of the result, and explain why its rate is independent of the dimension

Define the action-value function and its Bellman operator, and explain what it saves at decision time

Derive the upward bias of a maximum over noisy estimates, and explain how decoupling selection from evaluation removes part of it

Prerequisites: fitted value iteration and its error bound (

previous chapter), basic probability (expectation, variance, the central limit theorem, Jensen’s inequality).

hierarchy.lvl2: Two Expectations in Every Fitted Update
Two Expectations in Every Fitted Update

records.content:
Where do integrals appear in a fitted Bellman update, and what does
approximating them do to the fixed point?

They appear in two places. The first is inside the operator: the transition
expectation \int v(s')\,p(ds'|s,a) that every target contains. The second
is over the states: Galerkin and least-squares conditions integrate the
residual against test functions, and a regression averages the fitting error
over the states where targets were computed. Collocation has only the first
integral, which is one reason it was the simplest case.

Write \BellmanQuad for the Bellman operator with the transition
expectation replaced by a numerical rule, deterministic or random, and let
fitted value iteration run with it, v_{k+1} = \Proj\,\BellmanQuad v_k. The
error after one iteration splits into three pieces by the triangle
inequality. With v^\star = \Bellman v^\star,\begin{aligned}
\|v^\star - v_{k+1}\| &= \|v^\star - \Proj \BellmanQuad v_k\| \\
&\le \underbrace{\|v^\star - \Proj \Bellman v^\star\|}_{\text{best approximation}} + \underbrace{\|\Proj \Bellman v^\star - \Proj \Bellman v_k\|}_{\text{contraction of the current error}} + \underbrace{\|\Proj \Bellman v_k - \Proj \BellmanQuad v_k\|}_{\text{integration error}} .
\end{aligned}

The first term is the best the basis can do, the second shrinks with the
iterations when \Proj\Bellman is a contraction, and the third is the error
of the integration rule, which does not shrink as the iterations proceed. In
the language of 

Theorem 1, the integration error is one
more contribution to the per-iteration error \varepsilon, and it is
amplified by the same 1/(1-\gamma). This is why the accuracy of the
integration rule should match the accuracy of the basis. A degree-10
Chebyshev basis represents a smooth value function to about 

10-8, but
with a rectangle rule for the expectation the integration error, of order
h^2, dominates the sum, and the basis is wasted.

For low-dimensional problems with a smooth, explicit transition density,
deterministic quadrature is the right tool, and the rule is chosen to match
the basis: Gauss–Chebyshev nodes with Chebyshev polynomials, Gauss–Legendre
with Legendre, Gauss–Hermite with Hermite polynomials and Gaussian shocks,
midpoint or trapezoidal rules with piecewise-constant or piecewise-linear
elements. With orthogonal collocation the nodes of the basis double as the
nodes of the quadrature, and the expectations of the basis functions at the
successors of each node can be precomputed once into a matrix, so that each
iteration costs a matrix product and a maximization. The fishery used
Gauss–Hermite quadrature over its log-normal shock in this way. The same
pairing principle governed continuous-time trajectory optimization, where the
cost integral and the dynamics were discretized on the same nodes.

Deterministic quadrature needs three things: a state of low dimension, a
density that can be evaluated at the nodes, and a cheap model. The problems
this part of the book is heading for have none of them. The state of the
eight-dimensional stopping problem needs N^8 quadrature nodes for a product
rule with N nodes per axis. A simulator provides draws of s' and no
density. And a logged transition provides exactly one draw, which cannot be
chosen. Monte Carlo integration handles all three.

How do random samples trade the bias of a deterministic rule for variance,
and why does their rate not depend on the dimension?

Monte Carlo integration approximates an expectation by the average of
independent draws. For J = \mathbb{E}[f(X)] with X \sim p, draw
X^{(1)}, \ldots, X^{(N)} \sim p and form\hat{J}_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N f\big(X^{(n)}\big).

Two properties of this estimator carry the whole chapter. It is unbiased,
\mathbb{E}[\hat{J}_N] = J, by linearity of expectation. And its variance is
\sigma^2/N with \sigma^2 = \mathrm{Var}[f(X)], by independence of the
draws, so by the central limit theorem\sqrt{N}\,(\hat{J}_N - J) \Longrightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2),

and the error decays as N^{-1/2}. The rate is slow next to high-order
quadrature in one dimension, and it is the same in every dimension: Monte
Carlo pays in variance, never in an exponential number of nodes. It is also a
quadrature rule, with random nodes and equal weights 1/N. Importance
sampling changes the distribution of the nodes and compensates with unequal
weights, and the view of Monte Carlo as randomized quadrature covers it too.

The cell below checks both properties on a Gaussian with mean 2 and
standard deviation 3, with 4,000 repetitions for each sample size. Before
looking at the figure, predict what multiplying N by four does to the root
mean squared error.

import sys
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

code_directory = Path.cwd() / "code"
if str(code_directory) not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(code_directory))
from book_figure_theme import INK, MUTED, PALETTE, figure_style, show

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
true_mean, sigma, trials = 2.0, 3.0, 4000
sample_sizes = 2 ** np.arange(0, 11)
means, rmse = [], []
for n in sample_sizes:
    estimates = rng.normal(true_mean, sigma, size=(trials, n)).mean(axis=1)
    means.append(estimates.mean())
    rmse.append(np.sqrt(np.mean((estimates - true_mean) ** 2)))

with figure_style():
    fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.0, 2.4))
    ax.axhline(true_mean, color=MUTED, lw=.8, ls="--")
    ax.plot(sample_sizes, means, "o-", color=PALETTE["blue"], ms=3.5, lw=1)
    ax.text(1.2, true_mean + .045, "true mean", color=MUTED, fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_xscale("log", base=2)
    ax.set_xticks([1, 4, 16, 64, 256, 1024], ["1", "4", "16", "64", "256", "1024"])
    ax.set_ylim(true_mean - .15, true_mean + .15)
    ax.set_xlabel("draws $N$")
    ax.set_ylabel("average estimate")
    ax.set_title("(a) No bias at any $N$")

    bx.plot(sample_sizes, sigma / np.sqrt(sample_sizes), color=INK, lw=1)
    bx.plot(sample_sizes, rmse, "o", color=PALETTE["blue"], ms=3.5)
    bx.text(40, 1.0, r"$\sigma/\sqrt{N}$", color=INK, fontsize=9)
    bx.set_xscale("log", base=2)
    bx.set_yscale("log")
    bx.set_xticks([1, 4, 16, 64, 256, 1024], ["1", "4", "16", "64", "256", "1024"])
    bx.set_xlabel("draws $N$")
    bx.set_ylabel("root mean squared error")
    bx.set_title(r"(b) Error falls as $N^{-1/2}$")
    fig.tight_layout(w_pad=2)
show(fig)

Figure 1:The sample mean of N draws from a Gaussian with mean 2 and standard deviation 3, over 4,000 repetitions for each N. (a) The average estimate stays at the true mean whatever N: the estimator is unbiased. (b) Its root mean squared error (dots) follows \sigma/\sqrt{N} (line), a slope of -1/2 in log-log axes, so four times as many draws halve the error.

For a fixed value function v and a state-action pair (s,a), the
transition part of the Bellman operator is the expectation
\mathbb{E}[v(S') \mid S = s, A = a]. If next states
S'^{(1)}, \ldots, S'^{(N)} can be drawn from p(\cdot \mid s,a), by calling
a simulator or by acting in the real system, the sample average estimates it.
When the reward is random as well, the draws are pairs
(r^{(n)}, S'^{(n)}), and the one-step return is estimated by\widehat{G}_N(s,a) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N \Big[r^{(n)} + \gamma\, v\big(S'^{(n)}\big)\Big],

which is unbiased for \mathbb{E}[r + \gamma v(S') \mid s, a] as long as
v is fixed. Substituting it into the operator gives the Monte Carlo
Bellman operator(\widehat{\Bellman}_N v)(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \widehat{G}_N(s,a).

Nothing about approximation or projection has entered yet. For a fixed v,
Monte Carlo provides unbiased, noisy evaluations of (\Bellman v)(s) at any
state, from draws alone. The maximum over the noisy estimates, however, is
not unbiased, and the last section of the chapter is about that.

The second expectation, over the states, is estimated the same way. Galerkin
and least-squares conditions have the form
\int R(s;\theta)\, p_i(s)\, \xi(ds) = 0 for a distribution \xi over
states, and the weighted norm of the residual is \int R(s;\theta)^2\,\xi(ds).
The weight w of the previous chapters could be any positive function; for
sampling it must be a probability distribution that can be drawn from, which
is \xi after normalization, or any other distribution with importance
weights w/\xi. If states S^{(1)}, \ldots, S^{(M)} are drawn from \xi,
each condition becomes a sample average,\int R(s;\theta)\, p_i(s)\, \xi(ds) \approx \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^M R\big(S^{(m)};\theta\big)\, p_i\big(S^{(m)}\big),

and the least-squares objective becomes the empirical risk
\frac{1}{M}\sum_m R(S^{(m)};\theta)^2. This is the regression of the
previous chapter: targets at sampled states, and a fit that minimizes the
average error over them. In reinforcement learning \xi is rarely chosen; it
is the distribution of the states that the data happen to contain, which the
previous chapter showed to matter for convergence and the


next chapter shows to matter for coverage.

With both expectations sampled, the fitted update isv_{k+1} = \Proj_M\, \widehat{\Bellman}_N\, v_k,

a fit at M sampled states of targets that each average N sampled
successors. It needs no transition density and no state distribution in
closed form, only the ability to draw from them. In the typical
reinforcement-learning setting N = 1: each recorded transition
(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i) supplies one successor, and the target
r_i + \gamma v(s'_i) has the full variance of a single draw. The variance
is then reduced by the fit, which pools information across neighboring
states, and by the number of transitions rather than by averaging at a fixed
(s,a). The section after next returns to this choice.

Once the operator is evaluated from samples, what does acting on the result
cost, and how can that cost be moved into training?

The greedy policy of a value function v is\pi(s) = \arg\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \Big\{ r(s,a) + \gamma \int v(s')\,p(ds'|s,a) \Big\},

one transition expectation per action at every decision. With a model and a
quadrature rule this is a computation; with a simulator it is a Monte Carlo
estimate per action, repeated each time the state is visited; with a log it
is impossible, because no new successors can be drawn at decision time. The
expectation can instead be computed once, during training, and stored. The
action-value function of v,q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \int v(s')\,p(ds'|s,a),

caches the backup of every action, and the greedy policy becomes
\pi(s) = \arg\max_{a} q(s,a), a maximization over stored values with no
integral and no model. The optimal action-value function q^\star satisfies
its own Bellman equation, obtained by substituting v^\star(s') = \max_{a'}
q^\star(s',a'):q^\star(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \int p(ds'|s,a)\, \max_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_{s'}} q^\star(s',a').

The right-hand side defines the Bellman operator on action-value functions,
(\Bellman q)(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[\max_{a'} q(s',a') \mid s,a],
and it is a \gamma-contraction in the sup norm by the same argument as for
v: the maximum over a' does not increase sup-norm distances, and the
expectation does not either. Everything in the previous chapter transfers.
Fitted value iteration on q is fitted Q-iteration, its error bounds
hold with (s,a) in place of s, averagers remain safe, and the function
class now takes the action as an input or has one output per action. What
changes is the cost accounting: the expectations are evaluated during the
iterations, at the state-action pairs where targets are computed, and acting
afterwards is cheap.

Fitted Q-Iteration with a Model

Input Given an MDP (S, A, P, R, \gamma), base points \mathcal{B} \subset S, function approximator class q(s,a; \boldsymbol{\theta}), maximum iterations N, tolerance \varepsilon > 0, initial parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}_0

Output Parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} for Q-function approximation

Initialize \boldsymbol{\theta}_0 (e.g., random initialization)

n \leftarrow 0

repeat

\mathcal{D} \leftarrow \emptyset

For each (s,a) \in \mathcal{B} \times A:

y_{s,a} \leftarrow r(s,a) + \gamma \int p(ds'|s,a)\max_{a' \in A} q(s',a'; \boldsymbol{\theta}_n)

\mathcal{D} \leftarrow \mathcal{D} \cup \{((s,a), y_{s,a})\}

\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n+1} \leftarrow \texttt{fit}(\mathcal{D}, \boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{init}}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_0, K=\infty)

\delta \leftarrow \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}||A|}\sum_{(s,a) \in \mathcal{D} \times A} (q(s,a; \boldsymbol{\theta}_{n+1}) - q(s,a; \boldsymbol{\theta}_n))^2

n \leftarrow n + 1

until (\delta < \varepsilon or n \geq N)

return \boldsymbol{\theta}_n

The expectation in the target can be computed by quadrature when the model
allows it, or estimated by N draws of the successor from p(\cdot|s,a),
averaging \max_{a'} q(s'_i, a') over them. The fitting step is the one of
the previous chapter, with its initialization \boldsymbol\theta_{\text{init}}
and its optimization budget K written out because the


next chapter varies both.

Most reinforcement learning algorithms do not draw N successors per
state-action pair. They work with a data set of transition tuples
\mathcal{D} = \{(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)\}_{i=1}^M, each recording the one
successor that was observed when a_i was executed in s_i, and the target
of a tuple is y_i = r_i + \gamma \max_{a'} q(s'_i, a'), with N = 1.

This design has two origins. In some settings it is a constraint. A robot
that executes an action observes one outcome and cannot rewind to the same
state to sample another; the same holds for a clinical trial, a
manufacturing process, or any interaction that costs something. Many settings
in which reinforcement learning is applied have no such constraint. Game
emulators save and restore states, physics simulators reset to any
configuration, and software environments are cloned for free. The second
origin is historical. Reinforcement learning grew out of models of animal
learning, in which an organism experiences one consequence per action and
learns from a stream of experience, and temporal-difference learning,
Q-learning and the actor-critic methods were designed for that stream.

The convention persisted where the constraint did not, and it shaped the
algorithms. They store and manipulate tuples rather than state-action pairs
with several successors. They reduce variance through the function
approximator, which pools targets from nearby states, and through the number
of transitions, rather than by averaging at a fixed (s,a). And they treat
the two expectations asymmetrically: the outer one, over states, is sampled
with whatever budget is convenient, a whole data set, a replay buffer of a
million transitions, or one transition per step, while the inner one is
sampled once. In a domain with a cheap, resettable simulator and
high-variance targets, averaging several successors per (s,a) is a direct
variance reduction that current practice rarely uses.

What systematic error appears when the same noisy estimates are used both to
select an action and to value it?

Each estimate \widehat{G}_N(s,a) is unbiased, and the maximum over them is
not. Fix a state s and a value function v, and write the true continuation
value and its estimate as\mu(s,a) = \int v(s')\,p(ds' \mid s,a), \qquad \hat{\mu}_N(s,a) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N v(s'_i), \quad s'_i \sim p(\cdot|s,a),

so that (\widehat{\Bellman}_N v)(s) = \max_a \{r(s,a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}_N(s,a)\}.
Let a^\star be the action that maximizes the true backup. The maximum of a
collection is at least as large as any of its members, so\mathbb{E}\big[\max_a \{r(s,a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}_N(s,a)\}\big] \ge \mathbb{E}\big[r(s,a^\star) + \gamma \hat{\mu}_N(s,a^\star)\big] = r(s,a^\star) + \gamma \mu(s,a^\star) = (\Bellman v)(s).

The inequality is strict whenever more than one action has a nonzero
variance: the maximization picks whichever action received a positive noise,
and that inflated estimate becomes the target. This is Jensen’s inequality
for the maximum, \mathbb{E}[\max_a Y_a] \ge \max_a \mathbb{E}[Y_a], since
the maximum is convex. The same inequality is the reason that deterministic
policies are optimal in MDPs (

Theorem 2), where it
says that randomizing over actions cannot beat the best one; here it says
that maximizing over noisy estimates cannot be unbiased.

The bias does not average out with more draws of the same estimate, and it
compounds. Monte Carlo value iteration v_{k+1} = \widehat{\Bellman}_N v_k
builds its targets at iteration k+1 from a v_k that is already biased
upward, so \mathbb{E}[v_k] \ge \mathbb{E}[v_{k-1}] \ge \cdots \ge v^\star,
and the inflated values feed back into the next maximization. The cell below
holds every true action value at zero, draws five noisy samples per action,
and measures the bias of the maximum as the number of actions grows, next to
the estimator of the next subsection.

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
replications, samples_per_action = 6000, 5
action_counts = [2, 4, 8, 16, 32]
bias = {"maximum": [], "double": []}
se = {"maximum": [], "double": []}
for actions in action_counts:
    selection = rng.normal(size=(replications, actions, samples_per_action)).mean(axis=2)
    evaluation = rng.normal(size=(replications, actions, samples_per_action)).mean(axis=2)
    chosen = selection.argmax(axis=1)
    for name, values in (("maximum", selection.max(axis=1)),
                         ("double", evaluation[np.arange(replications), chosen])):
        bias[name].append(values.mean())
        se[name].append(values.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(replications))

with figure_style():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.6, 2.7))
    ax.axhline(0, color=MUTED, lw=.8)
    for name, color in (("maximum", PALETTE["vermilion"]), ("double", PALETTE["blue"])):
        ax.errorbar(action_counts, bias[name], yerr=2 * np.array(se[name]), fmt="o-", color=color,
                    ms=3.5, lw=1, capsize=0, elinewidth=1)
    ax.text(32, bias["maximum"][-1] - .06, "maximum of the\nestimates", color=PALETTE["vermilion"],
            fontsize=8.5, ha="right", va="top")
    ax.text(32, .06, "select with one estimate,\nevaluate with the other", color=PALETTE["blue"],
            fontsize=8.5, ha="right", va="bottom")
    ax.set_xscale("log", base=2)
    ax.set_xticks(action_counts, [str(a) for a in action_counts])
    ax.set_xlabel("number of actions")
    ax.set_ylabel("bias")
show(fig)

Figure 2:Bias of two estimators of \max_a \mu_a when every true action value \mu_a is zero and each is estimated from five standard Gaussian draws, over 6,000 repetitions. The maximum of the estimates (vermilion) is biased upward, and more so with more actions. Selecting the action with one set of draws and evaluating it with an independent set (blue) removes the bias in this case, where all actions are equally good. Two standard errors of each estimate are smaller than the dots.

The bias comes from using one noisy estimate for two jobs. Decompose the
estimate into its mean and its noise, \hat{\mu}_N(s,a) = \mu(s,a) + \varepsilon_a
with \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_a] = 0. The standard target isY = r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \mu(s,\hat a) + \gamma \varepsilon_{\hat a}, \qquad \hat a = \arg\max_a \{r(s,a) + \gamma \mu(s,a) + \gamma \varepsilon_a\},

and the same \varepsilon_{\hat a} that made \hat a win is added to its
value. Double Q-learning 

Van Hasselt et al. (2016) breaks this coupling with two
independent estimates of every action, \hat{\mu}^{(1)}_N(s,a) = \mu(s,a) +
\varepsilon^{(1)}_a and \hat{\mu}^{(2)}_N(s,a) = \mu(s,a) + \varepsilon^{(2)}_a,
with \varepsilon^{(1)} and \varepsilon^{(2)} independent. The first
selects and the second evaluates:\hat a = \arg\max_{a} \big\{r(s,a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}^{(1)}_N(s,a)\big\}, \qquad Y = r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \hat{\mu}^{(2)}_N(s,\hat a).

The selected action \hat a is random, a function of \varepsilon^{(1)}
alone. Conditioning on it,\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon^{(1)}}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon^{(2)}}\big[r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \mu(s,\hat a) + \gamma \varepsilon^{(2)}_{\hat a} \mid \hat a\big]\Big] = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon^{(1)}}\big[r(s,\hat a) + \gamma \mu(s,\hat a)\big],

because \varepsilon^{(2)} is independent of \hat a, so that
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\hat a} \mid \hat a] = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^{(2)}_{\hat a}] = 0.
The evaluation noise contributes nothing on average. What remains is the
selection bias: \hat a is more often an action whose \varepsilon^{(1)}
was positive than one whose true value is highest, so
\mathbb{E}[\mu(s,\hat a)] \le \max_a \mu(s,a), and the double estimator is
biased downward. In 

Figure 2 the maximum estimator grows
more optimistic as the number of actions grows, while the double estimator
has no bias: every action has the same true value there, so selecting the
wrong one costs nothing and the selection bias is zero. When the true values
differ, the double estimator is biased downward instead, by much less than
the maximum is biased upward. Removing the evaluation bias, the reuse of
the winning noise, removes most of the overestimation.

Two Q-functions instead of two sets of draws

The argument assumes two independent sets of draws from p(\cdot|s,a) for every state-action pair, which a log never provides and a simulator provides only by resetting. The practical implementation keeps two Q-functions instead, trained on different data or updated at different times, for instance an online network and a slowly updated copy of it. Their errors are then less correlated than the errors of a single network used twice, which gives part of the independence that the argument needs. This is Double DQN, in the 

next chapter (

Double DQN).

The algorithm below writes the principle out with Monte Carlo targets. Two
Q-functions alternate roles: at line 9 the first selects the action and at
line 12 the second evaluates it, and lines 10 and 13 do the same with the
roles exchanged. The mechanism is the same whether the Q-functions are tables
or fitted functions, and with single-sample data (N = 1) the two
Q-functions are trained on different subsets or at different frequencies to
approximate the independence.

Double Q Value Iteration with Monte Carlo

Input: MDP, state sample \mathcal{S}, Monte Carlo sample size N, maximum iterations K

Output: Two Q-functions q^{(1)}, q^{(2)}

Initialize q^{(1)}_0(s,a) and q^{(2)}_0(s,a) for all s,a

k \leftarrow 0

repeat

\quad for each s \in \mathcal{S} do

\quad\quad for each a \in \mathcal{A}(s) do

\quad\quad\quad Draw N next states: s'_1, \ldots, s'_N \sim p(\cdot \mid s,a)

\quad\quad\quad // Compute targets using decoupled selection-evaluation

\quad\quad\quad for i = 1, \ldots, N do

\quad\quad\quad\quad a^{(1)}_i \leftarrow \arg\max_{a'} q^{(1)}_k(s'_i, a')

\quad\quad\quad\quad a^{(2)}_i \leftarrow \arg\max_{a'} q^{(2)}_k(s'_i, a')

\quad\quad\quad end for

\quad\quad\quad q^{(1)}_{k+1}(s,a) \leftarrow r(s,a) + \frac{\gamma}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N q^{(2)}_k(s'_i, a^{(1)}_i)

\quad\quad\quad q^{(2)}_{k+1}(s,a) \leftarrow r(s,a) + \frac{\gamma}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N q^{(1)}_k(s'_i, a^{(2)}_i)

\quad\quad end for

\quad end for

\quad k \leftarrow k+1

until convergence or k \geq K

return q^{(1)}_k, q^{(2)}_k

Three other approaches keep a single estimate and correct the maximum
itself. They differ in how much they assume about the noise.

The correction can be learned. 

Keane & Wolpin (1994) treated the bias
\delta(s) = \mathbb{E}[(\widehat{\Bellman}_N v)(s)] - (\Bellman v)(s) \ge 0
as a quantity to estimate and subtract. It cannot be computed directly, but
it depends on observable features of the state: the number of actions, the
sample size, and the spread of the action values, since the bias is large
when several actions are close and small when one dominates. At a small set
of states, they ran both a high-fidelity evaluation of the backup, with many
draws, and the N-draw estimate used by the iteration, and regressed the gap
on those features; during value iteration the predicted bias is subtracted
from the raw maximum. The template, simulate on a subset and interpolate
everywhere, is common in econometric dynamic programming. It has seen little
use in reinforcement learning, because the high-fidelity evaluations are
expensive and a misspecified regression feeds its own error back into the
values.

The correction can be derived, under a distributional assumption.


Lee et al. (2013)

Lee & Powell (2019) assumed Gaussian noise of
standard deviation \sigma on the estimates of M actions, in which case
the expected maximum of the noises follows from extreme value theory,\mathbb{E}\Big[\max_{a} \varepsilon_a\Big] \approx \sigma \left(\frac{C_{\mathrm{E}}}{b_M} + b_M\right), \qquad b_M = \sqrt{2\log M - \log\log M - \log 4\pi},

with C_{\mathrm{E}} \approx 0.5772 the Euler–Mascheroni constant, and the
target is corrected by subtracting this amount with \sigma estimated from
repeated rewards at the same (s,a). The formula is exact for a
single-state problem whose only noise is in the rewards, and it is a
first-order correction otherwise; with heavier tails than Gaussian it
undercorrects. It replaces the regression of the learned correction by a
closed form, at the price of the Gaussian assumption.

The maximum can be replaced. 

D'Eramo et al. (2016) weight each
action by the probability that it is the best one under a Gaussian model of
the estimates,
w_a = \mathbb{P}\big(a \in \arg\max_{a'} \hat{\mu}_{a'}\big), and use
\sum_a w_a \hat{\mu}_a in place of \max_a \hat{\mu}_a. The weighted
estimator sits between the optimism of the maximum and the pessimism of the
double estimator, and adapts to the gaps between actions: when one action
dominates its weight is near one and the estimator is the maximum, and when
several are close their estimates are averaged. It needs a variance estimate
per action and one integral per action, which limits it to small action sets.
The smooth Bellman operator of the 

regularized chapter
also replaces the hard maximum by an average, with weights set by a
temperature rather than by estimated uncertainty. A last option changes
neither the target nor the operator but the loss of the fit, so that
overestimates are penalized more than underestimates; the


next chapter takes it up with Gumbel regression.

Fitted Bellman updates contain two expectations, inside the operator and over
the states, and either can be estimated from samples. The sample average is
unbiased, its error falls as N^{-1/2} whatever the dimension, and it adds a
per-iteration error that the bound of the previous chapter absorbs. Sampling
makes the model optional: a simulator or a log of transitions suffices, which
is the setting of reinforcement learning. Acting on a sampled value function
would require sampling at decision time, so the action-value function
q(s,a) stores the backup of each action instead, and fitted Q-iteration is
fitted value iteration on q. The maximum over noisy estimates is biased
upward, and the bias compounds through the iterations; using one estimate to
select the action and an independent one to value it removes the larger part
of the bias, and learned, analytic or weighted corrections are the
alternatives.

The algorithms of this chapter still choose the states at which targets are
computed, and still draw as many successors as they like. 

Fitted Q-iteration
and DQN take the data as given: a fixed log of
transitions with one successor each, or a buffer that fills as the agent
acts, and a fit that is warm-started and stopped early. The remaining design
choices of the practical algorithms are choices about that data and that
fit.

Sample-mean rate

If independent samples have standard deviation \sigma, what is the standard deviation of their sample mean based on N samples?

Solution to 

Exercise 1

\sigma/\sqrt{N}. Reducing it by a factor of two therefore requires four times as many samples.

Sign before simulation

Several actions have equal true values and independent noisy estimates. What sign do you expect for the bias of their maximum?

Solution to 

Exercise 2

Positive. Maximization preferentially selects estimates with favorable noise, so the expected maximum exceeds the common true value.

Double estimation

Which dependence is broken when one estimate selects the maximizing action and an independent estimate evaluates it, and which bias remains?

Solution to 

Exercise 3

The evaluation noise is made independent of the lucky noise that caused the selection, which removes the reuse of the same positive error for both jobs. The selection bias remains: the chosen action is still more often one whose first estimate was lucky, so the double estimator is biased slightly downward.

Receding-horizon control supplies feedback by repeatedly solving one nominal
finite-horizon problem. How must that problem and its surrounding controller
change when the task is to track a reference or to maximize economic output,
when the problem contains uncertainty or discrete modes, or when the solver
misses its deadline?

Once the basic idea of receding-horizon control is clear, it is helpful to see how the same backbone accommodates many variations. In every case, we transcribe the continuous-time optimal control problem into a nonlinear program with the structure of the 

receding-horizon subproblem:\begin{aligned}
    \text{minimize} \quad & c_N(\mathbf{x}_N) + \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \\
    \text{subject to} \quad & \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{f}_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \\
                            & \mathbf{g}_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \leq \mathbf{0} \\
                            & \mathbf{x}_{\min} \leq \mathbf{x}_k \leq \mathbf{x}_{\max} \\
                            & \mathbf{u}_{\min} \leq \mathbf{u}_k \leq \mathbf{u}_{\max} \\
    \text{given} \quad & \mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{x}_{\text{current}} \enspace .
\end{aligned}

The components in this NLP come from discretizing the continuous-time problem over a prediction horizon of N steps of length \Delta t, starting at the current time. The discrete transition \mathbf{f}_k is determined by the integration scheme, and each stage cost c_k includes the quadrature weight of its interval, as in the 

collocation transcriptions. With this blueprint in place, the rest is a matter of interpretation: how we define the cost, how we handle uncertainty, how we treat constraints, and what structure we exploit.

How should the finite-horizon objective penalize deviation from a time-varying
reference trajectory?

The most common setup is reference tracking. Here, we are given time-varying target trajectories (\mathbf{x}_k^{\mathrm{ref}}, \mathbf{u}_k^{\mathrm{ref}}), and the controller’s job is to keep the system close to these. The cost is typically quadratic:\begin{aligned}
    c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) &= \| \mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_k^{\mathrm{ref}} \|_{Q}^2 + \| \mathbf{u}_k - \mathbf{u}_k^{\mathrm{ref}} \|_{R}^2 \\
    c_N(\mathbf{x}_N) &= \| \mathbf{x}_N - \mathbf{x}_N^{\mathrm{ref}} \|_{P}^2 \enspace .
\end{aligned}

When dynamics are linear and constraints are polyhedral, this yields a convex quadratic program at each time step.

What changes when the target is a fixed equilibrium rather than a moving
reference?

In regulation tasks, we aim to bring the system back to an equilibrium point (\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{eq}}, \mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{eq}}), typically in the presence of disturbances. This is simply tracking MPC with constant references, so the stage cost no longer depends on k:\begin{aligned}
    c(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) &= \| \mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{eq}} \|_{Q}^2 + \| \mathbf{u}_k - \mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{eq}} \|_{R}^2 \\
    c_N(\mathbf{x}_N) &= \| \mathbf{x}_N - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{eq}} \|_{P}^2 \enspace .
\end{aligned}

To guarantee stability, it is common to include a terminal constraint \mathbf{x}_N \in \mathcal{X}_f, where \mathcal{X}_f is a control-invariant set under a known feedback law.

Can the controller optimize production or revenue directly when the best
operation need not remain near a prescribed setpoint?

Tracking and regulatory MPC penalize deviation from a prescribed reference. An economic controller instead optimizes the quantity produced by operating the system. The optimal state may vary continuously because there is no fixed reference trajectory.

A hinged flap extracts energy from oscillating water through a power-take-off (PTO) device. A single rotational mode gives the modelI\ddot q+b\dot q+kq=\tau_{\mathrm{wave}}(t)-\rho(t)\dot q,

where q is flap angle and \rho is the commanded PTO damping. The PTO torque and captured power are\tau_{\mathrm{PTO}}=-\rho\dot q,
\qquad
P_{\mathrm{capture}}=-\tau_{\mathrm{PTO}}\dot q=\rho\dot q^2.

Restricting \rho\geq0 keeps the PTO passive because \tau_{\mathrm{PTO}}\dot q=-\rho\dot q^2\leq0. The actuator can remove mechanical energy from the flap, but it cannot inject energy into it.

A frozen-state calculation suggests using as much damping as possible. At \dot q=0.4 rad/s, damping values of 900 and 1900 N m s/rad yield instantaneous capture rates of 144 and 304 W. The calculation holds velocity fixed. In the dynamical system, stronger damping reduces future velocity, so captured energy need not increase monotonically with \rho. The constant-damping sweep below measures that delayed effect.

The experiment uses a deterministic sum of three wave-torque components for 45 s. The controller updates every h=0.12 s and predicts N=18 steps, or 2.16 s, into the future. Its finite-horizon problem is\begin{aligned}
\max_{\rho_{0:N-1}}\quad &
h\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\rho_j\omega_j^2
-\lambda\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}
\left(\frac{\rho_j-\rho_{j-1}}{\rho_{\max}}\right)^2 \\
\text{subject to}\quad &
\mathbf{x}_{j+1}=F_h(\mathbf{x}_j,\rho_j,\tau_{\mathrm{wave}}), \\
&0\leq\rho_j\leq2400\ \mathrm{N\,m\,s/rad},\\
&|q_j|\leq0.55\ \mathrm{rad},\\
&|\rho_j\omega_j|\leq2800\ \mathrm{N\,m},\\
&|\rho_j-\rho_{j-1}|/h\leq5000\ \mathrm{N\,m\,s^{-2}/rad}.
\end{aligned}

Here F_h is one Runge-Kutta step of the flap model and \rho_{-1} is the damping applied during the previous control interval. Only \rho_0 is applied. The flap state is measured again, the horizon advances, and the nonlinear program is solved from the shifted previous solution.

Two passive controllers provide matched baselines. Constant damping requests \rho=900 N m s/rad. A phase-aware heuristic raises damping when the measured product \tau_{\mathrm{wave}}\dot q is positive and lowers it otherwise. All three requests pass through the same damping, torque, and damping-rate projection before reaching the plant. The stroke constraint differs because it depends on predicted state evolution rather than on the current actuator command.

Before inspecting the trajectories, predict whether constant damping should maximize total captured energy. Also predict which controller should use the most actuator variation. The economic objective can favor operation close to the state and torque limits.

def solve_economic_mpc(
    time: float,
    state: np.ndarray,
    previous_damping: float,
    params: WaveParameters | None = None,
    *,
    warm_start: np.ndarray | None = None,
    max_iterations: int = 45,
) -> MPCStep:
    """Maximize predicted harvested energy under plant and actuator constraints."""

    params = params or WaveParameters()
    params.validate()
    state = np.asarray(state, dtype=float)
    if state.shape != (2,) or not np.all(np.isfinite(state)):
        raise ValueError("state must have shape (2,) and contain finite values")
    horizon = params.horizon_steps
    if warm_start is None:
        initial = np.full(horizon, previous_damping, dtype=float)
    else:
        warm_start = np.asarray(warm_start, dtype=float)
        if warm_start.shape != (horizon,):
            raise ValueError("warm_start has the wrong horizon")
        initial = warm_start.copy()

    initial[0] = project_damping(initial[0], state[1], previous_damping, params)
    for k in range(1, horizon):
        change_limit = params.damping_rate_limit * params.control_period
        initial[k] = np.clip(
            initial[k],
            max(0.0, initial[k - 1] - change_limit),
            min(params.damping_max, initial[k - 1] + change_limit),
        )

    def objective(normalized: np.ndarray) -> float:
        sequence = params.damping_max * normalized
        prediction = predict_trajectory(time, state, sequence, params)
        velocity = prediction[:-1, 1]
        energy = params.control_period * np.sum(sequence * velocity**2)
        changes = np.diff(np.concatenate([[previous_damping], sequence]))
        slew = np.sum((changes / params.damping_max) ** 2)
        return float(-energy / 1_000.0 + params.slew_weight * slew)

    def constraints(normalized: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        sequence = params.damping_max * normalized
        prediction = predict_trajectory(time, state, sequence, params)
        return _constraint_margins(sequence, prediction, previous_damping, params)

    started = perf_counter()
    result = minimize(
        objective,
        initial / params.damping_max,
        method="SLSQP",
        bounds=[(0.0, 1.0)] * horizon,
        constraints={"type": "ineq", "fun": constraints},
        options={"maxiter": max_iterations, "ftol": 2e-6, "disp": False},
    )
    elapsed = perf_counter() - started
    sequence = np.asarray(
        params.damping_max * result.x if np.all(np.isfinite(result.x)) else initial
    )
    prediction = predict_trajectory(time, state, sequence, params)
    margins = _constraint_margins(sequence, prediction, previous_damping, params)
    maximum_violation = float(max(0.0, -np.min(margins)))
    success = bool(result.success and maximum_violation <= 2e-4)
    if not success:
        sequence = initial
        prediction = predict_trajectory(time, state, sequence, params)
        margins = _constraint_margins(sequence, prediction, previous_damping, params)
        maximum_violation = float(max(0.0, -np.min(margins)))

    first = project_damping(sequence[0], state[1], previous_damping, params)
    sequence = sequence.copy()
    sequence[0] = first
    return MPCStep(
        damping=first,
        sequence=sequence,
        predicted_state=prediction,
        objective=float(objective(sequence / params.damping_max)),
        success=success,
        max_predicted_violation=maximum_violation,
        solve_time_s=elapsed,
    )

This model assumes an accurate short-term wave forecast and one rigid flap mode. Real devices include radiation-memory effects, additional structural modes, losses, measurement error, and forecast uncertainty. Those omissions affect both predicted capture and constraint margins. Robust or stochastic MPC can represent some of this uncertainty, while data can be used to estimate the unmodeled residual dynamics.

How can feasibility and performance be protected against every disturbance in
a bounded uncertainty set?

Some systems are exposed to external disturbances or small errors in the model. In those cases, we want the controller to make decisions that will still work no matter what happens, as long as the disturbances stay within some known bounds. This is the idea behind robust MPC.

Instead of planning a single trajectory, the controller plans a “nominal” path (what would happen in the absence of any disturbance) and then adds a feedback correction to react to whatever disturbances actually occur. This looks like:\mathbf{u}_k = \bar{\mathbf{u}}_k + K (\mathbf{x}_k - \bar{\mathbf{x}}_k) \enspace ,

where \bar{\mathbf{u}}_k is the planned input and K is a feedback gain that pulls the system back toward the nominal path if it deviates.

Because we know the worst-case size of the disturbance, we can estimate how far the real state might drift from the plan, and “shrink” the constraints accordingly. The result is that the nominal plan is kept safely away from constraint boundaries, so even if the system gets pushed around, it stays inside limits. This is often called tube MPC because the true trajectory stays inside a tube around the nominal one.

The main benefit is that we can handle uncertainty without solving a complicated worst-case optimization at every time step. All the uncertainty is accounted for in the design of the feedback K and the tightened constraints.

What becomes possible when uncertainty is represented by probabilities rather
than only worst-case bounds?

If disturbances are random rather than adversarial, a natural goal is to optimize expected cost while enforcing constraints probabilistically. This gives rise to stochastic MPC, in which:

The cost becomes an expectation:\mathbb{E} \left[ c_N(\mathbf{x}_N) + \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \right]

Constraints are allowed to be violated with small probability:\mathbb{P}[\mathbf{g}_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \leq \mathbf{0}] \geq 1 - \varepsilon

In practice, expectations are approximated using a finite set of disturbance scenarios drawn ahead of time. For each scenario, the system dynamics are simulated forward using the same control inputs \mathbf{u}_k, which are shared across all scenarios to respect non-anticipativity. The result is a single deterministic optimization problem with multiple parallel copies of the dynamics, one per sampled future. This retains the standard MPC structure, with only moderate growth in problem size.

Despite appearances, this is not dynamic programming. There is no value function or tree of all possible paths. There is only a finite set of futures chosen a priori, and optimized over directly. This scenario-based approach is common in energy systems such as hydro scheduling, where inflows are uncertain but sample trajectories can be generated from forecasts.

Risk constraints are typically enforced across all scenarios or encoded using risk measures like CVaR. For example, one might penalize violations that occur in the worst (1 - \alpha)\% of samples, while still optimizing expected performance overall.

How can mode switches, on-off devices, and logical decisions enter the same
finite-horizon optimization?

When systems involve discrete switches (e.g., on/off valves, mode selection, or combinatorial logic), the MPC problem must include integer or binary variables. These show up in constraints like\boldsymbol{\delta}_k \in \{0,1\}^{n_\delta}, \qquad \mathbf{u}_k \in \mathcal{U}(\boldsymbol{\delta}_k)

where n_\delta counts the binary decisions at each step, along with mode-dependent dynamics and costs. The resulting formulation is a mixed-integer nonlinear program (MINLP). The receding-horizon idea is the same, but each solve is more expensive due to the combinatorial nature of the decision space.

When one optimization is too large or ownership is distributed, which
information must local controllers exchange to coordinate their plans?

Large-scale systems often consist of interacting subsystems. Distributed MPC decomposes the global NLP into smaller ones that run in parallel, with coordination constraints enforcing consistency across shared variables:\sum_{i} H^i \mathbf{z}^i_k = \mathbf{0} \qquad \text{(coupling constraint)}

Each subsystem solves a local problem over its own state and input variables, then exchanges information with neighbors. Coordination can be done via primal–dual methods, ADMM, or consensus schemes, but each local block looks like a standard MPC problem.

How can the prediction model improve from data without discarding the explicit
constraints enforced by MPC?

In practice, we may not know the true model \mathbf{f}_k or cost function c_k precisely. In adaptive MPC, these are updated online from data:\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{f}_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k; \boldsymbol{\theta}_t), \qquad
c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) = c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k; \boldsymbol{\psi}_t)

The parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}_t and \boldsymbol{\psi}_t are learned in real time, and the subproblem solved at time t uses their current estimates. When combined with policy distillation, value approximation, or trajectory imitation, this leads to overlaps with reinforcement learning where the MPC solutions act as supervision for a reactive policy.

What should the closed-loop system do when the preferred MPC problem is
infeasible, inaccurate, or unfinished at the control deadline?

The wave-energy example assumes that every optimization finishes before the next control update and that its prediction model remains accurate over the horizon. An operational MPC controller must also handle incompatible constraints, modeling errors, and missed computation deadlines.

A disturbance can move the measured state to a point from which the requested target is unreachable within the horizon. Model mismatch can make a trajectory feasible in prediction and infeasible on the plant. A solver can also stop because of an ill-conditioned local model or a changing active set. These cases require an explicit hierarchy of hard constraints, soft objectives, and fallback actions. The following mechanisms modify the finite-horizon problem or its deployment without changing the receding-horizon principle.

Which constraints may be violated at a quantified price so that the optimizer
can still return a usable action?

The first approach to handling infeasibility recognizes that not all constraints carry equal importance. A chemical reactor’s temperature must never exceed the runaway threshold: this is a hard constraint that cannot be violated. However, maintaining temperature within an optimal efficiency band is merely desirable. This can be treated as a soft constraint that we prefer to satisfy but can relax when necessary.

This hierarchy motivates reformulating the optimization problem using slack variables:\begin{aligned}
\min_{\mathbf{u}, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}} \quad & \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} \left( \|\mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_k^{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{Q}^2 + \|\mathbf{u}_k\|_{R}^2 + \mathbf{w}^\top \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_k \right) \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{f}_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \\
& \mathbf{g}_{\text{hard}}(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \leq \mathbf{0} \\
& \mathbf{g}_{\text{soft}}(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \leq \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_k \\
& \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_k \geq \mathbf{0}
\end{aligned}

The penalty weights \mathbf{w} encode our priorities. Safety constraints might use w_j = 10^6, while comfort constraints use w_j = 1. This reformulated problem is always feasible as long as the hard constraints alone admit a solution. That is: we can always make the slack variables \boldsymbol{\epsilon} sufficiently large to satisfy the soft constraints.

Rather than treating constraints as binary hard/soft categories, we can establish a constraint hierarchy that enables graceful degradation:\begin{aligned}
\text{Safety:} \quad & T_{\text{reactor}} \leq T_{\text{runaway}} - 10 \quad & w = \infty \text{ (hard)} \\
\text{Equipment:} \quad & 0 \leq u_{\text{valve}} \leq 100 \quad & w = 10^4 \\
\text{Efficiency:} \quad & T_{\text{optimal}} - 5 \leq T \leq T_{\text{optimal}} + 5 \quad & w = 10^2 \\
\text{Comfort:} \quad & |T - T_{\text{setpoint}}| \leq 1 \quad & w = 1
\end{aligned}

As conditions deteriorate, the controller abandons objectives in reverse priority order, maintaining safety even when optimality becomes impossible.

How do deadlines, thermal limits, forecast error, and solver time interact in a
receding-horizon controller for a real computing workload?

The offline frequency schedule in 

Trajectory Optimization
cannot react when a burst arrives earlier than forecast. Receding-horizon
control uses the same aggregate model but replaces the initial forecast after
each second. Measured NVIDIA L4 service-rate and phase-power curves calibrate
the model, while the request and queue trajectories remain simulation outputs.
The scheduling rule remains fixed at the reduced 512-token interleaved
chunked-prefill model from the modeling chapter, so the comparison isolates
feedback through the GPU clock.

At control time t, the statex_t=(p_t,d_t,T_t,f_{t-1})

contains queued prefill work, unfinished decode work, temperature, and the last
applied clock. The controller forecasts ten one-second transitions. Arrivals
are predicted from the trailing 30-second rate, while expected output work uses
the empirical output-length distribution from the trace. The request-level
plant receives the realized requests and output lengths instead.

The finite-horizon problem uses the normalized objectiveJ_t=\sum_{k=0}^{9}\left[
\frac{E_k}{E_{\max}}
+20\delta_{k,\mathrm{TTFT}}^2
+10\delta_{k,\mathrm{TPOT}}^2
+0.05\Delta f_k^2
+1000(s_{P,k}^2+s_{T,k}^2)
\right]+20B_{10}^2,

where, as in the receding-horizon subproblem, k counts seconds after the
control time t. The variables \delta_{k,\mathrm{TTFT}} and
\delta_{k,\mathrm{TPOT}} are normalized overruns of two aggregate delay
estimates. The first divides predicted queued prefill tokens by the profiled
prefill rate. The second divides the predicted number of active decode requests
by the profiled decode rate. These estimates enter the optimization but do not
equal realized request-level TTFT and TPOT; the detailed simulation computes
the latter. The frequency difference \Delta f_k is normalized by the profiled
clock range.
The slacks s_{P,k} and s_{T,k} penalize violations of the experimental
power and thermal limits, and B_{10} penalizes unfinished work at the end of
the horizon. SLSQP receives at most 50 iterations and a tolerance of 

10-6.
Only the first frequency is applied. The continuous result is rounded downward
to the nearest profiled requested clock before the next state is observed. The
replay reports the corresponding measured median realized clock separately,
since the requested and realized values can differ under the experimental power
cap.

A solver result is rejected if it is infeasible, non-finite, or arrives after
the 0.8-second control budget. The fallback is a hysteretic reactive governor:
it raises the clock by one profile level when weighted queue pressure reaches
eight or the oldest prompt has waited one second, and lowers it by one level
when temperature reaches 72 degrees C or pressure falls to one. Every fallback
appears in the recorded trajectory rather than being removed from the
aggregate metrics.

The comparison asks whether replanning improves the response to the shifted
burst without hiding its energy cost. Four controllers receive identical
requests and initial conditions:

maximum clock throughout the experiment;

the reactive governor used as the MPC fallback;

the open-loop schedule optimized for the nominal trace;

receding-horizon MPC.

The live experiment asks which clock policy uses the least measured GPU energy
while meeting common request-level latency limits. We use development measurements
to select a fixed clock and to set the limits on the 95th percentile of time to first
token and of per-request mean inter-token latency. The planned confirmation compares this
fixed clock, maximum clock, the governor, and MPC including its fallback. A
constant clock or governor can be the preferred policy if it meets both limits
with lower measured energy.

Development and confirmation each use 32 requests from disjoint portions of
the recorded trace, under steady and bursty arrival schedules. Each arrival
window spans at least 240 seconds. The GPU has a 40 W board power cap and a
6,251 MHz requested memory clock. Service rates and idle power require fresh
measurements at this cap; the original 64.8 W calibration remains archived.
The live state distinguishes requests awaiting their first output from requests
already streaming. A transition model fitted on mixed-serving data must pass
whole-run validation before it can support MPC. These measurements test queue
drainage under the workload the controller will actually encounter.

For confirmation, we plan five paired repetitions per schedule across three
independent acquisitions, with counterbalanced method order. Each pair uses
identical requests and arrival times. Energy includes the final request drain;
an efficiency claim requires all five valid pairs and both methods to meet both
frozen latency limits. Invalid trials and fallback decisions remain in the
record. Development qualification and a frozen comparison protocol are still
needed before confirmation can begin.

In two earlier development acquisitions, the GPU completed the full steady workload at
210 MHz, using 8.55 and 8.30 kJ, but could not return to its startup temperature
references before the cooling timeout. A subsequent qualification warms the GPU
with the full steady workload before selecting its reference from a stable
300-second cooling window. Its final 60-second mean fixes the reference for the
remaining trials; this stability criterion does not establish thermal equilibrium.

That warm-reference acquisition qualified both requested settings, 210 and
660 MHz, on the two designated arrival patterns. All 32 requests completed
validly in each of the four trials. The separate warm-up does not count toward
qualification. Energy was 7.65 and 8.29 kJ for the 210 MHz bursty and steady
trials, and 7.09 and 8.43 kJ for the corresponding 660 MHz trials. Clock labels
name requested settings: the 660 MHz request produced lower measured clocks
during active inference, with medians of 360 MHz for bursty and 300 MHz for
steady arrivals. These operating-point checks establish neither a common latency
target nor an energy winner. Controller development and a frozen comparison
protocol are still required before confirmation.

The controller in the recorded replay constrains a junction temperature
predicted by a one-state thermal model. None of the simulated controllers violates that
constraint, but this establishes feasibility only for the model used inside
the optimizer.

A power-matched pair of workloads exposes the modeling problem. During the
held-out experiment, a 55 W decode pulse and a 55 W prefill pulse consumed
nearly the same electrical energy, with a difference of 0.2 percent. The
measured peak temperature rise during prefill was nevertheless 2.00 degrees C
larger than during decode. A one-state model driven only by board power receives
nearly the same input for both pulses and has no variable with which to represent
this difference.

The clock sweep used to calibrate the serving model was designed to measure
service rate and power. Its one-state thermal fit had R^2=0.0020, so a
separate experiment tested whether workload phase was needed in the thermal
input. Both candidate models used\dot T(t)
=
-\frac{T(t)-T_{\mathrm{amb}}}{\tau}
+\frac{R}{\tau}P_{\mathrm{eff}}(t).

Here T_{\mathrm{amb}} is an effective ambient temperature, \tau is the
thermal time constant, and R is the steady-state thermal resistance. The two
input models differ by one term:P_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)
=
\begin{cases}
P(t), & \text{power-only model},\\
P(t)\bigl(1+\beta I_{\mathrm{prefill}}(t)\bigr),
& \text{phase-gain model}.
\end{cases}

The indicator I_{\mathrm{prefill}} equals one during prefill and zero during
decode. The phase-gain model can therefore assign different effective thermal
inputs to two workloads with the same measured board power. Its state
dimension and measured input remain unchanged.

The order of the four training pulses was counterbalanced. Every pulse began
from a verified post-relock temperature within a one-degree-Celsius band. The
acquisition retained a 77 degree C safe-down threshold and a 79 degree C abort

Figure 6:The power-only model predicts similar responses for the power-matched pulses.
The phase-gain model separates them and lowers held-out RMSE, but its largest
trajectory and phase-contrast errors remain above the fixed one-degree-Celsius
acceptance boundary. The validation data were not used to fit either model.

On the held-out pair, the power-only model has an RMSE of 1.43 degrees C. Adding the workload-phase gain reduces this error to 0.87 degrees C. The fixed rule, however, requires all three validation errors to remain below 1 degree C. The phase-gain model reaches a worst trajectory error of 2.73 degrees C and a phase-contrast error of 1.43 degrees C, so the model is rejected.

The measured prefill peak rise exceeds the decode rise by 2.00 degrees C; the phase-gain model predicts a difference of 3.43 degrees C. Prefill draws 0.132 W less mean board power and consumes 6.66 J less energy than decode, with an energy ratio of 0.99797. Higher measured electrical input therefore cannot explain the larger prefill temperature rise in this pair.

These measurements come from one NVIDIA L4 serving Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with vLLM 0.28.0. They do not establish a hardware-safety model or justify a mixed-serving thermal constraint.

The fitted gain gives prefill 1.147 times the effective thermal input of decode.
This parameter is reproducible across the ten optimization starts. The training
Jacobian also has full numerical rank, with condition number 384. These checks
reduce concern about an ambiguous parameter fit, but they do not establish that
one thermal state is sufficient. The validation residuals miss the rapid
initial temperature rise and later reverse sign. Inherited thermal state,
sensor timing and filtering, and phase-dependent heating remain possible
explanations; these pulse measurements do not isolate their contributions.

    def _solve(self, observation: ServingObservation, arrival_rate: float) -> tuple[np.ndarray, bool, float]:
        profile = self.plant.profile
        minimum = profile.minimum_clock_mhz
        maximum = profile.maximum_clock_mhz
        initial_prefill_tokens = observation.prefill_remaining_tokens
        initial_decode_tokens = estimate_decode_remaining_tokens(
            observation.decode_active,
            observation.generated_decode_tokens,
            self.mean_output_tokens,
        )
        prompt_arrivals = np.full(
            self.horizon_steps,
            arrival_rate * self.mean_prompt_tokens * self.control_period_s,
        )
        initial = np.full(self.horizon_steps, self.current_clock)
        maximum_power = max(profile.prefill_power_w[-1], profile.decode_power_w[-1])

        def objective(sequence: np.ndarray) -> float:
            (
                prefill_tokens,
                decode_tokens,
                active_decode,
                temperature,
                normalized_power,
                ttft_proxy,
                tpot_proxy,
            ) = _mpc_fluid_rollout(
                sequence,
                initial_prefill_tokens=initial_prefill_tokens,
                initial_decode_tokens=initial_decode_tokens,
                initial_active_decode=float(observation.decode_active),
                prompt_arrivals=prompt_arrivals,
                mean_prompt_tokens=self.mean_prompt_tokens,
                mean_output_tokens=self.mean_output_tokens,
                plant=self.plant,
                control_period_s=self.control_period_s,
                initial_temperature_c=observation.temperature_c,
            )
            normalized_frequency = (sequence - minimum) / (maximum - minimum)
            previous_normalized = (self.current_clock - minimum) / (maximum - minimum)
            changes = np.diff(
                np.concatenate([[previous_normalized], normalized_frequency])
            )
            ttft_slack = np.maximum(0.0, ttft_proxy - profile.ttft_slo_s) / max(
                profile.ttft_slo_s, 1e-12
            )
            tpot_slack = np.maximum(
                0.0,
                tpot_proxy - profile.tpot_slo_s,
            ) / max(profile.tpot_slo_s, 1e-12)
            power_slack = np.maximum(
                0.0,
                normalized_power - self.plant.power_limit_w / maximum_power,
            )
            thermal_slack = np.maximum(0.0, temperature[1:] - self.plant.thermal_limit_c)
            terminal_backlog = (
                prefill_tokens[-1] / profile.prefill_tokens_per_s[-1]
                + decode_tokens[-1] / profile.decode_tokens_per_s[-1]
            )
            return float(
                np.sum(normalized_power)
                + 20.0 * np.sum(ttft_slack**2)
                + 10.0 * np.sum(tpot_slack**2)
                + 0.05 * np.sum(changes**2)
                + 1_000.0 * np.sum(power_slack**2 + thermal_slack**2)
                + 20.0 * terminal_backlog**2
            )

        start = perf_counter()
        solution = minimize(
            objective,
            initial,
            method="SLSQP",
            bounds=[(minimum, maximum)] * self.horizon_steps,
            options={"maxiter": 50, "ftol": 1e-6, "disp": False},
        )
        elapsed = perf_counter() - start
        candidate = np.asarray(solution.x, dtype=float)
        success = bool(
            solution.success
            and np.all(np.isfinite(candidate))
            and elapsed <= self.solve_time_limit_s
        )
        return candidate, success, elapsed


def run_mpc(
    workload: Sequence[Request],
    plant: ServingPlant,
    scheduler: Scheduler = chunked_prefill_scheduler,
    *,
    horizon_s: float = 10.0,
    control_period_s: float = 1.0,
    solve_time_limit_s: float = 0.8,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> ServingResult:
    """Run receding-horizon frequency control on the detailed plant."""

    controller = _MPCClockController(
        workload,
        plant,
        horizon_s=horizon_s,
        control_period_s=control_period_s,
        solve_time_limit_s=solve_time_limit_s,
    )
    return simulate(
        workload,
        plant,
        scheduler,
        controller,
        seed,
        controller_name="MPC",
        scheduler_name="512-token interleaved chunked-prefill surrogate",
    )
