What Goes Wrong Without Terminal Ingredients

records.content:
Remove the terminal cost and the terminal set from the stick controller and
keep everything else. 

Figure 3 shows the closed loop from the
same initial state for several horizons, on the exact model and without
disturbances.



Figure 3:Closed-loop angle without terminal ingredients for N=1,3,5,10 (orange
shades), and with terminal cost and set for N=10 (blue), on the exact model.
A cross marks the first infeasible subproblem. With N=5 the stick settles
at \theta\approx0.32 rad and stays there.

The failures differ in kind, and each one has a clear cause.

With N=1, the objective is c(\mathbf x_0,u_0), and the next state does
not enter it. Since \mathbf x_0 is fixed, the minimizer is the cheapest
command, u_0=0, unless a constraint on \mathbf x_1 forces more. The
controller does nothing until the angle limit is about to be crossed, and by
then no admissible command can prevent it: the subproblem at step 3 is
infeasible.

With N=3, the horizon covers 0.15 s, less than half the time the tilt
needs to grow by a factor e. Within that window, pushing the stick back
costs command effort and returns little angle cost, so the plan does only
what is needed to keep the predicted angle under its limit. The subproblem
again becomes infeasible at step 3.

With N=5, every subproblem is feasible, but the closed loop converges to
\theta\approx0.32 rad, not to the upright position. There, each plan holds
the stick with a constant command and keeps the predicted angle just inside
the limit at the end of the horizon. The replanning law has acquired a
second equilibrium. Convergence to the target is therefore not implied by
feasibility.

With N=10, the horizon is long enough, and the stick returns upright. Its
closed-loop cost is 20.83, against 20.15 with terminal ingredients. The
remaining gap is the price of a horizon that sees only part of the recovery.

A long enough horizon eventually stabilizes the system without any terminal
ingredients, and there is a theory that quantifies “long enough”


Grüne & Pannek (2017). The required length depends on the system and the
initial state, and nothing in the subproblem reports when it is too short. The
terminal ingredients make a different trade. They give a certificate that
holds for every horizon, at the cost of a smaller feasible set: with the
terminal set, the same initial state is infeasible for every N\le 8.

To provide theoretical guarantees, the finite-horizon MPC problem is augmented with three interconnected components. The terminal cost c_N(\mathbf{x}) approximates the cost-to-go beyond the horizon, providing a surrogate for the infinite-horizon tail that cannot be explicitly optimized. The terminal constraint set \mathcal{X}_f defines a region where we have local knowledge of how to stabilize the system. Finally, the terminal controller \pi_f(\mathbf{x}) is a local feedback policy that stabilizes the system within \mathcal{X}_f.

These components must satisfy specific compatibility conditions to provide
theoretical guarantees. The statement below is for regulation to the origin
with time-invariant dynamics \mathbf f, stage cost c, and constraints
\mathbf g(\mathbf x,\mathbf u)\le\mathbf 0, which include the state and input
bounds. It follows 

Mayne et al. (2000).

Recursive Feasibility and Asymptotic Stability

Assume that \mathbf f(\mathbf 0,\mathbf 0)=\mathbf 0, that the stage cost
satisfies c(\mathbf x,\mathbf u)\ge\gamma\|\mathbf x\|^2 for some
\gamma>0, and that c_N\ge 0. Let the terminal set \mathcal X_f contain
the origin, and let the local controller \pi_f satisfy two conditions.

Control invariance: For all \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}_f, we have \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, \pi_f(\mathbf{x})) \in \mathcal{X}_f (the set is invariant) and \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}, \pi_f(\mathbf{x})) \leq \mathbf{0} (constraints remain satisfied).

Lyapunov decrease: For all \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}_f:c_N(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, \pi_f(\mathbf{x}))) - c_N(\mathbf{x}) \leq -c(\mathbf{x}, \pi_f(\mathbf{x}))

where c is the stage cost.

Suppose that the plant follows the prediction model exactly. Then, for every
initial state \mathbf x_0\in\mathcal X_N, the closed loop
\mathbf x_{t+1}=\mathbf f(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t)) has the
following properties:

Recursive feasibility: \mathbf x_t\in\mathcal X_N for all t, so
every subproblem has a solution.

Value decrease: V_N(\mathbf x_{t+1})\le V_N(\mathbf x_t)-c(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t)).

Cost bound and convergence:
\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}c(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t))\le V_N(\mathbf x_0),
and \mathbf x_t\to\mathbf 0.

Asymptotic stability, in the sense of a Lyapunov function, also needs V_N to
be bounded above by a multiple of \|\mathbf x\|^2 near the origin. This
holds, for example, when c_N is quadratic and the origin lies in the
interior of \mathcal X_f 

Rawlings et al. (2017). The three
properties listed are the ones a practitioner relies on, and they follow from
one construction.

Fix \mathbf x\in\mathcal X_N and let
(\mathbf u_0^\star,\ldots,\mathbf u_{N-1}^\star) be an optimal solution of
the subproblem from \mathbf x, with predicted states
\mathbf x_0^\star=\mathbf x,\mathbf x_1^\star,\ldots,\mathbf x_N^\star and
\mathbf x_N^\star\in\mathcal X_f. The controller applies
\mathbf u_0^\star, and since the model is exact, the next state is
\mathbf x^+=\mathbf x_1^\star.

A feasible candidate from \mathbf x^+. Consider the shifted sequence\tilde{\mathbf u}=\big(\mathbf u_1^\star,\ldots,\mathbf u_{N-1}^\star,\ \pi_f(\mathbf x_N^\star)\big).

From \mathbf x^+, its first N-1 commands reproduce the predicted states
\mathbf x_2^\star,\ldots,\mathbf x_N^\star, and these satisfy the
constraints because they did in the original solution. The last command
satisfies \mathbf g(\mathbf x_N^\star,\pi_f(\mathbf x_N^\star))\le\mathbf 0,
and the new terminal state
\mathbf f(\mathbf x_N^\star,\pi_f(\mathbf x_N^\star)) lies in
\mathcal X_f, both by control invariance. Hence \tilde{\mathbf u} is
feasible, so \mathbf x^+\in\mathcal X_N. Induction on t proves property 1.

Its cost. The candidate drops the first stage of the original solution and
adds one stage under \pi_f at the end. Its cost is\tilde V=V_N(\mathbf x)-c(\mathbf x,\mathbf u_0^\star)
+\Big[c(\mathbf x_N^\star,\pi_f(\mathbf x_N^\star))
+c_N\big(\mathbf f(\mathbf x_N^\star,\pi_f(\mathbf x_N^\star))\big)
-c_N(\mathbf x_N^\star)\Big].

The bracket is non-positive by the Lyapunov decrease condition. Since
V_N(\mathbf x^+) is the optimal cost from \mathbf x^+, it does not exceed
the cost of any feasible candidate:V_N(\mathbf x^+)\le\tilde V\le V_N(\mathbf x)-c(\mathbf x,\kappa_N(\mathbf x)).

This is property 2.

Summing. Adding property 2 over t=0,\ldots,T-1 telescopes to\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}c(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t))\le V_N(\mathbf x_0)-V_N(\mathbf x_T)\le V_N(\mathbf x_0),

using V_N\ge0. Letting T\to\infty gives the cost bound. A convergent
series of non-negative terms has terms tending to zero, so
\gamma\|\mathbf x_t\|^2\le c(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t))\to0.

The proof never uses optimality of the plan beyond the first step. It compares
the new optimum with one feasible candidate. Two practical consequences follow.
First, the guarantees survive an inexact solver as long as each returned plan
is feasible and costs no more than the shifted candidate. Many real-time
implementations check this explicitly and apply the candidate when the solver
fails to improve on it. Second, the exact-model assumption enters at exactly
one place, \mathbf x^+=\mathbf x_1^\star. With model error or disturbances,
the measured state differs from the predicted one, and the candidate need not
be feasible from it. In 

Figure 1, the recorded values
V_N(\mathbf x_t) decrease at every step until the tap, then jump from 0.61
to 3.23. Restoring guarantees under such errors is the subject of robust
MPC in the 

next chapter.

The bound in property 3 also gives a quantitative statement that the stick
experiment can check. With terminal ingredients and N=10, the closed-loop
cost from \mathbf x_0=(0.2,0.6) is 20.15, equal to V_{10}(\mathbf x_0) to
solver precision. The next two subsections explain why the bound is tight here.

hierarchy.lvl3: Constructing Terminal Ingredients for Linear Systems
Constructing Terminal Ingredients for Linear Systems

records.content:
The conditions of 

Theorem 1 look abstract, but for a linear
system \mathbf x_{k+1}=A\mathbf x_k+B\mathbf u_k with quadratic stage cost
\mathbf x^\top Q\mathbf x+\mathbf u^\top R\mathbf u, they can be met with
two matrix computations and one scalar.

Terminal controller and cost. Choose a linear terminal controller
\pi_f(\mathbf x)=K\mathbf x whose closed-loop matrix A_K=A+BK has all
eigenvalues inside the unit circle, and a quadratic terminal cost
c_N(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x. Substituting into the Lyapunov
decrease condition gives\mathbf x^\top\big(A_K^\top PA_K-P+Q+K^\top RK\big)\mathbf x\le0\qquad\text{for all }\mathbf x\in\mathcal X_f .

The condition holds with equality for every \mathbf x when P solves the
discrete Lyapunov equationA_K^\top PA_K-P+Q+K^\top RK=0 .

Because A_K is stable, the solution is unique and equals the series
P=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(A_K^\top)^k(Q+K^\top RK)A_K^k. Hence
\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x is exactly the cost of following
\mathbf u=K\mathbf x forever from \mathbf x, provided no constraint is
violated along the way. With this choice, the terminal cost is no longer a
guess at the tail. It is the cost of one admissible tail.

Any stabilizing K works. The natural choice is the gain that makes this tail
as cheap as possible, the infinite-horizon linear-quadratic regulator. Its
P solves the discrete algebraic Riccati equation and its gain is
K=-(R+B^\top PB)^{-1}B^\top PA. These formulas are derived by dynamic
programming in 

Finite-Horizon Dynamic Programming.
The argument here needs only the Lyapunov equation, which the LQR pair
satisfies.

Terminal set. The tail cost is meaningful only where K\mathbf x respects
the constraints for all future steps. Take an ellipsoid
\mathcal E_\alpha=\{\mathbf x:\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x\le\alpha\}. It is
invariant under A_K for every \alpha: by the Lyapunov equation,(A_K\mathbf x)^\top P(A_K\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x-\mathbf x^\top(Q+K^\top RK)\mathbf x\le\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x\le\alpha .

It remains to choose \alpha so that every constraint holds inside
\mathcal E_\alpha. Write each constraint, after substituting
\mathbf u=K\mathbf x, as a pair of half-spaces \pm\mathbf a^\top\mathbf x\le h.
For the stick, the rows are \mathbf a=K^\top with h=u_{\max}, and
\mathbf a=(1,0) with h=\theta_{\max}. The largest value of
\mathbf a^\top\mathbf x on \mathcal E_\alpha is
\sqrt{\alpha\,\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a}, a short Lagrange-multiplier
computation that the exercises ask for. Hence the largest admissible level is\alpha=\min_{\text{rows}}\ \frac{h^2}{\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a}.

With \mathcal X_f=\mathcal E_\alpha, both conditions of the theorem hold.
Invariance and constraint satisfaction hold by construction, and the decrease
holds with equality. This is the construction of 

Chen & Allgöwer (1998),
specialized to linear models. For a nonlinear model, the same recipe is
applied to the linearization at the equilibrium, with \alpha reduced until
the neglected nonlinear terms are dominated.

For the stick, the LQR gain is K=(-23.69,\,-7.55), and the input bound is
the binding row, giving \alpha=4.02. The initial state of the experiments has
\mathbf x_0^\top P\mathbf x_0=15.98, well outside \mathcal X_f, which is
why at least nine steps are needed to reach it. Two numerical checks in the
build script confirm the construction. Iterating the finite-horizon Riccati
recursion from P=Q converges to the same P to within 3\times10^{-12},
and on 2000 random points of \mathcal X_f, the largest value of
c_N(A_K\mathbf x)-c_N(\mathbf x)+c(\mathbf x,K\mathbf x) is of order


10-15, which is zero to rounding.

How does the finite-horizon value V_N(\mathbf x) compare with the
infinite-horizon value V_\infty(\mathbf x) of the constrained problem? The
answer depends on the terminal ingredients, and the three choices used on the
stick give three different answers. 

Figure 4 plots them.



Figure 4:Optimal finite-horizon value from \mathbf x_0=(0.2,0.6) as a function of
the horizon, for three terminal choices. Without terminal ingredients the
value rises toward V_\infty from below. With the LQR terminal cost alone it
can also lie below V_\infty. With terminal cost and terminal set the problem
is infeasible for N\le8 (shaded), and equals V_\infty to solver precision
from N=9 on.

Without terminal ingredients, V_N is a lower bound. Take the optimal
infinite sequence and keep its first N commands. They are feasible for the
N-step problem, and their cost omits only non-negative tail terms. Hence
V_N(\mathbf x)\le V_\infty(\mathbf x). The same argument shows that V_N
is non-decreasing in N. On the stick, V_1=0.76 and V_{10}=13.57, against
V_\infty=20.15.

With a terminal cost alone, V_N is neither. The LQR terminal cost
\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x is the cost of the unconstrained tail
\mathbf u=K\mathbf x. Outside \mathcal X_f, that tail violates a
constraint, and its cost can be lower than that of any admissible tail. With
N=1, the stick gives V_1=17.38<V_\infty. An upper bound cannot be
obtained without the terminal set.

With terminal cost and terminal set, V_N is an upper bound. Every
feasible N-step plan, extended by \pi_f from its terminal state, is an
admissible infinite sequence. By the Lyapunov equation, its cost equals the
N-step objective, because c_N is exactly the cost of the extension. The
infinite-horizon problem can choose among more sequences, so
V_\infty(\mathbf x)\le V_N(\mathbf x) on \mathcal X_N. The bound requires
that c_N be at least the cost of following \pi_f from every point of
\mathcal X_f. A terminal cost that underestimates that tail loses the upper bound.

The interesting question is bounding the approximation error
\varepsilon_N=V_N(\mathbf x)-V_\infty(\mathbf x)\ge0 in the third case. It
represents the cost of being forced to use \pi_f beyond the horizon rather
than continuing to optimize.

Let (\mathbf{u}_0^\star, \mathbf{u}_1^\star, \ldots) denote the infinite-horizon optimal control sequence with corresponding state trajectory (\mathbf{x}_0^\star, \mathbf{x}_1^\star, \ldots) where \mathbf{x}_0^\star = \mathbf{x}. The infinite-horizon cost is:V_\infty(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} c(\mathbf{x}_k^\star, \mathbf{u}_k^\star)

Suppose the horizon is long enough that this optimal trajectory has entered
the terminal set by step N, so that \mathbf x_N^\star\in\mathcal X_f. Then
its first N commands are feasible for the N-step problem, with cost\tilde{V}_N(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c(\mathbf{x}_k^\star, \mathbf{u}_k^\star) + c_N(\mathbf{x}_N^\star)

where c_N(\mathbf{x}_N^\star) approximates the tail cost \sum_{k=N}^{\infty} c(\mathbf{x}_k^\star, \mathbf{u}_k^\star).

Since V_N(\mathbf{x}) is the optimal N-horizon cost (which may do better than this particular truncated sequence), we have V_N(\mathbf{x}) \leq \tilde{V}_N(\mathbf{x}). The approximation error therefore satisfies:\varepsilon_N \leq \tilde{V}_N(\mathbf{x}) - V_\infty(\mathbf{x}) = c_N(\mathbf{x}_N^\star) - \sum_{k=N}^{\infty} c(\mathbf{x}_k^\star, \mathbf{u}_k^\star)

This bound shows that the approximation error depends on how well the
terminal cost approximates the optimal tail cost along the infinite-horizon
optimal trajectory, once that trajectory has entered \mathcal X_f. If
\mathbf x_N^\star\notin\mathcal X_f, the truncated sequence is infeasible for
the N-step problem and the bound says nothing.

The stick shows the extreme case. Inside \mathcal X_f, the LQR law satisfies
every constraint, so it is optimal for the constrained problem too, and
c_N=V_\infty there. The bound then gives \varepsilon_N=0 as soon as
\mathbf x_N^\star\in\mathcal X_f, which is what 

Figure 4
shows from N=9 on. Combined with property 3 of the theorem,V_\infty(\mathbf x_0)\le\sum_{t}c(\mathbf x_t,\kappa_N(\mathbf x_t))\le V_N(\mathbf x_0)=V_\infty(\mathbf x_0),

so the closed-loop cost equals V_\infty, as measured. On systems where the
optimal tail is not linear, \varepsilon_N is positive and shrinks with N
at a rate set by how fast optimal trajectories approach \mathcal X_f.

Receding-horizon control turns a finite-horizon optimizer into feedback by
reinitializing it from each measured state and applying only the first planned
action. The result is a state-feedback law \kappa_N, defined on the feasible
set \mathcal X_N and evaluated by optimization. On the balancing stick,
replanning with a wrong model keeps the stick upright, while under the same plan
executed open loop the stick falls within a second.

A short horizon alone guarantees nothing. It can leave an unstable system
uncontrolled, lose feasibility, or create a spurious equilibrium near a
constraint. A terminal cost, a terminal set, and an invariant local controller
connect the truncated problem to the infinite-horizon one. The shifted
candidate sequence then proves recursive feasibility, a decreasing value, and
a closed-loop cost no larger than V_N(\mathbf x_0). For linear systems, the
terminal cost solves a Lyapunov equation, and the terminal set is an
ellipsoid whose size follows from the constraints in closed form.

The basic loop leaves several design choices unresolved. How should the same
replanning mechanism represent tracking, economic objectives, uncertainty,
hybrid decisions, solver failures, and hard real-time deadlines? 

MPC variants
and reliable operation organize those choices.
The guarantees here also assumed an exact model, and the robust and
stochastic formulations of that chapter address what replaces them.

A scalar unstable plant

Consider x_{k+1}=2x_k+u_k with |u_k|\le1 and stage cost x^2+u^2.

Show that one-step MPC without terminal ingredients applies u=0 from
every state, and conclude that it does not stabilize the origin.

Take the terminal controller u=Kx with K=-3/2. Solve the scalar
Lyapunov equation for P, and verify the decrease condition.

Find the largest \alpha such that \{x:Px^2\le\alpha\} satisfies the
input bound under u=Kx. Express the terminal set as an interval.

Solution to 

Exercise 1

With N=1, the objective is x_0^2+u_0^2, and x_0 is fixed, so the
minimizer is u_0=0. The closed loop is x_{t+1}=2x_t, which diverges
from every nonzero state.

A_K=2-\tfrac32=\tfrac12 and Q+K^\top RK=1+\tfrac94=\tfrac{13}4. The
Lyapunov equation \tfrac14P-P+\tfrac{13}4=0 gives P=\tfrac{13}3. The
decrease holds with equality:
P(\tfrac12x)^2-Px^2+\tfrac{13}4x^2=(\tfrac{13}{12}-\tfrac{13}3+\tfrac{13}4)x^2=0.

|Kx|\le1 means |x|\le\tfrac23. The formula gives
\alpha=h^2/(a^2/P)=1/(\tfrac94\cdot\tfrac3{13})=\tfrac{52}{27}, and
\{x:\tfrac{13}3x^2\le\tfrac{52}{27}\}=\{|x|\le\tfrac23\}.

One step with the LQR terminal cost

Let P solve the discrete algebraic Riccati equation for (A,B,Q,R), and
let K=-(R+B^\top PB)^{-1}B^\top PA. Show that one-step MPC with terminal
cost \mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x and no active constraints applies exactly
\mathbf u=K\mathbf x. Which curve of 

Figure 4 does this
explain at N=1, and why does that value lie below V_\infty?

Solution to 

Exercise 2

The objective is
\mathbf x^\top Q\mathbf x+\mathbf u^\top R\mathbf u+(A\mathbf x+B\mathbf u)^\top P(A\mathbf x+B\mathbf u).
Setting its gradient in \mathbf u to zero gives
(R+B^\top PB)\mathbf u=-B^\top PA\mathbf x, which is \mathbf u=K\mathbf x.
Without constraints, its value is \mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x by the Riccati
equation, the unconstrained infinite-horizon cost. This is the green curve at
N=1. From \mathbf x_0=(0.2,0.6), the unconstrained LQR tail exceeds the
command bound, so it is cheaper than every admissible tail, and the value
17.38 lies below the constrained V_\infty=20.15.

Support function of an ellipsoid

Let P be symmetric positive definite and \alpha>0. Show that
\max\{\mathbf a^\top\mathbf x:\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x\le\alpha\}=\sqrt{\alpha\,\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a},
and deduce the formula for the terminal level \alpha.

Solution to 

Exercise 3

The maximum of a linear function over the ellipsoid is attained on its
boundary. Stationarity of
\mathbf a^\top\mathbf x-\lambda(\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x-\alpha) gives
\mathbf x=P^{-1}\mathbf a/(2\lambda). Substituting into
\mathbf x^\top P\mathbf x=\alpha gives
2\lambda=\sqrt{\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a/\alpha}, and the value is
\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a/(2\lambda)=\sqrt{\alpha\,\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a}.
The half-space \mathbf a^\top\mathbf x\le h contains the ellipsoid exactly
when this value is at most h, that is, when
\alpha\le h^2/(\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a). By symmetry, the same
condition covers -\mathbf a^\top\mathbf x\le h. Taking the minimum over all
rows gives \alpha.

The spurious equilibrium

Using code/receding_horizon.py, run the controller without terminal
ingredients with N=5 from (0.2,0.6) for 200 steps. Inspect the final
state, the applied command, and the predicted trajectory of the last
subproblem. Explain why the state is a fixed point of the closed loop, and why
it is not a fixed point of the open-loop dynamics with u=0. Find the
smallest horizon for which the stick returns upright from this initial state.

Solution to 

Exercise 4

The closed loop settles at \dot\theta=0, \theta\approx0.32 rad, with a
constant command close to -(g/\ell)\,\theta\approx-3.1 rad/s^2, which
cancels the gravitational acceleration. The last plan holds the stick nearly
still, and its predicted angle approaches the limit at the end of the horizon.
Within five steps, pushing the stick back costs more command effort than it
saves in angle cost, so the plan that holds the state is optimal, and applying
its first command reproduces the same state. With u=0, the same state falls
away. With N=6, the stick still parks, near \theta\approx0.29 rad. N=7
is the smallest horizon that returns it upright within 200 steps, with
closed-loop cost 34.1, and N=8 lowers that cost to 24.1.

Where the proof breaks under model error

Repeat the replanning experiment of 

Figure 1, and record
V_N(\mathbf x_t) along the closed loop. Identify each step where
V_N(\mathbf x_{t+1})>V_N(\mathbf x_t)-c(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf u_t). Which line of
the proof of 

Theorem 1 fails at those steps? Then shorten
the plant’s stick further and find the length at which the replanned
controller first meets an infeasible subproblem.

Solution to 

Exercise 5

The proof assumes \mathbf x^+=\mathbf x_1^\star. The tap violates that
assumption by 0.5 rad/s in one step, and V_N jumps from 0.61 to
3.23. The shorter stick violates it by a small amount at every step, so the
decrease inequality can fail by a margin even where V_N keeps decreasing.
The shifted candidate is built from the predicted state, so it need not be
feasible from the measured one. Recursive feasibility is no longer guaranteed,
and for a short enough stick it fails. The threshold depends on the tap and
the initial state, which is why robust MPC tightens the constraints by bounds
on the prediction error.

A rate limit in the terminal set

Add the constraint |\dot\theta_k|\le1 rad/s to the stick through
StickParameters(rate_max=1.0). Recompute \alpha and state which row is now
binding. Recompute the feasible sets of 

Figure 2 and
check whether \kappa_{20} still agrees with \operatorname{sat}(K\mathbf x).

Solution to 

Exercise 6

The terminal level becomes the minimum over three rows. For the rate row,
\mathbf a=(0,1) and h=1 give h^2/(\mathbf a^\top P^{-1}\mathbf a)\approx4.39.
For the angle row the value is 8.99, and for the input row 4.02. The input
bound still binds, so \alpha and \mathcal X_f do not change, although the
rate bound comes close. The function terminal_level performs the same
computation. The feasible sets are cut by the horizontal lines
\dot\theta=\pm1. Where the rate bound becomes active along the optimal
predicted path, the first command can differ from the saturated linear law, so
measure the gap rather than assume it.

The model, the MPC subproblem, and the checks are in one module, and the
figures and numbers are produced by one script:

Balancing-stick model and linear MPC

Experiment and figure builder

Numbers quoted in this chapter

Run uv run python scripts/build_receding_horizon_artifacts.py from the
repository root to regenerate the four figures and the metrics, in about one
minute. Normal book builds read the saved figures. The tests in
tests/test_receding_horizon.py check the Lyapunov equation, the terminal
level, the shifted-candidate inequality, recursive feasibility, and the
bounds on V_N on short runs.

Receding horizon

An MPC solver returns a sequence (\mathbf{u}_0^\star,\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{N-1}^\star). Which controls are normally applied before the problem is solved again?

Solution to 

Exercise 7

Only the first control (or first short control block) is applied. The state is measured again and the horizon is shifted before re-optimizing.

Terminal ingredients

What roles do a terminal cost and a terminal constraint play in finite-horizon MPC?

Solution to 

Exercise 8

The terminal cost approximates value beyond the horizon; the terminal constraint can keep the endpoint in a region from which a known controller remains feasible and stable.

Disturbance response

Why does resolving the same finite-horizon optimization after each measurement provide feedback even if the prediction model is deterministic?

Solution to 

Exercise 9

The newly measured state contains the accumulated effect of disturbances and model error. Reinitializing the optimization from that state changes the planned controls accordingly.

Infinite-horizon dynamic programming selects actions with a hard maximum. That
operator is nondifferentiable at ties and produces a deterministic greedy
choice. Can a modified control objective produce both a smooth Bellman operator
and a stochastic optimal policy? Convex regularization supplies the link.

While the standard Bellman optimality equations use the max operator to determine the best action, an alternative formulation known as the smooth or soft Bellman optimality equations replaces it with a smooth approximation of the maximum. The history of these equations runs across two communities that rarely read each other. They appear in the work of the structural econometrician John Rust on the replacement of bus engines 

Rust (1987), together with an inverse problem and an algorithm to solve it. 

Ng & Russell (2000), who are usually credited with introducing inverse reinforcement learning, cite Rust, but the connection was then largely lost. 

Ziebart et al. (2008) rediscovered the same equations as maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning, named after the maximum entropy principle. 

Haarnoja et al. (2017) built on Ziebart to obtain soft Q-learning, and soft actor-critic 

Haarnoja et al. (2018), one of the most widely used deep RL algorithms for continuous control, followed a year later.

In the infinite-horizon setting, the smooth Bellman optimality equations take the form:v^\star_\beta(s) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp\left(\beta\left(r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j | s, a) v^\star_\beta(j)\right)\right)

We write v^\star_\beta for this smooth value function, to keep it apart from the optimal value v^*_\gamma of the hard Bellman equation.

Adopting an operator-theoretic perspective, we can define a nonlinear operator \mathrm{L}_\beta such that the smooth value function of an MDP is then the solution to the following fixed-point equation:(\mathrm{L}_\beta \mathbf{v})(s) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)\right)\right)

As \beta \to \infty, \mathrm{L}_\beta converges to the standard Bellman operator \Bellman. Furthermore, it can be shown that the smooth Bellman operator is a contraction mapping in the supremum norm, and therefore has a unique fixed point. However, as opposed to the usual “hard” setting, the fixed point of \mathrm{L}_\beta is associated with the value function of an optimal stochastic policy defined by the softmax distribution:\pi(a|s) = \frac{\exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v^\star_\beta(j)\right)\right)}{\sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a') + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a') v^\star_\beta(j)\right)\right)}

Despite the confusing terminology, the above “softmax” policy is the smooth counterpart of the argmax in the original optimality equation, not of the max: it is a soft-argmax. The smooth counterpart of the max is the log-sum-exp. The same policy is also called a Boltzmann or Gibbs policy. As the temperature 1/\beta goes to zero, the softmax concentrates on the maximizing actions and we recover the greedy policy and the hard Bellman equation.

hierarchy.lvl3: Stochastic Policies: Exploration and the Partition Function
Stochastic Policies: Exploration and the Partition Function

records.content:
Moving from the argmax to the softmax turns deterministic policies into stochastic ones, which is both useful and costly. It is useful because noise in the actions is a way to explore. In RL the agent usually gathers its own data, and if it always took the action it currently believes best it would never learn about the others. The problem is not specific to RL. An engineer identifying a model of a plant must also choose inputs that reveal the dynamics, and in system identification this is called exciting the system: a persistently exciting input is one rich enough for the parameters to be identifiable from the data.

It is costly when the action set is continuous. The softmax policy is then a density \pi(a \mid s) \propto \exp(\beta q(s,a)) whose normalizing constant, the partition function \int \exp(\beta q(s,a))\, da, is an integral with no closed form in general. The log-sum-exp value has the same problem, since it is the logarithm of that integral. This is the intractable partition function familiar from energy-based models and probabilistic graphical models. Numerical quadrature is an option in low dimension but is rarely used. 

Haarnoja et al. (2017) sampled from the softmax policy over continuous actions with amortized Stein variational gradient descent, which proved expensive; soft actor-critic 

Haarnoja et al. (2018) instead fits a tractable parametric policy to the softmax, an idea we return to in the chapters on fitted value methods and policy learning. The notation for continuous actions, and what changes when sums become integrals, is in 

Continuous Action and State Spaces.

This formulation is interesting for several reasons. First, smoothness is a desirable property from an optimization standpoint. Unlike \gamma, we view \beta as a hyperparameter of our algorithm, which we can control to achieve the desired level of accuracy.

Second, we presented the equations pragmatically, by replacing the max with the log-sum-exp (a smooth maximum) and the argmax with the softmax (a smooth argmax). The same equations come out of two other starting points, and this chapter follows all three routes:

Smoothing the operator. Replace every max by a log-sum-exp, as above. This is the route of the next subsection, and the justification is computational: a smooth operator has gradients everywhere.

Noise on the rewards. Keep the hard Bellman equation, but suppose that each action’s reward is perturbed by independent Gumbel noise that the decision maker sees and the modeler does not. Integrating the noise out gives the log-sum-exp (

Gumbel Noise on the Rewards). This is how 

Rust (1987) motivated the equations, following the discrete choice models of econometrics.

Entropy regularization. Keep the rewards, but add a bonus proportional to the entropy of the policy in every state. The regularized Bellman equation is again the log-sum-exp equation (

Regularized Markov Decision Processes). This is the reading behind maximum entropy RL and soft actor-critic.

Each route brings its own tools: smoothness gives differentiability, the noise model gives a likelihood for observed behavior, and the regularization view gives convex duality. A fourth reading, close to the third, starts from the energy-based models of supervised learning, where a softmax turns unnormalized scores into a distribution; this is essentially what 

Ziebart et al. (2008) did. It connects to probabilistic graphical models, where finding an optimal smooth policy becomes an inference problem. This is the idea of control as inference, whose converse, inference as control, is now used to derive samplers and amortized inference methods with RL 

Levine et al. (2018).

Before iterating \mathrm{L}_\beta, we should check that iterating it is the right thing to do, that is, that it is a contraction. It is, in the sup-norm and with the same factor \gamma as the hard Bellman operator. The proof uses the same three facts as for \Bellman. The log-sum-exp is monotone, it commutes with adding a constant to all of its arguments, and \mathrm{L}_\beta maps a uniform shift c\mathbf{1} of v into a shift \gamma c\mathbf{1} of \mathrm{L}_\beta v. From v \le u + \|v-u\|_\infty\mathbf{1} we get \mathrm{L}_\beta v \le \mathrm{L}_\beta u + \gamma\|v-u\|_\infty\mathbf{1}, and exchanging u and v gives the contraction. A word of caution about the converse: failing to show that an operator is a contraction does not mean that its fixed point fails to exist or that no algorithm finds it. Contraction is a convenient sufficient condition, and other fixed-point theorems cover other cases.

Successive approximation applied to \mathrm{L}_\beta is smooth value iteration. It has the structure of value iteration, with a log-sum-exp wherever value iteration had a max and a softmax policy at the end where value iteration returned a greedy one.

Smooth Value Iteration

Input: MDP (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, r, p, \gamma), inverse temperature \beta > 0, tolerance \varepsilon > 0

Output: Value function v within \varepsilon/2 of v^\star_\beta and stochastic policy \pi

Initialize v(s) \leftarrow 0 for all s \in \mathcal{S}

repeat

\quad for each state s \in \mathcal{S} and action a \in \mathcal{A}_s do

\quad\quad q(s,a) \leftarrow r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)

\quad end for

\quad v_{\text{new}}(s) \leftarrow \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp(\beta \cdot q(s,a)) for all s \in \mathcal{S}

\quad \Delta \leftarrow \max_s |v_{\text{new}}(s) - v(s)|

\quad v \leftarrow v_{\text{new}}

until \Delta < \frac{\varepsilon(1-\gamma)}{2\gamma}

Extract policy: compute q(s,a) from v as in line 4, and set \pi(a|s) \leftarrow \frac{\exp(\beta \cdot q(s,a))}{\sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp(\beta \cdot q(s,a'))}

return v, \pi

Differences from standard value iteration:

Line 6 uses \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_a \exp(\beta \cdot q(s,a)) instead of \max_a q(s,a)

Line 10 extracts a stochastic policy using softmax instead of a deterministic argmax policy

As \beta \to \infty, the algorithm converges to standard value iteration

Lower \beta values produce more stochastic policies with higher entropy

What the stopping rule guarantees. Because \mathrm{L}_\beta is a \gamma-contraction, the a posteriori bound of the Banach fixed-point theorem applies unchanged, and the stopping test of line 9 guarantees \|v - v^\star_\beta\|_\infty \le \varepsilon/2. The proof that value iteration returns an \varepsilon-optimal policy also carries over, with one change of meaning. The softmax policy satisfies \mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega} v = \mathrm{L}_\beta v for the entropy-regularized evaluation operator of 

Regularized Bellman Operators, with regularizer \Omega(\pi(\cdot|s)) = \frac{1}{\beta}\sum_a \pi(a|s)\log\pi(a|s), just as a greedy policy satisfies \mathrm{L}_\pi v = \Bellman v. Repeating the proof of 

Proposition 2 with these operators shows that the returned policy is \varepsilon-optimal for the entropy-regularized objective. How far is that from optimal for the original rewards? Since \max_a x_a \le \frac{1}{\beta}\log\sum_a e^{\beta x_a} \le \max_a x_a + \frac{\log|\mathcal{A}|}{\beta}, where |\mathcal{A}| is the largest number of actions in any state, the two fixed points satisfyv^*_\gamma \;\le\; v^\star_\beta \;\le\; v^*_\gamma + \frac{\log |\mathcal{A}|}{\beta(1-\gamma)}\mathbf{1},

and the softmax policy returned by the algorithm loses at most \varepsilon + \frac{\log|\mathcal{A}|}{\beta(1-\gamma)} against the optimal value of the unregularized MDP. The temperature therefore adds a bias that does not shrink with more iterations; it is the price of smoothness and of exploration.

Why does adding independent Gumbel perturbations to action rewards produce a
log-sum-exp value before the perturbation is observed?

We can obtain the smooth Bellman equation by considering a setting in which we have Gumbel noise added to the reward function. This derivation provides theoretical insight and also connects to practical modeling scenarios where rewards have random perturbations.

hierarchy.lvl3: Step 1: Define the Augmented MDP with Gumbel Noise
Step 1: Define the Augmented MDP with Gumbel Noise

records.content:
At each time period and state s, we draw an action-indexed shock vector:\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t(s) = \big(\epsilon_t(s,a)\big)_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s}, \quad \text{where } \epsilon_t(s,a) \text{ i.i.d.} \sim \mathrm{Gumbel}(\mu_\epsilon, 1/\beta)

These shocks are independent across time periods, states, and actions, and are independent of the MDP transition dynamics p(\cdot | s, a).

The Gumbel distribution with location parameter \mu and scale parameter 1/\beta has probability density function:f(x; \mu, 1/\beta) = \beta\exp\left(-\beta(x-\mu)-\exp(-\beta(x-\mu))\right)

To generate a Gumbel-distributed random variable, we can use inverse transform sampling: X = \mu - \frac{1}{\beta} \log(-\log(U)) where U is uniform on (0,1).

Zero-Mean Shocks

To ensure the shocks have zero mean, we set \mu_\epsilon = -\gamma_E/\beta where \gamma_E \approx 0.5772 is the Euler-Mascheroni constant. This choice eliminates an additive constant that would otherwise appear in the smooth Bellman equation. For simplicity, we will adopt this convention throughout.

We now define an augmented MDP with:

Augmented state: \tilde{s} = (s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) where s \in \mathcal{S} and \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}_s|}

Augmented reward: \tilde{r}(\tilde{s}, a) = r(s,a) + \epsilon(a)

Augmented transition: \tilde{p}(\tilde{s}' | \tilde{s}, a) = p(s' | s, a) \cdot p(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}')

The transition factorizes because the next shock vector \boldsymbol{\epsilon}' is drawn independently of the current state and action (conditional independence).

The Augmented State Space is Uncountable

Even if the original state space \mathcal{S} and action space \mathcal{A} are finite, the augmented state space \tilde{\mathcal{S}} = \mathcal{S} \times \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}|} is uncountably infinite because each shock vector \boldsymbol{\epsilon} is a continuous random variable. The space has finite dimension, |\mathcal{A}| coordinates for the shocks, but a value function on it is an element of an infinite-dimensional function space. The shocks are also unbounded, so the rewards r(s,a)+\epsilon(a) are unbounded and the sup-norm theory of the previous chapter does not apply as stated. Nothing breaks, because the shocks have finite mean and enter additively, but it is one more reason not to work on this space directly. Therefore:

We cannot enumerate the augmented states

Tabular dynamic programming methods do not apply directly

The augmented value function \tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) maps a continuous space to \mathbb{R}

This motivates why we immediately marginalize over the shocks to obtain a finite-dimensional representation.

hierarchy.lvl3: Step 2: The Hard Bellman Equation on the Augmented State Space
Step 2: The Hard Bellman Equation on the Augmented State Space

records.content:
The Bellman optimality equation for the augmented MDP is:\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ r(s,a) + \epsilon(a) + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}'}\left[\tilde{v}(s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}') \mid s, a\right] \right\}

Here the expectation is over the next augmented state (s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}'), which includes both the next state s' \sim p(\cdot | s, a) and the next shock vector \boldsymbol{\epsilon}' \sim p(\cdot).

This is a perfectly well-defined Bellman equation, and an optimal stationary policy exists:\pi(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) \in \operatorname{argmax}_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ r(s,a) + \epsilon(a) + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}'}\left[\tilde{v}(s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}') \mid s, a\right] \right\}

However, this equation is computationally intractable because:

The state space is continuous (uncountable), so \tilde v is a function on a continuum

The shocks are fresh each period

We would need to solve for \tilde{v} over an uncountable domain

We never solve this equation directly. Instead, we use it as a mathematical device to derive the smooth Bellman equation.

hierarchy.lvl3: Step 3: Define the Ex-Ante (Inclusive) Value Function
Step 3: Define the Ex-Ante (Inclusive) Value Function

records.content:
The idea here is to consider the expected value before observing the current shocks. We define what some authors in econometrics call the inclusive value or ex-ante value:v(s) := \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\big[\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon})\big]

This is the value of being in state s before we observe the current-period shock vector \boldsymbol{\epsilon}.

Two Different Value Functions

It is crucial to distinguish:

\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}): the value after observing shocks (conditional on \boldsymbol{\epsilon}), defined on the augmented state space

v(s): the value before observing shocks (marginalizing over \boldsymbol{\epsilon}), defined on the original state space

The function v(s) is what we actually compute and care about. The augmented value \tilde{v} exists only as a proof device.

hierarchy.lvl3: Step 4: Separate the Deterministic and Random Components
Step 4: Separate the Deterministic and Random Components

records.content:
Now we take the expectation of the augmented Bellman equation with respect to the current shocks only (everything that does not depend on the current \boldsymbol{\epsilon} can be pulled out).

First, note that by the law of iterated expectations and independence of shocks across time:\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}'}\big[\tilde{v}(s', \boldsymbol{\epsilon}')\big] = v(s')

This follows from our definition of v and the fact that the next shock is independent of everything else.

Now define the deterministic part of the right-hand side:x_a(s) := r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)

This is the expected return from taking action a in state s without the shock. Using this notation, the augmented Bellman equation becomes:\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ x_a(s) + \epsilon(a) \right\}

Taking the expectation over \boldsymbol{\epsilon} on both sides:v(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ x_a(s) + \epsilon(a) \right\}\right]

Expectation of a Max, Not Max of an Expectation

Notice carefully: we have \mathbb{E}[\max(\cdot)], not \max \mathbb{E}[\cdot]. We are not swapping max and expectation.

The expression \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}[\max_a \{x_a + \epsilon(a)\}] is the expected value of the maximum of Gumbel-perturbed utilities. The Gumbel random utility identity evaluates this quantity in closed form.

hierarchy.lvl3: Step 5: Apply the Gumbel Random Utility Identity
Step 5: Apply the Gumbel Random Utility Identity

records.content:
We now invoke a result from extreme value theory:

Gumbel Random Utility Identity

Let \epsilon_1, \ldots, \epsilon_m be i.i.d. \mathrm{Gumbel}(\mu_\epsilon, 1/\beta) random variables. For any deterministic values x_1, \ldots, x_m \in \mathbb{R}:\max_{i=1,\ldots,m} \{x_i + \epsilon_i\} \overset{d}{=} \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{i=1}^m \exp(\beta x_i) + \zeta

where \zeta \sim \mathrm{Gumbel}(\mu_\epsilon, 1/\beta) (same distribution as the original shocks).

Taking expectations:\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i=1,\ldots,m} \{x_i + \epsilon_i\}\right] = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{i=1}^m \exp(\beta x_i) + \mu_\epsilon + \frac{\gamma_E}{\beta}

where \gamma_E \approx 0.5772 is the Euler-Mascheroni constant.

With mean-zero shocks (\mu_\epsilon = -\gamma_E/\beta), the constant term vanishes:\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{i=1,\ldots,m} \{x_i + \epsilon_i\}\right] = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{i=1}^m \exp(\beta x_i)

Applying this identity to our problem (with mean-zero shocks):v(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[\max_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \{x_a(s) + \epsilon(a)\}\right] = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp(\beta x_a(s))

Substituting the definition of x_a(s):v(s) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j)\right)\right)

We have arrived at the smooth Bellman equation.

To recap the logical flow:

We constructed an augmented MDP with state (s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) where shocks perturb rewards

We wrote the standard Bellman equation for this augmented MDP (hard max, but over an uncountable state space)

We defined the ex-ante value v(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}[\tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon})] to eliminate the continuous shock component

We separated deterministic and random terms: \tilde{v}(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \max_a \{x_a(s) + \epsilon(a)\}

We applied the Gumbel identity to evaluate \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}[\max_a \{\cdots\}] in closed form as a log-sum-exp

The augmented MDP with shocks exists only as a mathematical device. We never approximate \tilde{v}, never discretize \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, and never enumerate the augmented state space. The only computational object we work with is v(s) on the original (finite) state space, which satisfies the smooth Bellman equation.

hierarchy.lvl3: The Original and Augmented MDPs Side by Side
The Original and Augmented MDPs Side by Side

records.content:
The derivation moves between two decision problems. The first is the original MDP solved with the smooth Bellman equation, or equivalently with an entropy bonus (

Regularized Markov Decision Processes). The second is the augmented MDP, in which the decision maker solves a hard Bellman equation but sees a fresh shock on every action’s reward. The table puts them next to each other. We write q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{j} p(j\mid s,a)\, v^\star_\beta(j), which is the x_a(s) of the derivation.



Original MDP, smooth Bellman equation

Augmented MDP, Gumbel shocks

State

s \in \mathcal{S}

(s, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) \in \mathcal{S} \times \mathbb{R}^{\lvert\mathcal{A}_s\rvert}

Noise

only the transitions p(j \mid s,a)

the transitions, plus a fresh i.i.d. Gumbel vector \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t each period

Reward of action a

r(s,a), plus the bonus \beta^{-1} H(\pi(\cdot \mid s))

r(s,a) + \epsilon(a)

Transition

p(j \mid s,a)

p(j \mid s,a)\, g(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}'), with g the Gumbel density

Bellman equation

v = \mathrm{L}_\beta v, a log-sum-exp

\tilde v(s,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \max_a \{q(s,a) + \epsilon(a)\}, a hard max

Optimal policy

stochastic, \pi_\beta(a \mid s) \propto \exp(\beta q(s,a))

deterministic, \sigma(s,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \operatorname{argmax}_a \{q(s,a) + \epsilon(a)\}

Value

v^\star_\beta(s)

\tilde v(s,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}), with \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}[\tilde v(s,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})] = v^\star_\beta(s)

Who sees what

the agent and the modeler both see s

the agent sees s and \boldsymbol{\epsilon}; the modeler sees only s

Figure 1 draws both problems as graphical models, one time slice after another.



Figure 1:(a) The original MDP under the softmax policy. The action a_t is a random child of s_t with conditional distribution \pi_\beta(\cdot \mid s_t). (b) The augmented MDP. A shock vector \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t (dashed) is drawn independently each period, and the augmented state is (s_t, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t) (dotted boxes). The action is a deterministic function of the augmented state (double circle). The shock has no arrow into s_{t+1} or \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t+1}. Integrating \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t out of each slice of (b) gives (a).

The figure shows why the construction works. In panel (b), \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t has a single child, the action a_t, and the action is a deterministic function of (s_t, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t). Integrating the shock out of slice t therefore changes only the conditional distribution of a_t:\mathbb{P}(a_t = a \mid s_t) = \int \mathbb{1}\{a = \sigma(s_t, \boldsymbol{\epsilon})\}\, g(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\, d\boldsymbol{\epsilon} = \pi_\beta(a \mid s_t),

by 

Lemma 2. Doing this in every slice turns graph (b) into graph (a): the two models give the same distribution over state-action trajectories (s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1, \ldots). The missing arrows matter. If \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t also influenced s_{t+1}, or if the shocks were correlated over time, integrating them out would leave a dependence on the past, and the marginal process would no longer be an MDP in s. 

Rust (1987) states this as a conditional independence assumption, and his estimator relies on it.

The rewards are not equal path by path. The augmented agent collects r(s_t,a_t) + \epsilon_t(a_t), while the original MDP pays r(s_t,a_t) and the entropy bonus. They are equal on average. Conditional on which action wins, the winning value \max_a\{q(s,a)+\epsilon(a)\} has the same distribution whatever the winner is, a property of the Gumbel distribution. Its mean is \frac{1}{\beta}\log\sum_{a'} \exp(\beta q(s,a')) by 

Lemma 1, so\mathbb{E}\big[\epsilon(a) \,\big|\, \sigma(s,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = a\big] = \frac{1}{\beta}\log\sum_{a'} e^{\beta q(s,a')} - q(s,a) = -\frac{1}{\beta}\log \pi_\beta(a \mid s).

The shock that the agent collects on the action it picks is, on average, -\frac{1}{\beta}\log\pi_\beta(a\mid s). Averaging over a \sim \pi_\beta(\cdot\mid s) gives \frac{1}{\beta}H(\pi_\beta(\cdot \mid s)), the entropy bonus. The per-action penalty -\alpha \log \pi(a \mid s) that appears later in the regularized formulation is this expected shock, with \alpha = 1/\beta. A rarely chosen action is chosen only when its shock is large, and the entropy bonus is the average of those large shocks.

The augmented MDP is a device for theory: it explains where the log-sum-exp comes from and gives a likelihood for observed choices, but nobody solves it to compute a policy. On a small problem we can still solve it by brute force and check that it gives the same answer as the original MDP. The cell below draws a random MDP with 5 states and 3 actions, sets \gamma = 0.9 and \beta = 2, and computes the solution in three ways.

Original MDP. Smooth value iteration with the log-sum-exp, then the softmax policy.

Original MDP, regularized reading. The value of that softmax policy with its entropy bonus, from the linear system (\mathbf{I}-\gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}_\pi + \beta^{-1}\mathbf{H}_\pi.

Augmented MDP. Value iteration with the hard max on the ex-ante value, v(s) \leftarrow \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}[\max_a\{r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_j p(j\mid s,a)v(j)+\epsilon(a)\}], with the expectation replaced by an average over 50,000 Gumbel draws and no log-sum-exp anywhere. We then simulate 20,000 episodes in which the agent sees fresh shocks at every step, takes the deterministic action \operatorname{argmax}_a\{q(s,a)+\epsilon(a)\}, and collects r + \epsilon(a).

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_states, n_actions, gamma, beta = 5, 3, 0.9, 2.0
P = rng.dirichlet(0.5 * np.ones(n_states), size=(n_states, n_actions))  # P[s, a, j]
r = rng.normal(size=(n_states, n_actions))
loc, scale = -np.euler_gamma / beta, 1 / beta  # mean-zero Gumbel shocks


def smooth_max(q):
    """(1/beta) log sum_a exp(beta q), computed stably along the last axis."""
    m = q.max(axis=-1)
    return m + np.log(np.exp(beta * (q - m[..., None])).sum(axis=-1)) / beta


# Original MDP: smooth value iteration, then the softmax policy.
v = np.zeros(n_states)
for _ in range(500):
    v = smooth_max(r + gamma * P @ v)
q = r + gamma * P @ v
pi = np.exp(beta * (q - v[:, None]))
entropy = -(pi * np.log(pi)).sum(axis=1)

# Original MDP, regularized reading: evaluate pi with its entropy bonus,
# (I - gamma P_pi) v = r_pi + H_pi / beta.
P_pi = np.einsum("sa,saj->sj", pi, P)
v_reg = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(n_states) - gamma * P_pi, (pi * r).sum(axis=1) + entropy / beta)

# Augmented MDP: hard Bellman equation, ex-ante value. The expectation over the
# current shocks is an average over n_draws fixed Gumbel draws; no log-sum-exp.
n_draws = 50_000
shocks = rng.gumbel(loc, scale, size=(n_draws, n_states, n_actions))
v_aug = np.zeros(n_states)
for _ in range(150):
    v_aug = (r + gamma * P @ v_aug + shocks).max(axis=2).mean(axis=0)
q_aug = r + gamma * P @ v_aug

# Simulate the augmented MDP: the agent sees fresh shocks every step and takes
# the deterministic action argmax_a q_aug(s, a) + eps(a).
n_episodes, horizon = 20_000, 150
s = np.zeros(n_episodes, dtype=int)
returns = np.zeros(n_episodes)
visits = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
shock_total = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
cdf = P.cumsum(axis=2)
for t in range(horizon):
    eps = rng.gumbel(loc, scale, size=(n_episodes, n_actions))
    a = (q_aug[s] + eps).argmax(axis=1)
    eps_a = eps[np.arange(n_episodes), a]
    returns += gamma**t * (r[s, a] + eps_a)
    np.add.at(visits, (s, a), 1)
    np.add.at(shock_total, (s, a), eps_a)
    s = (rng.random(n_episodes)[:, None] > cdf[s, a]).sum(axis=1)
freq = visits / visits.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
mean_shock = shock_total / visits

fmt = lambda x: " ".join(f"{y:6.3f}" for y in x)
lines = [
    "Values v(s)",
    f"  original, smooth value iteration        {fmt(v)}",
    f"  original, entropy-regularized eval      {fmt(v_reg)}",
    f"  augmented, hard max over Gumbel draws   {fmt(v_aug)}",
    f"  augmented, simulated return from s=0    {returns.mean():6.3f} +/- {2 * returns.std() / np.sqrt(n_episodes):.3f}",
    "",
    "Policy: softmax pi(a|s) vs. action frequencies of the augmented agent",
    "  s |  softmax pi(.|s)      |  frequency in augmented MDP",
]
lines += [f"  {i} | {fmt(pi[i])} | {fmt(freq[i])}" for i in range(n_states)]
lines += [
    "",
    "Shocks: -log pi(a|s)/beta vs. mean shock eps(a) when a is chosen",
    "  s |  -log pi(.|s)/beta    |  mean chosen shock",
]
lines += [f"  {i} | {fmt(-np.log(pi[i]) / beta)} | {fmt(mean_shock[i])}" for i in range(n_states)]
lines += [
    "",
    f"  entropy bonus H/beta per state     {fmt(entropy / beta)}",
    f"  mean chosen shock per state        {fmt(shock_total.sum(1) / visits.sum(1))}",
]
print("\n".join(lines))



The three value functions agree up to Monte Carlo error, which stays below 0.01 on values near 10, and the simulated return of the augmented agent from state 0 matches v^\star_\beta(0) within its confidence interval. The augmented agent never randomizes, yet the frequencies of its actions reproduce the softmax probabilities to the third decimal. The last two blocks check the shock identity: the mean shock on a chosen action matches -\beta^{-1}\log\pi_\beta(a\mid s), and its average per state matches the entropy bonus. The cost explains why the Gumbel route stays theoretical. One brute-force sweep evaluates 50{,}000 \times 5 \times 3 maxima, where the log-sum-exp needs 5 \times 3 exponentials, and the brute-force answer is still off in the third digit. ## Control as Inference Perspective

The smooth Bellman optimality equations can also be derived from probabilistic inference perspective. To see this, let's go back to the idea from the previous section in which we introduced an indicator function $I_a(\epsilon)$ to represent whether an action $a$ is optimal given a particular realization of the noise $\epsilon$:

$$ I_a(\epsilon) = \begin{cases} 
   1 & \text{if } a \in \operatorname{argmax}_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ r(s,a') + \epsilon(a') + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{s', \epsilon'}\left[v_\gamma^\star(s',\epsilon')\mid s, a'\right] \right\} \\
   0 & \text{otherwise}
   \end{cases} $$

When we took the expectation over the noise $\epsilon$, we obtained a soft version of this indicator:

$$ \begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}_\epsilon[I_a(\epsilon)] &= \mathbb{P}\left(a \in \operatorname{argmax}_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \left\{ r(s,a') + \epsilon(a') + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{s', \epsilon'}\left[v_\gamma^\star(s',\epsilon')\mid s, \epsilon, a'\right] \right\}\right) \\
&= \frac{\exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a) + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{s'}\left[v_\gamma^\star(s')\mid s, a\right]\right)\right)}{\sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp\left(\beta\left(r(s,a') + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{s'}\left[v_\gamma^\star(s')\mid s, a'\right]\right)\right)}
\end{align*} $$

Given this indicator function, we can "infer" the optimal action in any state. This is the intuition and starting point behind the control as inference perspective in which we directly define a continuous-valued "optimality" variable $O_t$ at each time step $t$. We define the probability of optimality given a state-action pair as:

$$ p(O_t = 1 | s_t, a_t) = \exp(\beta r(s_t, a_t)) $$

Building on this notion of soft optimality, we can formulate the MDP as a probabilistic graphical model. We define the following probabilities:

1. State transition probability: $p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t)$ (given by the MDP dynamics)
2. Prior policy: $p(a_t | s_t)$ (which we'll assume to be uniform for simplicity)
3. Optimality probability: $p(O_t = 1 | s_t, a_t) = \exp(\beta r(s_t, a_t))$

This formulation encodes the idea that more rewarding state-action pairs are more likely to be "optimal," which directly parallels the soft assignment of optimality we obtained by taking the expectation over the Gumbel noise.

The control problem can now be framed as an inference problem: we want to find the posterior distribution over actions given that all time steps are optimal:

$$ p(a_t | s_t, O_{1:T} = 1) $$

where $O_{1:T} = 1$ means $O_t = 1$ for all $t$ from 1 to T. 

### Message Passing 

To solve this inference problem, we can use a technique from probabilistic graphical models called message passing, specifically the belief propagation algorithm. Message passing is a way to efficiently compute marginal distributions in a graphical model by passing local messages between nodes. Messages are passed between nodes in both forward and backward directions. Each message represents a belief about the distribution of a variable, based on the information available to the sending node. After messages have been passed, each node updates its belief about its associated variable by combining all incoming messages.

In our specific case, we're particularly interested in the backward messages, which propagate information about future optimality backwards in time. Let's define the backward message $\beta_t(s_t)$ as:

$$ \beta_t(s_t) = p(O_{t:T} = 1 | s_t) $$

This represents the probability of optimality for all future time steps given the current state. We can compute this recursively:

$$ \beta_t(s_t) = \sum_{a_t} p(a_t | s_t) p(O_t = 1 | s_t, a_t) \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) \beta_{t+1}(s_{t+1}) $$


Taking the log and assuming a uniform prior over actions, we get:

$$ \log \beta_t(s_t) = \log \sum_{a_t} \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) \exp(\beta (r(s_t, a_t) + \gamma v(_{t+1}) + \frac{1}{\beta} \log \beta_{t+1}(s_{t+1}))) $$

If we define the soft value function as $V_t(s_t) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \beta_t(s_t)$, we can rewrite the above equation as:

$$ V_t(s_t) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{a_t} \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) \exp(\beta (r(s_t, a_t) + \gamma V_{t+1}(s_{t+1}))) $$

This is exactly the smooth Bellman equation we derived earlier, but now interpreted as the result of probabilistic inference in a graphical model.

### Deriving the Optimal Policy

The backward message recursion we derived earlier assumes a uniform prior policy $p(a_t | s_t)$. However, our goal is to find an optimal policy. We can extract this optimal policy efficiently by computing the posterior distribution over actions given our backward messages.

Starting from the definition of conditional probability and applying Bayes' rule, we can write:

$$ \begin{align}
p(a_t | s_t, O_{1:T} = 1) &= \frac{p(O_{1:T} = 1 | s_t, a_t) p(a_t | s_t)}{p(O_{1:T} = 1 | s_t)} \\
&\propto p(a_t | s_t) p(O_t = 1 | s_t, a_t) p(O_{t+1:T} = 1 | s_t, a_t) \\
&= p(a_t | s_t) p(O_t = 1 | s_t, a_t) \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) \beta_{t+1}(s_{t+1})
\end{align} $$

Here, $\beta_{t+1}(s_{t+1}) = p(O_{t+1:T} = 1 | s_{t+1})$ is our backward message.

Now, let's substitute our definitions for the optimality probability and the soft value function:

$$ \begin{align}
p(a_t | s_t, O_{1:T} = 1) &\propto p(a_t | s_t) \exp(\beta r(s_t, a_t)) \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) \exp(\beta \gamma V_{t+1}(s_{t+1})) \\
&= p(a_t | s_t) \exp(\beta (r(s_t, a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) V_{t+1}(s_{t+1})))
\end{align} $$

After normalization, and assuming a uniform prior $p(a_t | s_t)$, we obtain the randomized decision rule:

$$ d(a_t | s_t) = \frac{\exp(\beta (r(s_t, a_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t) V_{t+1}(s_{t+1})))}{\sum_{a'_t} \exp(\beta (r(s_t, a'_t) + \gamma \sum_{s_{t+1}} p(s_{t+1} | s_t, a'_t) V_{t+1}(s_{t+1})))} $$

The workhorse behind the theory of regularized MDPs is the Legendre-Fenchel transform, also known as the convex conjugate. For a strongly convex function \Omega: \Delta(\mathcal{A}_s) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, its Legendre-Fenchel transform \Omega^*: \mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{A}_s} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} is defined as:\Omega^*(q(s, \cdot)) = \max_{\pi(\cdot|s) \in \Delta(\mathcal{A}_s)} \langle \pi(\cdot | s), q(s, \cdot) \rangle - \Omega(\pi(\cdot | s))

An important property of this transform is that it has a unique maximizing argument, given by the gradient of \Omega^*:\nabla \Omega^*(q(s, \cdot)) = \arg\max_\pi \langle \pi(\cdot | s), q(s, \cdot) \rangle - \Omega(\pi(\cdot | s))

The gradient is also Lipschitz: if \Omega is \kappa-strongly convex, a change of q moves the maximizing policy by at most 1/\kappa times as much. A more strongly convex regularizer therefore makes the policy less sensitive to errors in q. An important example of a regularizer is the negative entropy, which gives rise to the smooth Bellman equations as we are about to see. Scaled by the temperature 1/\beta, it is (1/\beta)-strongly convex, so the softmax policy moves by at most \beta times the change in q (measuring q in the sup norm and policies in the \ell_1 norm).

How do the regularizer and its convex conjugate alter Bellman evaluation,
policy improvement, and their contraction properties?

With these concepts in place, we can now define the regularized Bellman operators:

Regularized Policy Evaluation Operator (\mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega}):[\mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega} v](s) = \langle q(s,\cdot), \pi(\cdot | s) \rangle - \Omega(\pi(\cdot | s))

Regularized Bellman Optimality Operator (\mathrm{L}_\Omega):[\mathrm{L}_\Omega v](s) = [\max_\pi \mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega} v ](s) = \Omega^*(q(s, \cdot))

It can be shown that the addition of a regularizer in these regularized operators still preserves the contraction properties, and therefore the existence of a solution to the optimality equations and the convergence of successive approximation.

The regularized value function of a stationary policy with decision rule \pi, denoted by v_{\pi,\Omega}, is the unique fixed point of the operator equation:\text{find $v$ such that } \enspace v = \mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega} v

Under the usual assumptions on the discount factor and the boundedness of the reward, the value of a policy can also be found in closed form by solving for \mathbf{v} in the linear system of equations:(\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi) \mathbf{v} =  \mathbf{r}_\pi - \boldsymbol{\Omega}_\pi

where [\boldsymbol{\Omega}_\pi](s) = \Omega(\pi(\cdot|s)) is the vector of regularization terms at each state.

The associated state-action value function q_{\pi,\Omega} is given by:\begin{align*}
q_{\pi,\Omega}(s, a) &= r(s, a) + \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} \gamma p(j|s,a) v_{\pi,\Omega}(j) \\
v_{\pi,\Omega}(s) &= \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \pi(a | s) q_{\pi,\Omega}(s, a) - \Omega(\pi(\cdot | s))
\end{align*}

The regularized optimal value function v^*_\Omega is then the unique fixed point of \mathrm{L}_\Omega in the fixed point equation:\text{find $v$ such that } v = \mathrm{L}_\Omega v

The associated state-action value function q^*_\Omega is given by:\begin{align*}
q^*_\Omega(s, a) &= r(s, a) + \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} \gamma p(j|s,a) v^*_\Omega(j) \\
v^*_\Omega(s) &= \Omega^*(q^*_\Omega(s, \cdot))\end{align*}

An important result in the theory of regularized MDPs is that there exists a unique optimal regularized policy. Specifically, if \pi^*_\Omega is a conserving decision rule (i.e., \pi^*_\Omega = \arg\max_\pi \mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega} v^*_\Omega), then the randomized stationary policy \boldsymbol{\pi} = \mathrm{const}(\pi^*_\Omega) is the unique optimal regularized policy.

In practice, once we have found v^*_\Omega, we can derive the optimal decision rule by taking the gradient of the convex conjugate evaluated at the optimal action-value function:\pi^*(\cdot | s) = \nabla \Omega^*(q^*_\Omega(s, \cdot))

Under this framework, we can recover the smooth Bellman equations by choosing \Omega to be the negative entropy scaled by the temperature 1/\beta, and obtain the softmax policy as the gradient of the convex conjugate. Let’s show this explicitly:

Using the scaled negative entropy regularizer:\Omega(\pi(\cdot|s)) = \frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \pi(a|s) \log \pi(a|s)

The convex conjugate:\Omega^*(q(s, \cdot)) = \frac{1}{\beta}\log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp \big(\beta q(s,a)\big)

Now, let’s write out the regularized Bellman optimality equation:v^*_\Omega(s) = \Omega^*(q^*_\Omega(s, \cdot))

Substituting the expressions for \Omega^* and q^*_\Omega:v^*_\Omega(s) = \frac{1}{\beta}\log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp \left(\beta\Big(r(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v^*_\Omega(j)\Big)\right)

This matches the form of the smooth Bellman equation we derived earlier, with the log-sum-exp operation replacing the max operation of the standard Bellman equation. With \beta = 1, the unscaled negative entropy gives the same equation at unit temperature.

Furthermore, the optimal policy is given by the gradient of \Omega^*:\pi^*(a|s) = \nabla \Omega^*(q^*_\Omega(s, \cdot))_a = \frac{\exp(\beta q^*_\Omega(s,a))}{\sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp(\beta q^*_\Omega(s,a'))}

This is the familiar softmax policy we encountered in the smooth MDP setting.

One identity links the log-sum-exp to the regularized evaluation operator. Let \pi_q(\cdot \mid s) be the softmax of \beta q(s,\cdot). Then\frac{1}{\beta}\log\sum_{a} \exp\big(\beta q(s,a)\big) = \sum_a \pi_q(a \mid s)\, q(s,a) + \frac{1}{\beta} H\big(\pi_q(\cdot \mid s)\big),

which one checks by substituting \log \pi_q(a \mid s) = \beta q(s,a) - \log\sum_{a'} \exp(\beta q(s,a')) into the entropy. Line 6 of 

Algorithm 1 can therefore be written as “form the softmax policy, then add its expected q and its entropy bonus”. Algorithms stated that way are sometimes called entropy-regularized value iteration, but they are smooth value iteration with the log-sum-exp expanded. Policy iteration is different: it evaluates each policy completely before improving it.

Smooth Policy Iteration

Input: MDP (\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, r, p, \gamma), inverse temperature \beta > 0, tolerance \varepsilon > 0

Output: Stochastic policy \pi, \varepsilon-optimal for the entropy-regularized objective, and its value v

Initialize \pi(a|s) \leftarrow 1/|\mathcal{A}_s| for all s \in \mathcal{S}, a \in \mathcal{A}_s (uniform policy)

repeat

\quad Evaluation: solve (\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}_\pi + \frac{1}{\beta}\mathbf{H}_\pi, where [\mathbf{r}_\pi](s) = \sum_a \pi(a|s) r(s,a) and [\mathbf{H}_\pi](s) = -\sum_a \pi(a|s)\log\pi(a|s)

\quad q(s,a) \leftarrow r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a) v(j) for all s \in \mathcal{S}, a \in \mathcal{A}_s

\quad \Delta \leftarrow \max_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \big(\frac{1}{\beta}\log\sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}_s}\exp(\beta q(s,a)) - v(s)\big), the Bellman residual \|\mathrm{L}_\beta v - v\|_\infty

\quad if \Delta < \varepsilon(1-\gamma) then return v, \pi

\quad Improvement: \pi(a|s) \leftarrow \frac{\exp(\beta q(s,a))}{\sum_{a' \in \mathcal{A}_s} \exp(\beta q(s,a'))} for all s \in \mathcal{S}, a \in \mathcal{A}_s

Properties of smooth policy iteration:

Entropy-regularized evaluation. Line 3 is the linear system for the regularized value v_{\pi,\Omega} of 

Regularized Bellman Operators, with the entropy vector \mathbf{H}_\pi on the right-hand side. Replacing the exact solve by a few sweeps of v \leftarrow \mathbf{r}_\pi + \frac{1}{\beta}\mathbf{H}_\pi + \gamma\mathbf{P}_\pi v gives the smooth version of 

Algorithm 4.

Stochastic improvement. Line 7 uses the softmax instead of the argmax. As \beta \to \infty the method recovers standard policy iteration, and lower \beta gives policies with more entropy. As in the hard case, the improvement does not need to be applied in every state for the method to make progress. The policy-iteration loops hidden inside actor-critic methods make use of this.

What the stopping rule guarantees. The residual in line 5 is nonnegative, because v is the regularized value of \pi and the softmax maximizes the regularized one-step objective, so \mathrm{L}_\beta v \ge \mathrm{L}_{\pi,\Omega} v = v. For any v, the triangle inequality and the contraction property give \|v - v^\star_\beta\|_\infty \le \|v - \mathrm{L}_\beta v\|_\infty + \gamma\|v - v^\star_\beta\|_\infty, so\|v - v^\star_\beta\|_\infty \le \frac{\|\mathrm{L}_\beta v - v\|_\infty}{1-\gamma}.

This is the a posteriori bound of 

Theorem 3 written for one step of \mathrm{L}_\beta from v. Since v is the exact regularized value of the current \pi, the test of line 6 guarantees that \pi itself is within \varepsilon of the optimal regularized value in every state. A test on the change of the policy, such as \|\pi - \pi_{\text{old}}\| < \varepsilon, would give no such guarantee.

Convergence. The algorithm converges to the unique optimal regularized value function and policy. Unlike standard policy iteration, it does not terminate after finitely many iterations: the softmax policies form a continuum and the iterates approach the optimum without reaching it, which is why the loop stops on a tolerance. The convergence is fast, since each iteration is a Newton step (

Smooth Policy Iteration Is Newton’s Method).

hierarchy.lvl3: Smooth Policy Iteration Is Newton’s Method
Smooth Policy Iteration Is Newton’s Method

records.content:
The link between policy iteration and the Newton-Kantorovich method (

Newton-Kantorovich and Policy Iteration) is easier to see here than in the hard case, because \mathrm{L}_\beta is differentiable everywhere and there are no ties to worry about. The derivative of the log-sum-exp with respect to its arguments is the softmax, so the Fréchet derivative of \mathrm{L}_\beta at v is\mathrm{L}_\beta'(v) = \gamma \mathbf{P}_{\pi_v}, \qquad \pi_v(a \mid s) = \frac{\exp(\beta q_v(s,a))}{\sum_{a'}\exp(\beta q_v(s,a'))}, \quad q_v(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_j p(j\mid s,a) v(j),

the transition matrix of the softmax policy. A Newton step on v - \mathrm{L}_\beta v = 0 solves(\mathbf{I} - \gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi_v})\, v_{\text{new}} = \mathrm{L}_\beta v - \gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi_v} v.

At the softmax policy the log-sum-exp equals the expected q plus the entropy bonus, \mathrm{L}_\beta v = \mathbf{r}_{\pi_v} + \gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi_v} v + \frac{1}{\beta}\mathbf{H}_{\pi_v}. The right-hand side is therefore \mathbf{r}_{\pi_v} + \frac{1}{\beta}\mathbf{H}_{\pi_v}, and the Newton step is exactly the entropy-regularized evaluation of the softmax policy. Smooth policy iteration is the Newton-Kantorovich method applied to the smooth Bellman equation, without the semismooth machinery that the hard max requires.

Rust (1987) solved his smooth Bellman equation this way. He did not call it policy iteration. He recognized an operator equation, a root-finding problem in a function space, and applied Newton-Kantorovich to it, after a few rounds of successive approximation to get close enough for Newton’s method to converge quickly.

hierarchy.lvl3: Equivalence Between Smooth Bellman Equations and Entropy-Regularized MDPs
Equivalence Between Smooth Bellman Equations and Entropy-Regularized MDPs

records.content:
We have now seen three ways to arrive at the smooth Bellman equation: as a smoothed maximum, from Gumbel noise on the rewards, and as the optimality equation of a regularized MDP. It is worth writing the third one as an optimization problem over policies, because that is the form used by maximum entropy RL. With entropy weight \alpha = 1/\beta, the entropy-regularized MDP is\max_\pi\; \mathbb{E}_\pi \left[ \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t \Big( r(s_t, a_t) + \alpha H\big(\pi(\cdot|s_t)\big) \Big) \right],
\qquad H(\pi(\cdot|s)) = -\sum_a \pi(a|s) \log \pi(a|s).

Since H(\pi(\cdot|s)) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi(\cdot|s)}[-\log \pi(a|s)], the entropy bonus in state s is the average of a per-action term, and the objective equals\mathbb{E}_\pi \left[ \sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t \big( r(s_t, a_t) - \alpha \log \pi(a_t|s_t) \big) \right].

Entropy regularization therefore amounts to paying -\alpha\log\pi(a|s) for taking action a, a cost that is high for actions the policy rarely takes. This is the form that sample-based methods such as soft actor-critic estimate, since it only needs the probability of the action that was taken. In the augmented MDP of 

The Original and Augmented MDPs Side by Side, the same quantity is the expected shock on the chosen action.

The Bellman optimality equation of this problem maximizes, in each state, over the distribution \pi(\cdot|s):v(s) = \max_{\pi(\cdot|s) \in \Delta(\mathcal{A}_s)} \sum_a \pi(a|s) \big( q(s,a) - \alpha \log \pi(a|s) \big),
\qquad q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j|s,a)\, v(j).

The inner problem is the convex conjugate of the scaled negative entropy, which we computed in “Recovering the Smooth Bellman Equations”. A direct check is also short. Writing \pi_q for the softmax of \beta q(s,\cdot), for any distribution \pi,\sum_a \pi(a|s) \big( q(s,a) - \alpha \log \pi(a|s) \big) = \alpha \log\sum_a \exp\big(q(s,a)/\alpha\big) - \alpha\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi(\cdot|s) \,\big\|\, \pi_q(\cdot|s)\big),

and the KL divergence is nonnegative and zero only at \pi = \pi_q. The maximum is the log-sum-exp with \beta = 1/\alpha, attained by the softmax policy. So the value function that solves the smooth Bellman equation is the optimal value of the entropy-regularized MDP, and the softmax policy is its optimal policy. The two descriptions differ only in how they present the problem: as smoothing the Bellman operator, or as trading off reward against policy entropy. Maximum entropy RL algorithms such as soft actor-critic use both, the smooth operator for its differentiability and the regularized objective to explain why the policy should stay stochastic.

What changes in the smooth Bellman equation when the sums over actions become integrals?

So far the action sets were finite. In control problems the action is usually a vector a \in \mathcal{A}_s \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m, a torque, a dose, a flow rate, and the state is often continuous too. The smooth Bellman equation carries over once we fix a reference measure \mu on the actions. For a finite set, \mu is the counting measure and integrals against it are sums. For a box or another bounded subset of \mathbb{R}^m, it is usually the Lebesgue measure da. It can also be a probability measure, a prior policy \pi_0(da \mid s). Continuous states only need the transition kernel to be written as a measure, p(ds' \mid s,a). The table translates the notation of this chapter.

Object

Continuous \mathcal{S} and \mathcal{A}_s \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m

\sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} p(j \mid s,a)\, v(j)

\int_{\mathcal{S}} v(s')\, p(ds' \mid s,a)

Policy average

\sum_a \pi(a \mid s)\, q(s,a)

\int_{\mathcal{A}_s} \pi(a \mid s)\, q(s,a)\, \mu(da)

H(\pi) = -\sum_a \pi(a)\log\pi(a) \ge 0

h_\mu(\pi) = -\int \pi(a)\log\pi(a)\, \mu(da), of either sign

\frac{1}{\beta}\log\sum_a e^{\beta q(s,a)}

\frac{1}{\beta}\log\int_{\mathcal{A}_s} e^{\beta q(s,a)}\, \mu(da)

Gibbs density \pi_\beta(a \mid s) = \exp\big(\beta(q(s,a) - v(s))\big)
