With this notation, the smooth Bellman equation readsv^\star_\beta(s) = \frac{1}{\beta}\log\int_{\mathcal{A}_s} \exp\big(\beta\, q(s,a)\big)\, \mu(da), \qquad
q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \int_{\mathcal{S}} v^\star_\beta(s')\, p(ds' \mid s,a),

and the optimal decision rule is the Gibbs density \pi_\beta(a \mid s) = \exp\big(\beta(q(s,a) - v^\star_\beta(s))\big), which integrates to one against \mu because v^\star_\beta(s) is the log-normalizer. The contraction argument of the smooth value iteration section uses only monotonicity and the constant shift, and both hold for the integral. The operator is therefore a \gamma-contraction in the sup norm, provided the integral is finite. With bounded rewards, it is finite when \mu(\mathcal{A}_s) < \infty, for example a box of actions under the Lebesgue measure or any prior policy.

The variational form. The regularized reading also carries over. For any density \nu with respect to \mu, write Z(s) = \int e^{\beta q(s,a)}\mu(da). Then\int \nu(a)\, q(s,a)\, \mu(da) - \frac{1}{\beta}\int \nu(a) \log \nu(a)\, \mu(da)
= \frac{1}{\beta}\log Z(s) - \frac{1}{\beta}\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\nu \,\big\|\, \pi_\beta(\cdot \mid s)\big),

as one checks by substituting \log \pi_\beta = \beta q - \log Z. The left side is the regularized objective of 

Regularized Bellman Operators with \Omega(\nu) = \frac{1}{\beta}\int \nu\log\nu\, d\mu. Since the KL divergence is nonnegative and vanishes only at \nu = \pi_\beta, the maximum over \nu is the log-integral and the maximizer is the Gibbs density. This is the continuous version of the Legendre-Fenchel pair (negative entropy, log-sum-exp), and in statistical physics it is called the Gibbs variational principle.

The reference measure matters. With a finite action set, relabeling the actions changes nothing. With continuous actions, the entropy depends on \mu, and that dependence shows up in three ways.

Prior policies give KL regularization. If \mu = \pi_0(\cdot \mid s) is a probability measure, then \int \nu \log \nu\, d\mu = \mathrm{KL}(\nu \,\|\, \pi_0) and the problem is KL-regularized RL: the agent is penalized for moving away from \pi_0. In the finite case, the uniform prior gives \mathrm{KL}(\nu\,\|\,\text{uniform}) = \log\lvert\mathcal{A}_s\rvert - H(\nu), so entropy and KL regularization differ by a constant per state and have the same optimal policy.

Differential entropy has no floor. Under the Lebesgue measure, h(\pi) = -\int \pi \log \pi\, da is the differential entropy, which is negative for concentrated densities: a Gaussian with variance \sigma^2 in one dimension has h = \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e \sigma^2), negative once \sigma^2 < 1/(2\pi e). It also depends on the units of the action. Rescaling a \mapsto c\,a in \mathbb{R}^m adds m \log\lvert c\rvert to h. That only shifts all values by a constant and leaves the policy unchanged, but a nonlinear change of variables, say from a torque to its logarithm, changes the optimal policy.

Unbounded action sets need care. If \mathcal{A}_s = \mathbb{R}^m with the Lebesgue measure and bounded rewards, the integral diverges and the smooth Bellman equation has no solution. The remedies are a bounded action set (soft actor-critic squashes its Gaussian samples through a \tanh into a box), a prior policy as reference measure, or rewards that decrease fast enough in \lVert a\rVert, such as a quadratic action cost.

How far from the hard maximum. The finite-action bound \max_a q \le \frac{1}{\beta}\log\sum_a e^{\beta q} \le \max_a q + \frac{\log\lvert\mathcal{A}\rvert}{\beta} keeps only its upper half: \frac{1}{\beta}\log\int e^{\beta q}\,d\mu \le \sup_a q(s,a) + \frac{\log \mu(\mathcal{A}_s)}{\beta}, which gives v^\star_\beta \le v^*_\gamma + \frac{\log \mu(\mathcal{A})}{\beta(1-\gamma)} when \mu(\mathcal{A}_s) \le \mu(\mathcal{A}) for all s. The lower bound fails, because a set of actions of small volume contributes little to the integral even if it contains the maximizer. The right tool is Laplace’s method. If q(s,\cdot) is twice differentiable with a unique maximizer a^\star(s) in the interior of \mathcal{A}_s, and \mathbf{H}(s) = -\nabla_a^2 q(s, a^\star(s)) is positive definite, then under the Lebesgue measure\frac{1}{\beta}\log\int_{\mathcal{A}_s} e^{\beta q(s,a)}\, da
= q(s,a^\star(s)) + \frac{m}{2\beta}\log\frac{2\pi}{\beta} - \frac{1}{2\beta}\log\det \mathbf{H}(s) + o(1/\beta).

The gap to the hard maximum shrinks like \frac{m\log\beta}{2\beta}, slightly slower than the 1/\beta rate of the finite case, and the Gibbs density concentrates around a^\star(s) like a Gaussian with covariance (\beta\mathbf{H}(s))^{-1}.

Quadratic q and linear-quadratic control. If q(s,a) = q_0(s) - \frac{1}{2}(a - \bar a(s))^\top \mathbf{H}(s)(a - \bar a(s)) is exactly quadratic in a with \mathbf{H}(s) \succ 0, Laplace’s formula is exact. The Gibbs policy is the Gaussian \mathcal{N}\big(\bar a(s), (\beta\mathbf{H}(s))^{-1}\big) and v^\star_\beta(s) = q_0(s) + \frac{1}{2\beta}\log\det\big(2\pi(\beta\mathbf{H}(s))^{-1}\big). Linear-quadratic problems are of this kind. With dynamics x' = Ax + Bu + w and reward -\frac{1}{2}x^\top Q x - \frac{1}{2}u^\top R u, a quadratic value -\frac{1}{2}x^\top P x + c makes q quadratic in u with \mathbf{H} = R + \gamma B^\top P B, which does not depend on x. The log-determinant term is then a constant, so P solves the same discounted Riccati equation as without regularization. The entropy-regularized LQR policy is Gaussian, with mean the usual linear feedback -\gamma(R + \gamma B^\top P B)^{-1} B^\top P A\, x and covariance \big(\beta(R + \gamma B^\top P B)\big)^{-1}. The regularization adds exploration noise around the LQR controller, more of it along the directions where the cost is flat, and does not change the gain.

Gumbel shocks over a continuum. The augmented-MDP construction needs one shock per action. Over a continuum of actions we cannot attach independent shocks to every point, since the supremum of uncountably many independent Gumbel variables is infinite. The replacement is a Gumbel process 

Maddison et al. (2014): a random function G on \mathcal{A}_s such that, for every measurable set B, the maximum \max_{a \in B} G(a) is Gumbel with location \log\mu(B) and unit scale, independently over disjoint sets. For such a process, \max_a\{\beta q(s,a) + G(a)\} is Gumbel with location \log\int e^{\beta q(s,a)}\mu(da), and its argmax has the Gibbs density. With \epsilon_t = G_t/\beta the derivation of 

Gumbel Noise on the Rewards goes through with a random function in place of a random vector, and 

Figure 1 still describes the model. It is even less a computational object than in the finite case. 

Maddison et al. (2014) use it to build an exact sampler, A* sampling, but the algorithms for continuous control, soft actor-critic among them, work with the Gibbs density directly and approximate it with a parametric policy.

hierarchy.lvl2: Rust’s Bus Engines and Inverse Reinforcement Learning
Rust’s Bus Engines and Inverse Reinforcement Learning

records.content:
What can we learn about a decision maker’s goals from records of what they did?

Rust’s 1987 paper is worth reading for three reasons: it contains the smooth Bellman equation, it poses what is now called inverse reinforcement learning, and it solves that problem with a bilevel method that relies on implicit differentiation, a tool that became popular in machine learning three decades later for hyperparameter optimization.

The problem. Harold Zurcher was the superintendent of maintenance at the Madison Metropolitan bus company. Rust had his maintenance records: for each bus, the odometer reading each month, and the months in which Zurcher replaced the engine. Replacing an engine is expensive, while keeping an old engine running costs more and more as the mileage grows. The question was how Zurcher decided when to replace. Rust is a structural econometrician. Structural econometrics does not stop at predicting behavior; it posits a mechanism that generates it, here a decision maker solving an MDP, and fits the parameters of that mechanism to data. The fitted mechanism can then answer questions the data alone cannot, such as how behavior would change if the price of an engine changed.

The model. The state s is the mileage since the last replacement, discretized into bins. Each month there are two actions, keep (a=0) or replace (a=1). Keeping costs c(s;\theta), increasing in s; replacing costs a fixed amount RC and resets the mileage. With parameters \theta collecting RC and those of c, the reward is r_\theta(s,0) = -c(s;\theta) and r_\theta(s,1) = -RC - c(0;\theta), and the mileage transitions are estimated directly from the odometer data. The data contradict any deterministic policy: two buses with the same mileage are sometimes treated differently. Rust’s answer was the Gumbel model of 

Gumbel Noise on the Rewards. Zurcher sees, in addition to s, a shock \epsilon(a) for each action that the econometrician does not see, and acts optimally given both. Integrating out the shocks gives the smooth Bellman equation and the softmax choice probabilitiesv_\theta = \mathrm{L}_{\beta,\theta}\, v_\theta, \qquad \pi_\theta(a \mid s) = \frac{\exp(\beta q_\theta(s,a))}{\sum_{a'}\exp(\beta q_\theta(s,a'))}.

This is the second, deeper reason Rust used these equations. Besides being smooth, they follow from the random-utility models of 

McFadden (1974), the standard statistical basis of discrete choice in econometrics, in the same way that least squares follows from assuming Gaussian noise. In machine learning terms, McFadden’s conditional logit is multiclass logistic regression with a structural interpretation.

The estimator. Given observed pairs (s_t, a_t), maximize the log-likelihood \ell(\theta) = \sum_t \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t). Every evaluation of \ell requires solving the smooth Bellman equation for the current \theta, so the problem is bilevel: an outer maximization over \theta around an inner fixed-point problem. Rust called his algorithm the nested fixed point (NFXP) algorithm. The gradient of \ell needs \partial v_\theta / \partial\theta, which the implicit function theorem provides without differentiating through the iterations of the inner solver. Differentiating v_\theta = \mathrm{L}_{\beta,\theta} v_\theta and using the derivative of \mathrm{L}_\beta from 

Smooth Policy Iteration Is Newton’s Method,\frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial \theta} = (\mathbf{I} - \gamma\mathbf{P}_{\pi_\theta})^{-1}\, \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_{\pi_\theta}}{\partial\theta}, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_{\pi_\theta}}{\partial\theta}(s) = \sum_a \pi_\theta(a\mid s)\, \frac{\partial r_\theta(s,a)}{\partial \theta}.

The matrix to invert is the one of policy evaluation, already factored by the Newton steps of the inner solver. For rewards linear in the parameters, r_\theta(s,a) = \theta^\top\phi(s,a), this derivative is the vector of expected discounted feature counts under the softmax policy, the quantity that 

Ziebart et al. (2008) matches to the empirical feature counts. The score of one observation is then\nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta(a\mid s) = \beta\Big(\nabla_\theta q_\theta(s,a) - \sum_{a'}\pi_\theta(a'\mid s)\,\nabla_\theta q_\theta(s,a')\Big), \qquad \nabla_\theta q_\theta(s,a) = \nabla_\theta r_\theta(s,a) + \gamma\sum_j p(j\mid s,a)\,\frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial \theta}(j).

Nested Fixed Point (NFXP) Maximum Likelihood

Input: Observed state-action pairs \{(s_t, a_t)\}, transition model p, discount \gamma, scale \beta, initial parameters \theta_0Output: Estimated reward parameters \hat\theta

repeat for k = 0, 1, \ldots

(Inner problem) Solve v = \mathrm{L}_{\beta,\theta_k} v: a few sweeps of 

Algorithm 1, then Newton steps (

Smooth Policy Iteration Is Newton’s Method), warm-started from the previous v

Compute \pi_{\theta_k}, q_{\theta_k} and \partial v_{\theta_k}/\partial\theta by the implicit-function formula above

Compute \nabla \ell(\theta_k) = \sum_t \nabla_\theta\log\pi_{\theta_k}(a_t\mid s_t)

(Outer step) \theta_{k+1} \leftarrow \theta_k + H_k^{-1}\nabla\ell(\theta_k), with H_k a positive definite curvature estimate (Rust used the outer product of the scores, the BHHH method)

until \|\nabla\ell(\theta_k)\| is small

return \hat\theta = \theta_k

What the model assumes. The setup is a strong one, and naming its assumptions explains why inverse RL is hard in general.

Rationality. The decision maker is assumed to solve the MDP exactly. People do not; the literature on bounded rationality studies how they fall short, and Rust himself has written skeptically about whether people follow Bellman’s principle of optimality. The assumption is still a useful starting point, in the same way a linear model is.

Observability. Rust observes the state and the action. In many applications one or both are missing. With logged prices, for instance, an unchanged price may be a decision to keep it or simply the absence of a decision, and the action itself must be inferred, which makes the problem partially observable.

Identifiability. Many reward functions explain the same behavior equally well. With hard maxima, a constant reward makes every policy optimal, and adding a shaping term \gamma\Phi(s') - \Phi(s) to any reward leaves the optimal policies unchanged 

Ng et al. (1999). The map from rewards to behavior is many-to-one, so the data can at best single out a set of candidate rewards. Structural econometrics restores identification by restricting the reward to a parametric family, fixing the discount factor and the scale \beta, and normalizing one action’s reward. Whether such restrictions are acceptable depends on the goal: predicting what Zurcher would do under new engine prices is a weaker demand than recovering what he “really” wanted.

Entropy regularization replaces hard action selection with a smooth conjugate
operator and produces a stochastic optimal policy. Gumbel perturbations,
log-sum-exp Bellman updates, and regularized policy iteration describe the same
construction from probabilistic, variational, and algorithmic viewpoints.
Drawn as graphical models, the original MDP and the Gumbel-augmented MDP differ
by one shock node per time step, and integrating it out recovers the softmax
policy; the expected shock on the chosen action is the entropy bonus. The same
equations hold for continuous actions once a reference measure is fixed, with
integrals in place of sums and a Gibbs density in place of the softmax, and the
choice of that measure becomes part of the model.
Smooth policy iteration is Newton’s method on the smooth Bellman equation, and
Rust’s nested fixed-point estimator uses the same derivative to recover reward
parameters from observed behavior.

The same log-sum-exp form appears over whole trajectories in continuous time.


Path-integral stochastic control examines
systems driven by Gaussian disturbances whose Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation
becomes linear under a logarithmic transformation, so that optimal feedback can
be estimated from weighted trajectories.

Smoothness changes the operator but does not remove the need to represent its
unknown value function. How can an infinite-dimensional functional equation be
reduced to finitely many coefficients and test conditions? 

Weighted-residual
methods provide the general approximation
machinery.

Temperature limit

What happens to a softmax policy as the entropy temperature \alpha approaches zero, assuming a unique maximizing action?

Solution to 

Exercise 1

Its probability concentrates on the maximizing action, so the soft policy approaches the ordinary greedy deterministic policy.

Smooth maximum

Why is log-sum-exp often easier to optimize through than a hard maximum?

Solution to 

Exercise 2

Log-sum-exp is differentiable and blends information from all actions. A hard maximum is nondifferentiable at ties and passes local gradient information only through selected maximizers.

Entropy as an expected shock

In the augmented MDP the agent never randomizes. Where does the entropy bonus of the original MDP come from in its rewards?

Solution to 

Exercise 3

From the shocks on the actions it picks. Given that action a wins, its shock has mean -\frac{1}{\beta}\log\pi_\beta(a\mid s), which is large for actions that rarely win. Averaging over the winning action gives \frac{1}{\beta}H(\pi_\beta(\cdot\mid s)), the entropy bonus.

Units of a continuous action

A one-dimensional action is measured in newton-metres, and you switch to kilonewton-metres. What happens to the entropy-regularized optimal value and policy under the Lebesgue reference measure? What if you switch to the logarithm of the torque?

Solution to 

Exercise 4

Dividing the action by 1000 subtracts \log 1000 from the differential entropy of every density, so every value shifts by the constant -\frac{\log 1000}{\beta(1-\gamma)} and the policy, mapped back to newton-metres, is unchanged. A logarithmic change of variables is nonlinear: the Lebesgue measure in the new variable is a different measure on torques, so the regularizer and the optimal policy both change.

DDPG and TD3 address continuous actions by learning a deterministic policy that amortizes the \arg\max_a q(s,a) operation. But deterministic policies have a fundamental limitation: they require external exploration noise (Gaussian perturbations in TD3) and can converge to suboptimal deterministic behaviors without adequate coverage of the state-action space.

Gradient estimators make stochastic actors trainable, while regularized dynamic
programming specifies the stochastic policy they should approach. Can these
pieces avoid both the continuous-action integral in the soft Bellman equation
and the repeated optimization of a hard maximum?

Entropy-regularized dynamic programming presents an alternative: MDPs where the agent maximizes expected return plus a bonus for policy randomness. This yields stochastic policies with exploration built into the objective itself. The smooth Bellman operator replaces the hard max with a soft-max:v^*(s) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \exp\left(\beta \cdot q^*(s,a)\right)

where \beta = 1/\alpha is the inverse temperature and \alpha is the entropy regularization weight. For finite action spaces, this log-sum-exp is easy to compute. But for continuous actions \mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^m, the sum becomes an integral:v^*(s) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \int_{\mathcal{A}} \exp\left(\beta \cdot q^*(s,a)\right) da

This integral is intractable. We face an infinite-dimensional sum over the continuous action space. The very smoothness that gives us stochastic policies creates a new computational barrier, distinct from but analogous to the \arg\max problem in standard FQI.

From Intractable Integral to Tractable Expectation

records.content:
How can the continuous-action log-partition integral be rewritten as an
expectation under the policy being learned?

Soft actor-critic (SAC) 

Haarnoja et al., 2018

Haarnoja et al., 2018 exploits an equivalence between the intractable integral and an expectation. The optimal policy under entropy regularization is the Boltzmann distribution \pi^*(a|s) \propto \exp(\beta \cdot q^*(s,a)). Under this policy, the soft value function becomes:v^*(s) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi^*(\cdot|s)}\left[q^*(s,a) - \alpha \log \pi^*(a|s)\right]

This converts the intractable integral into an expectation we can estimate by sampling. SAC learns a parametric policy \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} that approximates the Boltzmann distribution, enabling fast action selection via a single forward pass. For bootstrap targets, SAC samples \tilde{a}' \sim \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\cdot|s') and computes:y = r + \gamma \left[\min_{j=1,2} q^j_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\text{target}}}(s', \tilde{a}') - \alpha \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\tilde{a}'|s')\right]

The minimum over twin Q-networks applies the clipped double-Q trick from TD3. Exploration comes from the policy’s stochasticity rather than external noise.

hierarchy.lvl2: Learning the Policy: Matching the Boltzmann Distribution
Learning the Policy: Matching the Boltzmann Distribution

records.content:
Which divergence or equivalent stochastic objective moves the actor toward the
Boltzmann distribution induced by the soft Q-function?

The Q-network update assumes a policy \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} that approximates the Boltzmann distribution \pi^*(a|s) \propto \exp(\beta \cdot q^*(s,a)). Training such a policy presents a problem: the Boltzmann distribution requires the partition function Z(s) = \int_{\mathcal{A}} \exp(\beta \cdot q(s,a))da, the very integral we are trying to avoid. SAC sidesteps this by minimizing the KL divergence from the policy to the (unnormalized) Boltzmann distribution:\min_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathcal{D}}\left[D_{KL}\left(\pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\cdot|s) \| \frac{\exp(\beta \cdot q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(s,\cdot))}{Z_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(s)}\right)\right]

Since \log Z_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(s) does not depend on \boldsymbol{\phi}, this reduces to:\min_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\cdot|s)}\left[\alpha \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(a|s) - q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(s,a)\right]

This pushes probability toward high Q-value actions while the \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} term penalizes concentrating probability mass, maintaining entropy. The entropy bonus comes from the KL divergence structure rather than from an explicit regularization term.

To estimate gradients of this objective, we face a technical problem: the policy parameters \boldsymbol{\phi} appear in the sampling distribution \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}, making \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}[\cdot] difficult to compute. SAC uses a Gaussian policy \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(a|s) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s), \sigma_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s)^2) with the reparameterization trick. Express samples as a deterministic function of parameters and independent noise:a = f_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s, \epsilon) = \mu_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s) + \sigma_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s) \odot \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)

This moves \boldsymbol{\phi} out of the sampling distribution and into the integrand:\min_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathcal{D}}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)}\left[\alpha \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(f_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s,\epsilon)|s) - q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(s,f_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s,\epsilon))\right]

We can now differentiate through f_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} and the Q-network, as DDPG differentiates through a deterministic policy. SAC extends this by sampling noise \epsilon at each gradient step rather than outputting a single deterministic action.

Soft Actor-Critic (SAC)

Input: MDP (S, \mathcal{A}, P, R, \gamma), twin Q-networks q^1(s,a; \boldsymbol{\theta}^1), q^2(s,a; \boldsymbol{\theta}^2), policy \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}, learning rates \alpha_q, \alpha_\pi, replay buffer capacity B, mini-batch size b, EMA rate \tau, entropy weight \alpha

Output: Q-function parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}^1, \boldsymbol{\theta}^2, policy parameters \boldsymbol{\phi}

Initialize \boldsymbol{\theta}^1_0, \boldsymbol{\theta}^2_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}_0 randomly

\boldsymbol{\theta}^1_{\text{target}} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}^1_0, \boldsymbol{\theta}^2_{\text{target}} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}^2_0

Initialize replay buffer \mathcal{B} with capacity B

t \leftarrow 0

while training do

Observe state s

Sample action: a \sim \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_t}(\cdot|s) \quad // Stochastic policy provides exploration

Execute a, observe reward r and next state s'

Store (s,a,r,s') in \mathcal{B}, replacing oldest if full

Sample mini-batch \{(s_i,a_i,r_i,s_i')\}_{i=1}^b from \mathcal{B}

// Update Q-networks: bootstrap using single-sample soft value estimate

for each s'_i do sample \tilde{a}'_i \sim \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_t}(\cdot|s'_i)

y_i \leftarrow r_i + \gamma \left[\min(q^1(s'_i, \tilde{a}'_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}^1_{\text{target}}), q^2(s'_i, \tilde{a}'_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}^2_{\text{target}})) - \alpha \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_t}(\tilde{a}'_i|s'_i)\right]

\boldsymbol{\theta}^1_{t+1} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}^1_t - \alpha_q \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^b(q^1(s_i,a_i;\boldsymbol{\theta}^1_t) - y_i)^2

\boldsymbol{\theta}^2_{t+1} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}^2_t - \alpha_q \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^b(q^2(s_i,a_i;\boldsymbol{\theta}^2_t) - y_i)^2

// Update policy: minimize KL to Boltzmann distribution

for each s_i do sample \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I) and compute \hat{a}_i = f_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_t}(s_i, \epsilon_i) \quad // Reparameterization

\boldsymbol{\phi}_{t+1} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\phi}_t - \alpha_\pi \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^b \left[\alpha \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_t}(\hat{a}_i|s_i) - \min_{j=1,2} q^j(s_i, \hat{a}_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}^j_{t+1})\right]

// EMA update for Q-network targets

\boldsymbol{\theta}^1_{\text{target}} \leftarrow \tau \boldsymbol{\theta}^1_{t+1} + (1-\tau)\boldsymbol{\theta}^1_{\text{target}}

\boldsymbol{\theta}^2_{\text{target}} \leftarrow \tau \boldsymbol{\theta}^2_{t+1} + (1-\tau)\boldsymbol{\theta}^2_{\text{target}}

t \leftarrow t + 1

return \boldsymbol{\theta}^1_t, \boldsymbol{\theta}^2_t, \boldsymbol{\phi}_t

The algorithm interleaves three updates. The Q-networks (lines 7-10) follow fitted Q-iteration with the soft Bellman target: sample a next action \tilde{a}'_i from the current policy, compute the entropy-adjusted target y_i = r_i + \gamma[\min_j q^j_{\text{target}}(s'_i, \tilde{a}'_i) - \alpha \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\tilde{a}'_i|s'_i)], and minimize squared error. The minimum over twin Q-networks mitigates overestimation as in TD3. The policy (lines 12-13) updates to match the Boltzmann distribution induced by the current Q-function, using the reparameterization trick for gradient estimation. Target networks update via EMA (lines 15-16) to stabilize training.

The stochastic policy serves the same amortization purpose as in DDPG and TD3: it replaces the intractable \arg\max operation with a fast network forward pass. SAC’s entropy regularization produces exploration through the policy’s inherent stochasticity rather than external noise. This makes SAC more robust to hyperparameters and eliminates the need to tune exploration schedules.

Can a soft-optimal policy be trained by enforcing multi-step consistency
directly rather than constructing one-step Bellman targets?

DDPG, TD3, and SAC all follow the same solution template from fitted Q-iteration: compute Bellman targets using the current Q-function, fit the Q-function to those targets, repeat. This is successive approximation, the function iteration approach v_{k+1} = \Proj \Bellman v_k from the 

projection methods chapter.

Path Consistency Learning (PCL) 

Nachum et al., 2017 solves the Bellman equation differently. Instead of iterating the operator, it directly minimizes a residual. This is the least-squares approach from projection methods: solve \Residual(v) = 0 by minimizing \|\Residual(v)\|^2. The method exploits special structure (smooth Bellman operators under deterministic dynamics) that conventional methods cannot leverage.

Consider the Q-function Bellman equation from 

entropy-regularized dynamic programming. Under general stochastic dynamics, it involves an expectation over next states:q^*(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{s'}[v^*(s')]

Suppose the dynamics are deterministic: s' = f(s,a). The next state is uniquely determined, so the expectation disappears:q^*(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma v^*(f(s,a))

The value function relates to Q-functions through the soft-max:v^*(s) = \alpha \log \int_{\mathcal{A}} \exp(q^*(s,a)/\alpha) da

Contrast two cases: general policies versus the optimal Boltzmann policy.

For general policies, the value equals an expectation:v^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi(\cdot|s)}[q^\pi(s,a) - \alpha \log \pi(a|s)]

This is an average. For a single observed action a, we have:q^\pi(s,a) - \alpha\log\pi(a|s) = v^\pi(s) + \varepsilon(s,a)

where \varepsilon(s,a) is sampling error with \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi}[\varepsilon(s,a)] = 0. Individual actions give noisy estimates that fluctuate around the mean.

For the optimal policy under entropy regularization, the Boltzmann structure produces an exact pointwise identity. The optimal policy is:\pi^*(a|s) = \frac{\exp(q^*(s,a)/\alpha)}{\exp(v^*(s)/\alpha)}

Taking logarithms and rearranging:v^*(s) = q^*(s,a) - \alpha \log \pi^*(a|s) \quad \text{for all } a

This holds exactly for every action a, not just in expectation. There is no sampling error. The advantage q^*(s,a) - v^*(s) is encoded in the log-probability: suboptimal actions have low q^*(s,a) but also large -\alpha\log\pi^*(a|s) (low probability means large negative log-probability), and these terms balance exactly to give v^*(s).

Now take a trajectory segment (s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1, \ldots, s_d) where each transition follows the deterministic dynamics s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t). Start with q^*(s_0, a_0) = r_0 + \gamma v^*(s_1) and use equation 

(15) to substitute v^*(s_1) = q^*(s_1,a_1) - \alpha\log\pi^*(a_1|s_1) exactly:q^*(s_0, a_0) = r_0 + \gamma[q^*(s_1,a_1) - \alpha\log\pi^*(a_1|s_1)]

Substitute q^*(s_1,a_1) = r_1 + \gamma v^*(s_2):q^*(s_0, a_0) = r_0 + \gamma r_1 - \gamma\alpha\log\pi^*(a_1|s_1) + \gamma^2 v^*(s_2)

Continue this telescoping for d steps. Each substitution is exact:q^*(s_0, a_0) = \sum_{t=0}^{d-1} \gamma^t r_t - \alpha \sum_{t=1}^{d-1} \gamma^t \log\pi^*(a_t|s_t) + \gamma^d v^*(s_d)

Apply equation 

(15) once more to get v^*(s_0) = q^*(s_0,a_0) - \alpha\log\pi^*(a_0|s_0):v^*(s_0) = \sum_{t=0}^{d-1} \gamma^t [r_t - \alpha\log\pi^*(a_t|s_t)] + \gamma^d v^*(s_d)

Rearranging gives the path consistency residual:R(s_0:s_d; \pi^*, v^*) = v^*(s_0) - \gamma^d v^*(s_d) - \sum_{t=0}^{d-1} \gamma^t[r_t - \alpha\log\pi^*(a_t|s_t)] = 0

The telescoping produces an exact identity: R = 0 for every action sequence, not just in expectation. The behavior policy never appears because the constraint holds as a deterministic identity for any observed (s_0, a_0, \ldots, s_d). This enables off-policy learning without importance sampling.

Contrasting General Policies and Optimal Boltzmann Policies

The distinction between equations 

(12) and 

(15) is subtle but crucial.

For general policies (equation 

(12)), the value is an average over actions sampled from the policy. Individual actions give noisy estimates: if we draw a \sim \pi(\cdot|s), then q^\pi(s,a) - \alpha\log\pi(a|s) = v^\pi(s) + \varepsilon where \varepsilon is a zero-mean random variable. We need to average many samples to estimate v^\pi(s) accurately. Multi-step telescoping would accumulate these sampling errors \varepsilon_0, \varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_{d-1}, producing noisy residuals even at the true solution. Off-policy learning would require importance weights to correct for using actions from a different behavior policy.

For the optimal entropy-regularized policy (equation 

(15)), the Boltzmann structure collapses the expectation to a pointwise identity. The relationship v^*(s) = q^*(s,a) - \alpha\log\pi^*(a|s) holds exactly for every action a, optimal or not. A suboptimal action has low q^*(s,a) (low expected return) and low \pi^*(a|s) (low probability), making -\alpha\log\pi^*(a|s) large. These terms balance precisely to give v^*(s). No sampling error exists. The telescoping is exact, producing a residual that equals zero for every action sequence, not just in expectation. Off-policy learning works because the constraint holds as a deterministic identity for any observed path.

This property is unique to soft-max operators. For hard-max, v^*(s) = \max_a q^*(s,a) holds only when a is optimal. Suboptimal actions satisfy v^*(s) > q^*(s,a), an inequality that cannot be used to construct a residual.

records.content: PCL’s two structural requirements (deterministic dynamics and entropy regularization) are not arbitrary design choices. Each addresses a fundamental theoretical issue.

records.content:
Under stochastic dynamics, the Q-function Bellman equation has an expectation over next states:q^*(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \mathbb{E}_{s' \sim p(\cdot|s,a)}[v^*(s')]

The exact relationship 

(15) still holds, so we can write the path consistency constraint. But now consider what PCL minimizes: the squared residual \mathbb{E}[R^2] whereR = v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s_0) - \gamma^d v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s_d) - \sum_{t=0}^{d-1} \gamma^t[r_t - \alpha\log\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(a_t|s_t)]

At the true optimum (v^*, \pi^*), the constraint is \mathbb{E}[R] = 0, which implies (\mathbb{E}[R])^2 = 0. But PCL minimizes \mathbb{E}[R^2], and by Jensen’s inequality:\mathbb{E}[R^2] \geq (\mathbb{E}[R])^2

with equality only when R has zero variance. Under stochastic dynamics, even at optimality, individual trajectory residuals are random variables with mean zero but positive variance (due to transition noise). Minimizing \mathbb{E}[R^2] to zero would require driving \text{Var}(R) \to 0, which is impossible and pushes the solution away from the true optimum.

This is Baird’s double sampling problem 

Baird, 1995. To get an unbiased gradient of (\mathbb{E}[R])^2, we need:\nabla (\mathbb{E}[R])^2 = 2\mathbb{E}[R] \cdot \nabla \mathbb{E}[R] = 2\mathbb{E}[R] \cdot \mathbb{E}[\nabla R]

This requires two independent samples of the next state from the same (s,a) pair: one for estimating \mathbb{E}[R] and one for \mathbb{E}[\nabla R]. With a simulator, this is possible. With real trajectories, it is not.

Under deterministic dynamics, R is deterministic (no transition noise), so \mathbb{E}[R^2] = (\mathbb{E}[R])^2 and Jensen’s inequality holds with equality. Minimizing the squared residual is equivalent to solving \mathbb{E}[R] = 0.

records.content:
Attempt the same path consistency derivation with the hard-max Bellman operator. Under deterministic dynamics, the Q-function satisfies:q^*(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma v^*(f(s,a))

where v^*(s) = \max_{a'} q^*(s,a') and the optimal policy is \pi^*(s) = \arg\max_a q^*(s,a) (deterministic).

Now try to relate v^*(s) to an arbitrary observed action a. For the optimal action a^* \in \arg\max_{a'} q^*(s,a'), we have:v^*(s) = q^*(s,a^*)

But for a suboptimal action a \ne a^*:v^*(s) = \max_{a'} q^*(s,a') > q^*(s,a)

This is an inequality, not an equation. There is no formula expressing v^*(s) in terms of q^*(s,a) for suboptimal actions.

Attempt the multi-step telescoping. Start with q^*(s_0, a_0) = r_0 + \gamma v^*(s_1). To continue, we need to express v^*(s_1) using the observed action a_1. But we only have:v^*(s_1) \geq q^*(s_1, a_1)

with equality only if a_1 happens to be optimal at s_1. We cannot substitute this into the Q-function equation to get an exact telescoping. The derivation breaks at the first step.

Compare this to the soft-max case. The Boltzmann structure gives equation 

(15): v^*(s) = q^*(s,a) - \alpha\log\pi^*(a|s) for all actions a. The log-probability term compensates exactly for suboptimality: low-probability actions have large -\alpha\log\pi^*(a|s), which adds to the low q^*(s,a) to recover v^*(s). This enables exact substitution at every step:v^*(s_1) = q^*(s_1, a_1) - \alpha\log\pi^*(a_1|s_1) \quad \text{(exact for any } a_1\text{)}

The telescoping proceeds without inequalities or restrictions on which actions were chosen. Multi-step hard-max Q-learning lacks theoretical justification for off-policy data because when we observe a trajectory with suboptimal actions, we cannot write an exact path consistency constraint.

Both requirements are structural:

Requirement

Addresses

Deterministic dynamics

Double sampling bias: ensures \mathbb{E}[R^2] = (\mathbb{E}[R])^2

Entropy regularization

All-action consistency (equation 

(15))

Without deterministic dynamics, residual minimization is biased. Without entropy regularization, the constraint holds only for optimal actions.

Equation 

(20) provides a constraint that the optimal (v^*, \pi^*) must satisfy: the residual equals zero for every observed path. For parametric approximations (v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}, \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) that are not yet optimal, the residual is nonzero:R(s_0:s_d; \boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\phi}) = v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s_0) - \gamma^d v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s_d) - \sum_{t=0}^{d-1} \gamma^t[r_t - \alpha \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(a_t|s_t)]

PCL minimizes the squared residual over observed path segments:\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\phi}} \sum_{\text{segments}} \frac{1}{2} R(s_i:s_{i+d}; \boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\phi})^2

This is the least-squares residual approach from the 

projection methods chapter. SAC computes targets y_i and fits to them (successive approximation). PCL directly minimizes the residual without computing targets or performing a separate fitting step.

Gradient descent gives:\begin{align}
\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k+1} &= \boldsymbol{\theta}_k + \eta_\pi \sum_i R_i \cdot \alpha \sum_{t=0}^{d-1} \gamma^t \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_k}(a_{i+t}|s_{i+t}) \\
\boldsymbol{\phi}_{k+1} &= \boldsymbol{\phi}_k - \eta_v \sum_i R_i \left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_k}(s_i) - \gamma^d \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_k}(s_{i+d})\right]
\end{align}

where R_i = R(s_i:s_{i+d}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_k, \boldsymbol{\phi}_k). Large residuals drive larger updates.

Path Consistency Learning (PCL)

Input: MDP with deterministic dynamics s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t), policy \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}, value function v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}, entropy weight \alpha, path length d, learning rates \eta_\pi, \eta_v, replay buffer capacity B

Output: Policy parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}, value parameters \boldsymbol{\phi}

Initialize \boldsymbol{\theta}_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}_0

Initialize replay buffer \mathcal{R} with capacity B

k \leftarrow 0

while training do

Sample trajectory \tau = (s_0, a_0, r_0, \ldots, s_T) from \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_k} and store in \mathcal{R}

Sample trajectory \tau' from \mathcal{R}

for each d-step segment in \tau' do

Compute residual: R_i \leftarrow v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_k}(s_i) - \gamma^d v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_k}(s_{i+d}) - \sum_{t=0}^{d-1} \gamma^t[r_{i+t} - \alpha \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_k}(a_{i+t}|s_{i+t})]

Update policy: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{k+1} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}_k + \eta_\pi \alpha R_i \sum_{t=0}^{d-1} \gamma^t \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \log \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_k}(a_{i+t}|s_{i+t})

Update value: \boldsymbol{\phi}_{k+1} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\phi}_k - \eta_v R_i\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_k}(s_i) - \gamma^d \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\phi}} v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_k}(s_{i+d})\right]

Remove oldest trajectories if |\mathcal{R}| > B

k \leftarrow k + 1

return \boldsymbol{\theta}_k, \boldsymbol{\phi}_k

The algorithm collects trajectories from the current policy and stores them in a replay buffer. At each iteration, it samples a trajectory (possibly old) and performs gradient descent on the path residual for all d-step segments. The replay buffer enables off-policy learning: trajectories from old policies, expert demonstrations, or exploratory behavior all provide valid training signals.

Single-step case (d=1): The path residual becomes R(s:s'; \boldsymbol{\theta}, \boldsymbol{\phi}) = v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s) - \gamma v_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(s') - r + \alpha\log\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(a|s). For unified parameterization where v_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(s) = q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(s,a) - \alpha\log\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(a|s) exactly, this becomes R = q_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(s,a) - r - \gamma v_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(s'), the soft Bellman residual. Minimizing \sum_i R_i^2 is equivalent to soft Q-learning, though SAC solves this via successive approximation (compute targets, fit) rather than direct residual minimization.

No entropy (\alpha \to 0): The residual becomes R = v(s_i) - \gamma^d v(s_{i+d}) - \sum_t \gamma^t r_t, the negative d-step advantage. But unlike A2C/A3C where v tracks the current policy’s value, PCL’s value converges to v^* because the residual couples policy and value through the optimality condition.

Multi-step with hard-max: No analog exists. The hard-max Bellman operator \max_a q(s,a) does not have an exact pointwise relationship like equation 

(15). Multi-step telescoping would accumulate errors from the max operator, making the constraint valid only in expectation under the optimal policy. The soft-max structure enables exact off-policy path consistency.

hierarchy.lvl3: PCL vs SAC: Residual Minimization vs Successive Approximation
PCL vs SAC: Residual Minimization vs Successive Approximation

records.content:
Both methods solve entropy-regularized MDPs but use fundamentally different solution strategies:

Aspect

SAC

PCL

Solution method

Successive approximation: compute targets y_i, fit q to targets

Residual minimization: minimize \sum_i R_i^2 directly

Update structure

Target computation + regression step

Single gradient step on squared residual

Target networks

Required (mark outer-iteration boundaries)

None (residual constraint, not target fitting)

Temporal horizon

Single-step TD: y = r + \gamma V(s')

Multi-step paths: accumulate over d steps

Off-policy handling

Replay buffer with single-sample bias

No importance sampling (works for any trajectory)

Dynamics requirement

General stochastic transitions

Deterministic transitions s' = f(s,a)

Architecture

Twin Q-networks + policy network

Single Q-network (unified parameterization)

PCL requires deterministic dynamics. It gains multi-step telescoping and off-policy learning without importance weights, but only for deterministic systems (robotic manipulation, many control tasks). SAC works for general stochastic MDPs.

PCL amortizes at a different level than DDPG/TD3/SAC. Those methods amortize the action maximization: learn a policy network that outputs \arg\max_a q(s,a) directly. PCL amortizes the solution of the Bellman equation itself. Instead of repeatedly applying the Bellman operator (which requires \int_{\mathcal{A}} \exp(q/\alpha) da at every iteration), PCL samples path segments and minimizes their residual. The computational cost of verifying optimality across all states and path lengths is distributed across training through sampled gradient updates.

How does online trajectory optimization compare with amortizing action
selection into a learned policy?

The 

MPPI development constructs
a distribution over finite control sequences by exponentially tilting a
reference distribution toward low-cost trajectories. A shifted Gaussian
proposal makes these trajectories easier to sample. Importance weights then
correct for the change of proposal, and their weighted perturbations update
the nominal sequence. The controller applies its first action and shifts the
remaining sequence to initialize the next optimization.

This calculation shares an exponential form with the policies derived from
entropy regularization, but the distributions and optimization problems
require separate definitions. SAC regularizes a state-conditional action
policy. The information-theoretic MPPI construction regularizes a distribution
over trajectories relative to a specified reference law


Williams et al., 2017. In the separate


continuous-time path-integral derivation,
the reference law is generated by an uncontrolled
diffusion, and the quadratic control cost must match its noise covariance.
Neither derivation identifies an arbitrary MPPI implementation with SAC or
PCL’s soft Bellman solution.

The Gaussian mean update fits the tilted trajectory distribution by minimizing
KL divergence from that distribution to the Gaussian family. It need not
minimize the original expected-cost objective over Gaussian policies. Its
sampled implementation also has discretization and finite-sampling error.
The 

aircraft example
also estimates each candidate’s expected cost across possible wind futures.
For the matched stochastic-control model, the


Brownian passage examples
compare sampled feedback with analytic and numerical reference solutions.

An actor network distributes computation across training examples and returns
an action through a forward pass. MPPI spends model evaluations at the current
state, with a warm start from the previous plan. A new cost function can be
used in its next optimization, although finite computation and a poor proposal
can still prevent a useful update.

The computational comparison separates where effort is spent from the errors
that remain:

Aspect

Learned actor

MPPI

Action selection

Policy-network evaluation

Repeated batches of model rollouts

Reuse across decisions

Trained parameters

Shifted nominal control sequence

Model use at deployment

Often unnecessary

A rollout model is required

Approximation sources

Policy and value approximation, estimation, optimization

Model error, discretization, restricted proposal, finite sampling

Changed objective

Usually requires further training

Enters subsequent rollout costs

For a deterministic rollout model, one MPPI iteration with K sequences and
H time steps uses KH transition evaluations. Estimating each sequence’s
expected cost across L disturbance scenarios increases that count to KHL.
These evaluations can be batched across sequences and scenarios, while each
trajectory still advances through time. The practical choice depends on model
cost, available parallel computation, and the accuracy required at each
decision.

Can first-order optimality eliminate the value function and yield a functional
equation directly in the policy?

The methods developed in this chapter all parameterize policies, but they remain rooted in the Bellman equation. NFQCA, DDPG, TD3, and SAC learn Q-functions through successive approximation, then derive policies by maximizing these Q-functions. PCL minimizes a path residual derived from the soft Bellman equation. The policy serves as an amortized optimizer for a value-based objective.

There is a different approach, developed in computational economics 

Judd, 1992

Rust, 1996

Judd, 1998, that also parameterizes policies but solves an entirely different functional equation. Consider a control problem with continuous states and actions, deterministic dynamics s' = f(s,a), and differentiable reward r(s,a). The optimal action \pi^*(s) satisfies the first-order condition:\frac{\partial r(s,a)}{\partial a}\Big|_{a=\pi^*(s)}
+
\gamma\, \frac{\partial v^*(s')}{\partial s'}\Big|_{s'=f(s,\pi^*(s))}\,
\frac{\partial f(s,a)}{\partial a}\Big|_{a=\pi^*(s)}
=
0.

This Euler equation expresses optimality through derivatives rather than through the max operator. For problems with special structure (the Euler class, where dynamics are affine in the controlled state), envelope theorems eliminate v^* entirely, yielding a closed functional equation \mathcal{E}(\pi)(s) = 0 in the policy alone.

With a parameterized policy \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(s), we can discretize via collocation or Galerkin projection:G(\boldsymbol{\theta}) := \begin{bmatrix}
\mathcal{E}(\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})(s_1) \\
\vdots \\
\mathcal{E}(\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})(s_N)
\end{bmatrix} = 0.

This is root-finding, not fixed-point iteration. Newton-type methods replace the successive approximation of fitted Q-iteration. The Euler operator is not a contraction, so convergence guarantees are problem-dependent.

What does this mean for reinforcement learning? The Euler approach shares the amortization idea: learn a policy network that directly outputs actions. But the training objective comes from first-order optimality conditions rather than from Bellman residuals or Q-function maximization. This raises questions worth considering. Could Euler-style objectives provide useful training signals for actor-critic methods? When dynamics are known or learned, could first-order conditions offer advantages over value-based objectives? The connection between these traditions remains underexplored.

SAC converts the soft value integral into an expectation under a learned
stochastic policy. PCL instead minimizes a multi-step consistency residual, and
MPPI updates a finite-horizon trajectory distribution at each decision. The Euler approach supplies a further alternative: solve a
first-order policy equation rather than a Bellman fixed point.

MPPI avoids a persistent actor approximation by performing online sampling
and optimization. Its exponential weights resemble those of entropy-regularized
policies, but its reference distribution, horizon, and sampling assumptions
define a different optimization problem. Finite computation and model error
remain in either approach.

All of these objectives retain an optimality equation derived from a value or
path-consistency relation. Can expected return be differentiated directly
without first treating a Bellman equation as the training objective? 

Policy
gradients and actor-critic methods use the trajectory
score and bring value functions back as variance-reducing critics.

Compute trade-off

Contrast MPPI and an actor network in terms of online computation and approximation error.

Solution to 

Exercise 1

MPPI spends many model rollouts at every decision and avoids a persistent
actor approximation, but retains model, discretization, proposal, and
finite-sampling errors. An actor is cheap online but can introduce error
because its parameters only approximate the desired decision rule. A
warm-started MPPI sequence and a trained actor reuse computation in different
ways.

records.content:
Finite-horizon dynamic programming chooses an action from each state and time,
then follows one deterministic successor. How should the recursion change when
an action induces a distribution of successors and the decision rule itself may
be randomized or depend on history? Stochastic dynamic programming answers by
averaging continuation values under a transition kernel.

hierarchy.lvl1: Stochastic Dynamic Programming and Markov Decision Processes
Stochastic Dynamic Programming and Markov Decision Processes

records.content:
Which combinations of state, history, and randomization may a decision rule use
when selecting an action?

Before diving into stochastic systems, we need to establish terminology for the different types of strategies a decision maker might employ. In the deterministic setting, we implicitly used feedback controllers of the form u(\mathbf{x}, t). In the stochastic setting, we must be more precise about what information policies can use and how they select actions.

A decision rule is a prescription for action selection in each state at a specified decision epoch. These rules can vary in their complexity based on two main criteria:

Dependence on history: Markovian or History-dependent

Action selection method: Deterministic or Randomized

Markovian decision rules depend only on the current state, while history-dependent rules consider the entire sequence of past states and actions. Formally, a history h_t at time t is:h_t = (s_1, a_1, \ldots, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, s_t)

The set of all possible histories at time t, denoted H_t, grows exponentially with t:

H_1 = \mathcal{S} (just the initial state)

H_2 = \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{S}

H_t = \mathcal{S} \times (\mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{S})^{t-1}

Deterministic rules select an action with certainty, while randomized rules specify a probability distribution over the action space.

These classifications lead to four types of decision rules:

Markovian Deterministic (MD): \pi_t: \mathcal{S} \rightarrow \mathcal{A}_s

Markovian Randomized (MR): \pi_t: \mathcal{S} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}_s)

History-dependent Deterministic (HD): \pi_t: H_t \rightarrow \mathcal{A}_s

History-dependent Randomized (HR): \pi_t: H_t \rightarrow \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}_s)

where \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}_s) denotes the set of probability distributions over \mathcal{A}_s.

A policy \boldsymbol{\pi} is a sequence of decision rules, one for each decision epoch:\boldsymbol{\pi} = (\pi_1, \pi_2, ..., \pi_{N-1})

The set of all policies of class K (where K \in \{HR, HD, MR, MD\}) is denoted as \Pi^K. These policy classes form a hierarchy:\Pi^{MD} \subset \Pi^{MR} \subset \Pi^{HR}, \quad \Pi^{MD} \subset \Pi^{HD} \subset \Pi^{HR}

The largest set \Pi^{HR} contains all possible policies. We ask: under what conditions can we restrict attention to the much simpler set \Pi^{MD} without loss of optimality?

Notation: rules vs. policies

Decision rule (kernel). A map from information to action distributions:

Markov, deterministic:  \pi_t:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{A}_s

Markov, randomized:     \pi_t(\cdot\mid s)\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}_s)

History-dependent:       \pi_t(\cdot\mid h_t)\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}_{s_t})

Policy (sequence). \boldsymbol{\pi}=(\pi_1,\pi_2,\ldots).

Stationary policy. \boldsymbol{\pi}=\mathrm{const}(\pi) with \pi_t\equiv\pi \ \forall t.By convention, we identify \pi with its stationary policy \mathrm{const}(\pi) when no confusion arises.

hierarchy.lvl1: Stochastic Dynamic Programming and Markov Decision Processes
Stochastic Dynamic Programming and Markov Decision Processes

records.content:
How does a transition kernel replace the single deterministic successor in the
finite-horizon model?

In the stochastic setting, our system evolution takes the form:\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = \mathbf{f}_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t, \mathbf{w}_t)

Here, \mathbf{w}_t represents a random disturbance or noise term at time t due to the inherent uncertainty in the system’s behavior. The stage cost function may also incorporate stochastic influences:c_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t, \mathbf{w}_t)

In this context, our objective shifts from minimizing a deterministic cost to minimizing the expected total cost:\mathbb{E}\left[c_\mathrm{T}(\mathbf{x}_T) + \sum_{t=1}^{T-1} c_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t, \mathbf{w}_t)\right]

where the expectation is taken over the distributions of the random variables \mathbf{w}_t. The principle of optimality still holds in the stochastic case, but Bellman’s optimality equation now involves an expectation:J_k^\star(\mathbf{x}_k) = \min_{\mathbf{u}_k} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}_k}\left[c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_k) + J_{k+1}^\star(\mathbf{f}_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_k))\right]

In practice, this expectation is often computed by discretizing the distribution of \mathbf{w}_k when the set of possible disturbances is very large or even continuous. Let’s say we approximate the distribution with K discrete values \mathbf{w}_k^i, each occurring with probability p_k^i. Then our Bellman equation becomes:J_k^\star(\mathbf{x}_k) = \min_{\mathbf{u}_k} \sum_{i=1}^K p_k^i \left(c_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_k^i) + J_{k+1}^\star(\mathbf{f}_k(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_k^i))\right)

hierarchy.lvl1: Stochastic Dynamic Programming and Markov Decision Processes
hierarchy.lvl2: Optimality Equations in the Stochastic Setting

records.content:
How is the deterministic continuation value replaced by an expectation over
all possible next states?

When dealing with stochastic systems, a central question arises: what information should our control policy use? In the most general case, a policy might use the entire history of observations and actions. However, as we’ll see, the Markovian structure of our problems allows for dramatic simplifications.

Let h_t = (s_1, a_1, s_2, a_2, \ldots, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, s_t) denote the complete history up to time t. In the stochastic setting, the history-based optimality equations become:u_t(h_t) = \sup_{a\in A_{s_t}}\left\{ r_t(s_t,a) + \sum_{j\in S} p_t(j\mid s_t,a)\, u_{t+1}(h_t,a,j) \right\},\quad u_N(h_N)=r_N(s_N)

where we now explicitly use the transition probabilities p_t(j|s_t,a) rather than a deterministic dynamics function.

Principle of optimality for stochastic systems

Let u_t^* be the optimal expected return from epoch t onward. Then:

a. u_t^* satisfies the optimality equations:u_t^*(h_t) = \sup_{a \in A_{s_t}} \left\{ r_t(s_t, a) + \sum_{j \in S} p_t(j|s_t, a) u_{t+1}^*(h_t, a, j) \right\}

with boundary condition u_N^*(h_N) = r_N(s_N).

b. Any policy \pi^* that selects actions attaining the supremum (or maximum) in the above equation at each history is optimal.

Intuition: This formalizes Bellman’s principle of optimality: “An optimal policy has the property that whatever the initial state and initial decision are, the remaining decisions must constitute an optimal policy with regard to the state resulting from the first decision.” The recursive structure means that optimal local decisions (choosing the best action at each step) lead to global optimality, even with uncertainty captured by the transition probabilities.

A simplification occurs when we examine these history-based equations more closely. The Markov property of our system dynamics and rewards means that the optimal return actually depends on the history only through the current state:

State sufficiency for stochastic MDPs

In finite-horizon stochastic MDPs with Markovian dynamics and rewards, the optimal return u_t^*(h_t) depends on the history only through the current state s_t. Thus we can write u_t^*(h_t) = v_t^*(s_t) for some function v_t^* that depends only on state and time.

Following 

Puterman (1994) Theorem 4.4.2. We proceed by backward induction.

Base case: At the terminal time N, we have u_N^*(h_N) = r_N(s_N) by the boundary condition. Since the terminal reward depends only on the final state s_N and not on how we arrived there, u_N^*(h_N) = u_N^*(s_N).

Inductive step: Assume u_{t+1}^*(h_{t+1}) depends on h_{t+1} only through s_{t+1} for all t+1, \ldots, N. Then from the optimality equation:u_t^*(h_t) = \sup_{a \in A_{s_t}} \left\{ r_t(s_t, a) + \sum_{j \in S} p_t(j|s_t, a) u_{t+1}^*(h_t, a, j) \right\}

By the induction hypothesis, u_{t+1}^*(h_t, a, j) depends only on the next state j, so:u_t^*(h_t) = \sup_{a \in A_{s_t}} \left\{ r_t(s_t, a) + \sum_{j \in S} p_t(j|s_t, a) u_{t+1}^*(j) \right\}

Since the expression in brackets depends on h_t only through the current state s_t (the rewards and transition probabilities are Markovian), we conclude that u_t^*(h_t) = u_t^*(s_t).

Intuition: The Markov property means that the current state contains all information needed to predict future evolution. The past provides no additional value for decision-making. This result allows us to work with value functions v_t^*(s) indexed only by state and time, dramatically simplifying both theory and computation.

This state-sufficiency result, combined with the fact that randomization never helps when maximizing expected returns, leads to a dramatic simplification of the policy space:

Policy reduction for stochastic MDPs

For finite-horizon stochastic MDPs with finite state and action sets:\sup_{\pi \in \Pi^{\mathrm{HR}}} v_\pi(s,t) = \max_{\pi \in \Pi^{\mathrm{MD}}} v_\pi(s,t)

That is, there exists an optimal policy that is both deterministic and Markovian.

Sketch following 

Puterman (1994) Lemma 4.3.1 and Theorem 4.4.2. First, Lemma 4.3.1 shows that for any function w and any distribution q over actions, \sup_a w(a) \ge \sum_a q(a) w(a). Thus randomization cannot improve the expected value over choosing a single maximizing action. Second, by state sufficiency (Proposition 

Proposition 1 and 

Puterman (1994) Thm. 4.4.2(a)), the optimal return depends on the history only through (s_t,t). Therefore, selecting at each (s_t,t) an action that attains the maximum yields a deterministic Markov decision rule which is optimal whenever the maximum is attained. If only a supremum exists, \varepsilon-optimal selectors exist by choosing actions within \varepsilon of the supremum (see 

Puterman (1994) Thm. 4.3.4).

Intuition: Even in stochastic systems, randomization in the policy doesn’t help when maximizing expected returns: you should always choose the action with the highest expected value. Combined with state sufficiency, this means simple state-to-action mappings are optimal.

These results justify focusing on deterministic Markov policies and lead to the backward recursion algorithm for stochastic systems:

Backward Recursion for Stochastic Dynamic Programming

Input: Terminal cost function c_\mathrm{T}(\cdot), stage cost functions c_t(\cdot, \cdot, \cdot), system dynamics \mathbf{f}_t(\cdot, \cdot, \cdot), time horizon \mathrm{T}, disturbance distributions

Output: Optimal value functions J_t^\star(\cdot) and optimal control policies \pi_t^\star(\cdot) for t = 1, \ldots, T

Initialize J_T^\star(\mathbf{x}) = c_\mathrm{T}(\mathbf{x}) for all \mathbf{x} in the state space

For t = T-1, T-2, \ldots, 1:

For each state \mathbf{x} in the state space:

Compute J_t^\star(\mathbf{x}) = \min_{\mathbf{u}} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}_t}\left[c_t(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w}_t) + J_{t+1}^\star(\mathbf{f}_t(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w}_t))\right]

Compute \pi_t^\star(\mathbf{x}) = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u}} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}_t}\left[c_t(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w}_t) + J_{t+1}^\star(\mathbf{f}_t(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w}_t))\right]

End For

End For

Return J_t^\star(\cdot), \pi_t^\star(\cdot) for t = 1, \ldots, T

While SDP provides us with a framework for handling uncertainty, it makes the curse of dimensionality even more difficult to handle in practice. Both the state space and the disturbance space must be discretized. This can lead to a combinatorial explosion in the number of scenarios to be evaluated at each stage.

However, just as we tackled the challenges of continuous state spaces with discretization and interpolation, we can devise efficient methods to handle the additional complexity of evaluating expectations. This problem essentially becomes one of numerical integration. When the set of disturbances is continuous (as is often the case with continuous state spaces), we enter a domain where numerical quadrature methods could be applied. But these methods tend to scale poorly as the number of dimensions grows. This is where more efficient techniques, often rooted in Monte Carlo methods, come into play. Two ingredients tackle the curse of dimensionality:

Function approximation (through discretization, interpolation, neural networks, etc.)

Monte Carlo integration (simulation)

These two elements essentially distill the key ingredients of machine learning, which is the direction we’ll be exploring in this course.

records.content:
How does the reservoir policy change when each week’s release must be chosen
before that week’s inflow is known?

The previous chapter operated a 

seasonal hydroelectric
reservoir
against an inflow forecast and treated the forecast as exact. Its policy
refills the reservoir after the spring freshet, holds it at capacity from
September to late November, and releases exactly the forecast inflow in each of
those weeks. That plan is only as good as the forecast: in a week wetter than
forecast, the reservoir is already full and the extra water goes over the
spillway.
Stochastic dynamic programming has long been used to compute reservoir
operating policies that account for this risk 

Stedinger et al., 1984. We make
the inflow random and keep every other element of the deterministic model: 52
weekly stages, the storage and release limits, the head h(x), the price p_t
and the terminal value.

Let \bar w_t denote the forecast of the previous chapter. The inflow in week
t isw_t = \xi_t\,\bar w_t,
\qquad
\xi_t = \begin{cases}
0.6 & \text{with probability } 1/4, \\
1.0 & \text{with probability } 1/2, \\
1.4 & \text{with probability } 1/4,
\end{cases}

where the factors \xi_0, \ldots, \xi_{51} are independent. The mean inflow
equals the forecast, and one week in four is 40% wetter than forecast. The
inflow plays the role of the disturbance \mathbf{w}_t in the stochastic
dynamics above. Because the factors are independent, past inflows carry no
information about the next one, and storage alone remains a sufficient state,
as in 

Proposition 1.

The operator sets the release u_t at the start of the week, before the inflow
arrives. In a dry week the requested release can exceed the water available
above dead storage. The turbines then stop when the level reaches dead storage,
so the volume actually released is\tilde u_t = \min\{u_t,\ x_t + w_t - x_{\min}\}.

Storage evolves as x_{t+1} = \min\{x_t + w_t - \tilde u_t,\ \bar x\}, and the
week earns p_t\,\kappa\,h(x_t)\,\tilde u_t. Both the successor and the revenue
now depend on the disturbance, as \mathbf{f}_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t,
\mathbf{w}_t) and c_t(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t, \mathbf{w}_t) do in the
general formulation. Writing \xi^k for the three factors and q_k for their
probabilities, Bellman’s equation readsJ_t^\star(x) = \max_{u_{\min} \le u \le u_{\max}}
\sum_{k=1}^{3} q_k \Big[\, p_t\,\kappa\,h(x)\,\tilde u^k
+ J_{t+1}^\star\big(\min\{x + \xi^k \bar w_t - \tilde u^k,\ \bar x\}\big) \Big],
\qquad
\tilde u^k = \min\{u,\ x + \xi^k \bar w_t - x_{\min}\},

with the terminal value J_T^\star(x) = p_T\,\kappa\,h(x)\,(x - x_{\min}) as
before. The expectation sits inside the maximum because a single release has to
serve all three inflows.

The code below changes the deterministic solver in two places. The bracket is
averaged over the three inflows before the maximum over releases is taken. And
the successors x + 0.6\,\bar w_t - u and x + 1.4\,\bar w_t - u are in
general no longer multiples of the 10 hm³ grid step, so J_{t+1}^\star is
evaluated between grid points by linear interpolation, as in 

the interpolation
section
of the previous chapter. Given the single factor 1 with probability 1, the same
function solves the deterministic problem and returns its 74.1 M$ from
1100 hm³; with a known inflow, stopping a release at dead storage is the same
as forbidding it. This is the certainty-equivalent problem: the random inflow
is replaced by its mean, and the resulting policy is applied as if the forecast
were exact. The last lines operate both policies for 2000 simulated years, on
the same inflow sequences.

import numpy as np

# The deterministic model of the previous chapter.
T = 52
weeks = np.arange(T)
w_bar = 60 + 340 * np.exp(-((weeks - 19) / 3.5) ** 2) + 60 * np.exp(-((weeks - 43) / 4) ** 2)
w_bar = 10 * np.round(w_bar / 10)                    # inflow forecast (hm³/week)
p = 60 + 30 * np.cos(2 * np.pi * (weeks - 5) / 52)   # price ($/MWh)
x_min, x_max = 200, 2000
u_min, u_max = 30, 250
kappa, p_T = 2.45, 50

def head(x):
    return 40 + 40 * np.sqrt(x / x_max)

def terminal_value(x):
    return p_T * kappa * head(x) * (x - x_min)

dx = 10
X = np.arange(x_min, x_max + dx, dx)
U = np.arange(u_min, u_max + dx, dx)

# Random inflow w_t = xi_t * w_bar_t, with xi_t drawn independently each week.
factors = np.array([0.6, 1.0, 1.4])
probs = np.array([0.25, 0.5, 0.25])

def solve(factors, probs):
    J = np.zeros((T + 1, len(X)))
    policy = np.zeros((T, len(X)))
    J[T] = terminal_value(X)
    x, u = X[:, None], U[None, :]                     # all (storage, release) pairs
    for t in reversed(range(T)):
        value = np.zeros((len(X), len(U)))
        for factor, prob in zip(factors, probs):      # expectation over the inflow...
            inflow = factor * w_bar[t]
            release = np.minimum(u, x + inflow - x_min)       # turbines stop at dead storage
            x_next = np.minimum(x + inflow - release, x_max)  # water above capacity spills
            value += prob * (p[t] * kappa * head(x) * release
                             + np.interp(x_next, X, J[t + 1]))
        J[t] = value.max(axis=1)                      # ...inside the maximum over releases
        policy[t] = U[value.argmax(axis=1)]
    return J, policy

def simulate(policy, years, x0):
    """Operate the reservoir for many years at once: one row of factors per year."""
    x = np.full(len(years), float(x0))
    storage, revenue, spill = [x], 0.0, 0.0
    for t in range(T):
        inflow = years[:, t] * w_bar[t]
        requested = policy[t, np.round((x - x_min) / dx).astype(int)]
        release = np.minimum(requested, x + inflow - x_min)
        revenue = revenue + p[t] * kappa * head(x) * release
        spill = spill + np.maximum(x + inflow - release - x_max, 0)
        x = np.minimum(x + inflow - release, x_max)
        storage.append(x)
    return np.array(storage), revenue + terminal_value(x), spill

J_ce, policy_ce = solve([1.0], [1.0])         # certainty equivalent: inflow = forecast
J_sto, policy_sto = solve(factors, probs)     # stochastic dynamic programming

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
years = rng.choice(factors, size=(2000, T), p=probs)   # the same inflows for both policies
i0 = np.searchsorted(X, 1100)
results = {}
for name, J, policy in (("certainty equivalent", J_ce, policy_ce),
                        ("stochastic", J_sto, policy_sto)):
    storage, revenue, spill = simulate(policy, years, x0=1100)
    results[name] = (storage, revenue, spill)
    print(f"{name:<21} predicted {J[0, i0] / 1e6:5.2f} M$   simulated {revenue.mean() / 1e6:5.2f} M$"
          f"   spill {spill.mean():3.0f} hm³/year")



The two backward passes predict different things. The certainty-equivalent
pass predicts 74.06 M$, the revenue its policy would earn if every week’s
inflow matched the forecast, which never happens. On the simulated inflows the
same policy earns 73.05 M$ on average, about 1 M$ less, and spills water in
96% of the years. At a water value of about 11 k$ per hm³, the 85 hm³ it
spills each year account for most of the shortfall. The stochastic pass predicts
73.75 M$, and the simulation agrees within its standard error of 0.06 M$.
This agreement is expected: J_0^\star(1100) is the expected revenue of the
stochastic policy under the inflow model, and the average over simulated years
estimates the same expectation.

On the same inflows, the stochastic policy earns 0.68 M$ more per year than
the certainty-equivalent policy. Stochastic programming calls this difference
the value of the stochastic solution 

Birge & Louveaux, 2011. It is small next to
the total revenue, but most of that revenue comes from water that any rule would
sell. In the deterministic model, running the river without storing anything
earned 66.8 M$, and managing the storage added 7.3 M$. The loss from
ignoring the inflow uncertainty is about a tenth of that amount.

from pathlib import Path
import sys

code_directory = Path.cwd() / "code"
if str(code_directory) not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(code_directory))

from hydro_reservoir_stochastic import (
    make_stochastic_comparison_figure,
    make_stochastic_policy_figure,
)

water_value_ce = np.gradient(J_ce, dx, axis=1)    # dJ_t/dx on the grid, $ per hm³
water_value_sto = np.gradient(J_sto, dx, axis=1)
storage_ce, revenue_ce, spill_ce = results["certainty equivalent"]
storage_sto, revenue_sto, spill_sto = results["stochastic"]



make_stochastic_comparison_figure(storage_ce, storage_sto, revenue_ce,
                                  revenue_sto, x_max, first_week=30)

Figure 1:Both policies operated on the same 2000 simulated years from x_0 = 1100 hm³. Left, storage from August to December: median (solid) and 5th and 95th percentiles (dashed). The certainty-equivalent policy (orange) holds the reservoir at capacity and spills whenever a week is wetter than forecast; the stochastic policy (blue) holds it about 50 hm³ below. Right, the revenue of the stochastic policy minus that of the certainty-equivalent policy in each simulated year.



Because both policies face the same inflows, the gain can be measured year by
year, as in the right panel of 

Figure 1. Its
mean has a standard error of 0.01 M$, against 0.06 M$ for either mean revenue:
a wet or dry year raises or lowers the revenue of both policies alike, and this
common variation cancels in the difference. Evaluating competing policies on the
same random inputs is a variance-reduction technique known as common random
numbers. The stochastic policy earns more in 87% of the years. The other years
have dry autumns, in which the certainty-equivalent policy spills little and
the margin kept by the stochastic policy turns out to be unnecessary.

The gain comes almost entirely from the autumn, shown in the left panel. The
certainty-equivalent policy refills the reservoir to capacity in September and
holds it there, releasing the forecast inflow each week, so every week wetter
than forecast spills. The stochastic policy stops about 50 hm³ below capacity.
In late October the forecast inflow is 120 hm³ per week, and the wettest week
brings 0.4 \times 120 = 48 hm³ more than forecast. The policy keeps exactly
enough room to absorb it.

The size of this margin follows from the comparison that explained the
deterministic policy in the previous chapter: the turbines run when releasing
one more hm³, worth p_t\,\kappa\,h(x), earns more than keeping it, worth the
water value \partial J_{t+1}^\star/\partial x at the next storage. With random
inflow, the second term becomes an average over the three successors
x_{t+1}^k. For an inflow that fills the reservoir, an hm³ kept this week
spills and adds nothing next week, so those successors drop out of the
average. As long as the release is not cut short at dead storage, the
slope \partial Q_t/\partial u from the previous chapter becomesp_t\,\kappa\,h(x) \;-\; \sum_{k:\ x_{t+1}^k < \bar x} q_k\,
\frac{\partial J_{t+1}^\star}{\partial x}\big(x_{t+1}^k\big).

The rule becomes: run the turbines when the price exceeds the expected value of
the water kept, counting water that would spill as worth nothing. In late
October, near capacity, one hm³ earns about 10.3 k$ if released and has a
water value of about 11.2 k$ if kept. Below the margin, the kept hm³ never
spills, so keeping it is worth more. Above the margin, it spills in the wettest
week, with probability 1/4, and its expected value falls to
0.75 \times 11.2 = 8.4 k$, less than the 10.3 k$ from releasing it. The
policy therefore holds the storage level from which the wettest week just fills
the reservoir. In the deterministic model the inflow is known, so the policy can
fill the reservoir to capacity without spilling.

make_stochastic_policy_figure(w_bar, factors, X, policy_sto, storage_sto[:, :40],
                              14, water_value_ce[14], water_value_sto[14])

Figure 2:Solution of the stochastic problem. Left, the optimal release u_t^\star(x) below the inflow forecast (dark marks) and the range of the random inflow (light bars). White curves are 40 simulated years of operation from 1100 hm³. Right, the water value at the start of the freshet. With the inflow known (orange), it drops abruptly at the storage level from which the freshet fills the reservoir; with random inflow (blue), the drop is spread from about 1100 hm³ to capacity.



The same averaging changes the water value. The right panel of


Figure 2 shows it in week 14, early April, when the
freshet begins. In the certainty-equivalent model it drops abruptly at
1770 hm³: from that level on, the forecast freshet fills the reservoir, and any
additional hm³ is certain to spill. In the stochastic model the drop is spread
from about 1100 hm³ to capacity. An additional hm³ spills only if the freshet
is wet enough, and the probability of such a freshet rises gradually with
storage. More generally, each J_t^\star averages J_{t+1}^\star over three
successors, and this averaging smooths the kinks of the deterministic value
function at every step of the recursion.

The white curves in the left panel are 40 simulated years. In the deterministic
model a single path described the operation of the policy; here each year
follows its own. The paths spread out in January and February, while the policy
releases the minimum and storage follows the random inflow. They come back
together at the end of the winter drawdown, when every year reaches low storage
before the freshet, spread again during the freshet, whose volume differs from
year to year, and converge in autumn toward the level below capacity where the
policy holds them. The outcome of a policy under uncertainty is a distribution,
and estimating it takes many simulated trajectories. The same holds for the
reinforcement learning methods of later chapters: one good trajectory does not
show that a policy is good.

Question. If the operator could see each week’s inflow before choosing
the release, would the expected revenue from 1100 hm³ be above or below
73.75 M$? Which lines of solve would change?

Answer

Above, or at least equal. Seeing the inflow first allows a different release
for each of the three inflows, and choosing the same release for all three
remains possible, so the maximum cannot decrease. In Bellman’s equation the
maximum moves inside the expectation,
J_t^\star(x) = \sum_k q_k \max_u [\,\cdots]. In solve, each term is
maximized over releases before it is added, value += prob * (...).max(axis=1)
with value a vector over storage levels, and J[t] = value. The policy then
depends on the inflow as well as on the storage. The expected revenue becomes
74.01 M$, so knowing each week’s inflow in advance is worth 0.26 M$ per year.

Question. In this model the inflow factor is drawn independently each
week, so a wet April says nothing about May. Real freshets tend to be wet or
dry for weeks at a time, because they melt from a single snowpack. What would
the state have to contain for the backward recursion to remain valid, and
what would that cost?

Answer

With correlated inflows, storage is no longer a sufficient state: the
distribution of next week’s inflow depends on past inflows, and the argument of


Proposition 1 no longer applies to storage alone. If the factor
follows a Markov chain, adding last week’s factor to the state restores it. The
state becomes (x_t, \xi_{t-1}), with 181 \times 3 = 543 grid points instead
of 181, and the expectation uses the transition probabilities out of
\xi_{t-1}. A measured snowpack would be a continuous second state variable
with its own grid. Each such variable multiplies the size of the grid, which is
the curse of dimensionality again. A common alternative is to re-solve a
deterministic problem every week with an updated forecast, as in


receding-horizon control.
